title: How the recruiting landscape has changed through the eyes of Penn State coaches
author: Andrew Deal | The Daily Collegian
description:
Over the past five years, the recruiting landscape has changed drastically with the adoption of new rules and additional aspects of recruiting for coaches to adapt to in collegiate athletics.

Players have always had the option to transfer schools, but in the past, they had to sit out one year before playing for their new team. In 2018, the NCAA launched the official transfer portal so athletes could formally enter their name to switch schools.

Since then, the transfer portal has exploded. The NCAA eliminated the rule forcing players to sit out a year in 2021, but only gave them one chance to transfer. If an athlete transferred twice, they’d have to sit out a year at their second new destination.

“Recruiting is completely different. It's just a different world now with NIL, transfer portal,” associate head coach Terry Smith said.

2024 is when the transfer portal became what it is now, as the NCAA dropped the requirement for a player to sit out if they transfer twice. The transfer portal has continued to expand year by year.

Recruiting players became even more difficult with the threat of players transferring after a season — the 2025 transfer portal had over 3,000 football players seeking new teams 2026. Essentially, each coaching staff has to re-recruit their entire roster each offseason.

While it’s difficult for coaching staffs, the transfer portal provides the opportunity for players to get a fresh start. Penn State wide receiver Chase Sowell has now transferred four times and said Tuesday the portal has been a “blessing.”

“Obviously you get a lot of stories where it obviously doesn't go well,” Sowell said. “I'm just blessed that you know that I got the opportunity that I had because 2023 May, sitting in my dorm, I thought football was over for me, and I thought that's just what it was, and I was gonna accept it, but the transfer portal gave me another opportunity and kind of let me elevate myself.”

NIL and revenue sharing is just another aspect of the changes in recruiting. Players can now directly earn money, making college athletics mirror professional sports.

For example, 2027 Tennessee running back commit David Gabriel Georges will reportedly sign a 3-year deal worth around $2 million per year with the Volunteers following his senior year of high school. Additionally, he’s guaranteed to wear No. 0 and will have family travel benefits for all games, according to On3’s Hayes Fawcett.

Prior to 2021, that was unheard of in college football. Now, it’s becoming more common, with current Michigan quarterback Bryce Underwood expected to make north of $10 million during his time with the Wolverines. Those details all came together to help persuade him to flip his commitment from LSU.

“You have to be able to pay these guys a certain amount of money just to have a conversation with them. It's just different,” Terry Smith said.

With money now involved, so are agents who represent college athletes to help them with decision making and making the most money possible for their representatives.

Agents make college football even more like the NFL, and they’re still very new to collegiate athletics. What used to involve just talking to players, their families and high school coaches now pieces in agents, resulting in an added need for even more communication.

“Agents is probably the first thing that comes to my mind,” safeties coach Deon Broomfield said. “It kind of still feels weird, like, ‘Hey, you gotta talk to my agents.’ That's foreign.”

Another ripple in recruiting occurred in the most recent offseason. Collegiate athletics adopted a five-for-five rule, meaning every college athlete has five years of eligibility from when they first enroll in college or from their 19th birthday, whichever comes first.

That can completely change teams, but for Penn State, only six players could be affected by it after this season. From then on, roster construction will be even more complicated with this factor now in consideration.

“The five-for-five deal is interesting,” Broomfield said. “We'll see how that kind of affects us moving forward, just numbers and that. But recruiting is getting to know people and obviously making sure they're the right fit. And I think that part of it has not changed.”

It also throws away the redshirt concept, which many teams had to gameplan each week. Now, coaches don’t have to worry about which players appear in which weeks to maintain their redshirt status, which according to Terry “is really good” for Penn State.

In some ways, the recruiting process at Penn State has stayed the same under Matt Campbell and the new coaching staff. There’s still “blue collar” and “tradition” involved in the recruiting process when looking for “high character young men,” according to Huggins.

D’Anton Lynn, who joined the Nittany Lions as their defensive coordinator this offseason, played for Penn State from 2008 to 2011. His recruiting process back then was unlike anything that’d happen in this day and age, as no money was involved.

“I felt like you know when you're getting recruited, going through the recruiting process, what stuck out to that was different about Penn State was they had a standard off the field that was just as high as on the field, and it was very apparent,” Lynn said.

But the standard that came with committing to a school like Penn State in 2008 has not changed.

The Nittany Lions, and many of the other top programs in the country, can pitch playing for Penn State by telling a player they have the opportunity to play for a team that has so much history and tradition involved within the program.

Huggins is still looking for players “who love football” and “want to sit in the first two rows of class,” he said, which have remained the same within the program no matter who the head coach was.

“Makes it really easy, because I outline in every younger man's recruiting process what it is that we're looking for,” Huggins said. “If that doesn't align with what we're looking for, there is a means to an end.”

If Penn State gets players like that out of high school, edge rushers coach Christian Smith said he knows they’re not going to “come to school just because of how much NIL they're getting.”

However, a difficult aspect of pitching Penn State is the location, which benefits other major programs for top recruits. The Nittany Lions are “in the middle of nowhere” and surrounded by mountains and no major cities. Huggins said he makes sure he’s as transparent as possible when it comes to that, making clear the potential geographical disadvantage of Penn State.

“There's one way in and there's one way out,” Huggins said. “ I don't hide that in recruiting. Yes, ‘We have an unbelievable fan base,’ I said, ‘but at the same time, too, if you ain't handling your business, can you handle that as well?’ I think I address the elephants in the room right on.”

The Nittany Lions have uniformity throughout the entire coaching staff. The process starts from Campbell and works its way down, but it all stems back to players being in Happy Valley for the right reasons and working together as one team to build the best culture for the program.

“Coach Campbell's philosophy is, ‘We're gonna get the right type of human being that fits our culture, our kind of guys,’” Broomfield said. “I think for us, we still approach it from that manner, and then we kind of gotta weed through everything else.”

title: Satire | The best ways to warm up during Penn State’s cold months
author: Carolena Bongi | The Daily Collegian
description:
Unfortunately, the warm weather at Penn State can't last forever. Soon, the leaves will fall alongside your spirits, and students will once again remember that choosing a school in the middle of Pennsylvania comes with consequences.

While winter technically doesn't begin until December, anyone who has walked across campus knows Penn State follows its own calendar.

Here are some ways to stay warm as the weather gets colder.

Get really invested in Penn State football

If you're cold, you just probably aren't angry enough. Thankfully, Penn State football exists.

With Matt Campbell beginning a new era in Happy Valley, there’ll be plenty of opportunities to get your blood pressure high enough that you won't even remember the temperature outside.

I recommend spending four quarters screaming in Beaver Stadium, and by halftime you should have generated enough body heat to warm up. If you truly bleed blue and white, the hypothermia just adds to your gameday outfit.

And if that doesn't work, just start thinking about how Penn State is playing Michigan away instead of home.

Let downtown food save you

After spending four hours standing in Beaver Stadium, your hands will most likely have reached the point where you can no longer feel your fingers.

But once the game ends, head downtown and find somewhere warm to eat.

A hot slice of pizza from Benny Leone's or some chicken tenders and fries from Raising Cane’s will give you a reason to get out of the cold and recover before making the walk home. You can even test your luck at Champs Downtown.

Of course, that's only if you can manage to get to the restaurants before the rest of the stadium or have enough willpower to wait in line for another hour.

Wait in the HUB-Robeson Center Starbucks line

If you're looking for somewhere warm to spend an afternoon, get in the Starbucks line in the HUB. You'll definitely be able to find it because there's always a clump of people standing around, waiting eagerly for their orders.

Wait in the line and make yourself comfortable, because you’re going to be here for a long time.

Make sure you bring your laptop and some school work because by the time you get your coffee, it might be spring anyway.

Stand over the steam coming out of the sidewalk

We've all felt those random clouds of steam coming out of the sidewalks around campus. Who knows what kind of toxic fumes are actually leaking out of those vents?

Usually, you walk right past them, and might even be scared about what you're possibly breathing in, but this winter, it's time to take advantage.

Find one, stand directly over it and enjoy the warmth.

Wear all of your Penn State clothes at once

If you've been at Penn State for more than a semester, chances are half of your closet has a Penn State logo on it. Winter is finally your chance to put all of it to use.

Start with a Penn State T-shirt, then a crewneck and finish it off with the Penn State jacket. You can even add in those striped overalls that have been pushed to the back of your closet for some extra flair. For the cherry on top, head to McLanahan’s for a Penn State scarf and hat.

Walk up Shortlidge Road

If the cold is really getting to you, skip the bus and take a walk up Shortlidge Road.

Walking up that hill with your backpack will guarantee you’ll be sweating before you even make it halfway up. You might even find yourself wishing it was a little colder by the time you reach the top.

Become the Nittany Lion Mascot

If your winter coat isn't cutting it anymore, there’s one obvious solution: become the Nittany Lion.

There's a reason you never see him shivering on the sidelines at games. That suit has to be warmer than anything hanging in your closet.

Staying warm at Penn State might take a little creativity, but luckily we have plenty of options to help you get through.

title: Staff predictions | Will Penn State wrap up nonconference play with a win over Buffalo?
author: The Daily Collegian football staff
description:
Penn State’s final nonconference matchup of 2026 is on the horizon.

The Nittany Lions are set to take on Buffalo this Saturday at noon in Beaver Stadium for the THON game as they look to improve to 3-0.

Can Penn State get the job done after a less-than-ideal showing against Temple?

Andrew Deal: Penn State 38, Buffalo 7

Buffalo ranks right below Marshall in ESPN’s FPI rankings, so the teams are relatively similar to each other. If that’s the case, a result similar to Penn State’s 45-0 victory over Marshall should be in store on Saturday.

I believe the coaching staff will once again try to get the run game going before conference play starts the following week. With the consistent talk from Campbell and Taylor Mouser about the run game this week, I expect there to be added emphasis to run the ball well against Buffalo’s defense.

With that, the score won’t be as much of a blowout as many expect against a Buffalo team who’s coming off a loss to FIU in Week 2. Running the ball consistently will naturally take more time off the clock, leading to less opportunities for the Nittany Lions to put points on the board.

Buffalo’s offense runs through wide receiver Chance Morrow, who’s responsible for 34% of the Bulls’ offensive yards through two weeks. With the growth of Penn State’s defensive back room, I expect Morrow to have a quieter game, leading to Buffalo struggling to move the ball.

Penn State will once again be in control, but this time will have a large enough lead to put in younger or depth players earlier in the game, which is key for the development of young players, especially quarterback Alex Manske.

The Nittany Lions will put on a dominant showing and run away with the game, defeating Buffalo 38-7, with the running backs showing more glimpses of consistency that hasn’t been seen in the past two weeks.

Andrew Mercer: Penn State 48, Buffalo 0

After a slower start to Penn State’s first road trip, the Nittany Lions are going to want to dash any doubts going into the conference schedule, and I believe that Penn State is going to take Buffalo by storm with its second shutout of the season.

Penn State’s secondary is one of the highest-performing aspects of D’Anton Lynn’s defense, and with the Bulls’ offense primarily stemming from Morrow, I think the Nittany Lions’ pass defense will keep Buffalo off the scoreboard.

The Nittany Lions’ passing game will be the focus once again as Mouser continues to work on slowly but surely improving the ground game. Although I believe the running backs will have another meager showing overall, I predict that either Carson Hansen or James Peoples will find the end zone.

Ryan Barker will nail a pair of field goals when the running backs falter throughout the game. Additionally, I think the Nittany Lions will score their first special teams touchdown with Zay Robinson taking a punt return to the end zone.

Other than that, it’ll once again be the Rocco Becht show until Manske takes over. There were plenty of explosive plays against both Marshall and Temple, and if Becht continues to trust the deep ball, the receivers and tight ends will continue to produce at a high level.

Lexie Linderman: Penn State 41, Buffalo 6

To no one’s surprise, everyone is going to be focused on Penn State’s run game against Buffalo this weekend. Will Quinton Martin Jr. play? Can Hansen prove he’s the guy?

Those questions will be answered this Saturday when the Nittany Lions pick up their third and final nonconference win of the season. This matchup is crucial for Penn State to no longer be a “hair off” in the run game, as Mouser put it, ahead of the beginning of Big Ten play on Sept. 26.

There will definitely be an emphasis on running the ball against the Bulls in an effort to get that aspect of the offense moving, so Becht might not have as flashy of a game as he’s had the last two weeks.

I also expect the Nittany Lions to try and get some different people the ball, especially considering Mouser said he wants to find tight end Finn Furmanek in the end zone and Andrew Rappleyea is also waiting to have his big game.

As for the defense, Penn State will keep on rolling after allowing just nine points through the first two games, six of which came in garbage time against Temple. The secondary will continue to shine in pass coverage, while the defensive line will have some reinforcements with defensive tackles Armstrong Nnodim and Alijah Carnell set to return from injury.

Noah Aberegg: Penn State 52, Buffalo 3

Two weeks ago, Penn State laid down the hammer against Marshall, winning 45-0 in dominant fashion. A week later, the offense got off to a slow start and struggled in the run game, putting up just 27 points.

Against Buffalo, I think the Nittany Lions will have things figured out and get off to a faster start with more success in the run game. I think Hansen will be more decisive in his reads and utilize better blocking from the offensive line and tight ends — including Gabe Burkle, as he’ll likely play more snaps than last week.

Following a breakout by Koby Howard in Week 1 and Benjamin Brahmer in Week 2, I think all aspects of the passing game will be flowing. Becht’s confidence has grown stronger through each game and that’ll likely continue against Buffalo.

Defensively, the Nittany Lions will be looking for answers against Morrow, who has the team’s only five touchdowns this year. However, Penn State’s secondary has performed amongst the best in the nation, allowing the fifth-lowest passing yards per game.

Penn State will look to fill the gap left by Max Granville — who Campbell announced was out for the season due to injury postgame last week. The defensive line’s depth will alleviate Granville’s absence and record numerous sacks against the Bulls.

title: ‘I love this human’ | TE Andrew Rappleyea brings toughness to Penn State offense
author: Noah Aberegg | The Daily Collegian
description:
Tight end Andrew Rappleyea walked into a meeting room with Matt Campbell shortly after he was hired to meet the guy who could be his head coach for the next few years.

From his first conversation with Rappleyea, Campbell was all-in on what he brought to the Nittany Lions.

“The first time I met him, I was like, 'Ooh, I love this human,’” Campbell said.

Rappleyea was one of 52 players who returned to Penn State’s squad after James Franklin was fired, and his commitment to the Nittany Lions was one of the key things that drew Campbell’s attention.

Campbell’s first question to each player during the introductory meeting was about why they came to Penn State, a question Rappleyea answered “with passion and with just this infectious energy,” Campbell said.

“You knew that that was somebody that you wanted to build the program around,” Campbell said. “Then to watch how he works, what he comes in with, that competitive endurance that he comes everyday with.”

On the other side of things, Rappleyea had spent the last three years playing for James Franklin, but didn’t follow his tight ends coach Ty Howle or Franklin. Instead, he was committed to what Campbell brought to the table and gave him a chance.

“This is the right guy for the job,” Rappleyea said. “He’s a great human being and as a coach, I just love playing for him.”

As one of the key returners to Penn State’s squad, Rappleyea helped bring the team together, despite not necessarily being the top player in his position group.

“We had a bunch of new guys coming from all over the place and really just getting comfortable with them,” Rappleyea said. “Lining up now, I feel like there’s not a doubt in my mind we’re going to get the job done.”

Through two games this season, Rappleyea has recorded just two receptions for 23 yards. But what’s not on the stat sheet is made up for in his blocking.

Rappleyea’s shorter but bigger frame has allowed him to eat up blocks on run plays. With Gabe Burkle sidelined for Week 1 and playing a limited role against Temple, Rappleyea has been key with blocking what he believes can be a dominant rushing attack.

“We have the best backs in the country, the best line, best tight end group,” Rappleyea said.

In all aspects of his game, Rappleyea brings a physicality aspect that draws praise from his coaching staff.

“It doesn't matter if it's ping pong or it doesn't matter if it's basketball,” Campbell said. “If Rapp's got something to say, he's going to try to attack you in everything he does.”

In Campbell and Taylor Mouser’s offensive system, Rappleyea has been a part of a tight-end heavy lineup, at times playing in 14-personnel, which he said was “awesome.”

While Rappleyea hasn’t had his big game or shining moment yet, he’s embraced every moment to play and be on the field.

“I just love football, I love the physicality of it,” Rappleyea said. “I love doing my job and helping the team win.”

title: ‘Just me being myself’ | Penn State WR Zay Robinson’s confidence, energy key to success
author: Andrew Mercer | The Daily Collegian
description:
When Zay Robinson first got to Iowa State, fellow wide receiver Chase Sowell originally found him obnoxious, but later grew to appreciate his loud, energetic character. There was a certain swagger about him baked into his nature as a football player and as a person.

Robinson was the kind of player that told his teammates exactly what he was going to do on the field, and then executed the plan to perfection, something Sowell grew to see not as arrogance, but as confidence.

Sowell took Robinson under his wing and the pair forged a brotherly bond at Iowa State that carried over to Penn State.

“There's nobody else I'd rather have in my corner, and I'll do anything to give him advice and keep giving him the wisdom that I have,” Sowell said Tuesday.

Robinson hasn’t changed one bit since transferring to Penn State. He’s still the dancing, kind and infectiously charismatic teammate and is one of the Nittany Lions’ most vocal players.

“That was just me being myself,” Robinson said Wednesday. “I'm loud, I'm nice, I like to dance. I just like to be that spark of energy. It wasn't me ‘talking the talk.’ It was me just being confident in myself, and that's what I'll always have.”

The redshirt freshman equated his charismatic personality to the confidence he’s built over the course of his life. He said the belief he has in himself stems from his family’s influence, naming his grandmother, mother and the rest of his “tight family.”

Robinson’s self-confidence is already being shown on the field. Although he’s lower in a depth chart, he has found ways to make an impact in the short duration of his appearance.

He said staying “locked in” on his process and making on-the-fly adjustments depending on how his body feels is crucial to his ability to perform when his name is called. Robinson’s confidence is reinforced by the faith he has in his preparation.

When Matt Campbell and Taylor Mouser called his number these past two weeks, Robinson put that confidence on full display.

Robinson’s only target against Marshall was a 39-yard touchdown reception. He caught three passes on three targets for 34 yards against Temple, including a catch through heavy traffic, which Robinson had full faith in himself and Rocco Becht to make the connection.

“I gotta just be ready for any moment because it can happen at any time,” Robinson said. “That goes with how my process is throughout the week. Getting my sleep, eating right, just doing everything, all the little things, so I can be ready for those moments when they come.”

However, Robinson has provided an even bigger on-field impact this season as Penn State’s starting kick and punt returner, a position he’s accepted with enthusiastic joy. He was a returner for West Des Moines Valley High School, and he said he likes the “isolation” of the job.

“I had the opportunity to just go back there one time and try it, and I liked it,” Robinson said. “It helps the team, so I want to do whatever I can do. Get the ball, and just get to make plays.”

So far, Robinson’s averaged 20.5 yards per kick return and 12.6 yards per punt return through two games. However, he said he’s only a “man or two away” from a breakthrough return, noting that the blocks are there and he needs to improve on slipping tackles.

Robinson’s not worried about whether he’ll get more playing time at wide receiver. He said he just needs to stay consistent, continue to trust himself and never let off the gas.

“It's just nice to have an opportunity to be out there with my guys and to be able to help however I can,” Robinson said.

title: Penn State notebook | Matt Campbell discusses Buffalo, TEs at weekly presser
author: Andrew Deal | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State concludes its nonconference schedule with a home matchup against Buffalo on Saturday.

Matt Campbell met with the media on Wednesday to talk about the Bulls, the tight end room and his team’s performance so far.

Here’s what Campbell had to say.

Assessing Buffalo

Campbell has experience coaching a MAC team that’s going on the road to a ranked Power Four stadium. In 2015, his Toledo team went down to No. 18 Arkansas and defeated the Razorbacks 16-12. With that, he understands Buffalo’s perspective heading into Saturday.

“Anybody can beat anybody on any Saturday, and I think the reality of the world we live in today, it's why you're straining to be the best,” Campbell said.

Buffalo enters with a 1-1 record, coming off a 33-20 loss against Florida International, but Campbell saw glimpses of what the Bulls can be in the second half when sophomore Jason Wright entered the game.

Campbell recognized the experience that Buffalo coach Pete Lambo has with multiple years under his belt as the associate head coach at South Carolina. That background isn’t going unnoticed by Campbell and his staff.

“He's coached at some great places, and I think you just watch how this Buffalo team plays,” Campbell said. “Their kids play really, really hard. I think they found themselves a great quarterback in the second half of the game last week.”

Wright stepped into the starting role and put up a fight against Florida International despite the large deficit he had. With that, he continued to find a connection with leading receiver Chance Morrow, who’s far and away the Bulls’ top target.

Morrow has 218 receiving yards on the season, with the next highest coming from tight end Clint Walker with 46. Campbell highlighted the difficulties Morrow could give to the Nittany Lions’ defense.

“He's got an elite catch radius,” Campbell said. “He's long. He's got the ability to threaten you with his speed down the field, but he's also you watch some of those catches in tight spaces. He's a real challenge”

Tight end development

It’s been no secret that Penn State has multiple potential stars at tight end this season. Both Gabe Burkle and Benjamin Brahmer were named to the John Mackey Award watch list. Joining them in the room is Andrew Rappleyea, who stood out to Campbell from the moment he met with him in the offseason.

“(Rappleyea)’s got this infectious energy,” Campbell said. “The first time that I met him, I was like, ‘Ooh, I love that human.’ And I just think the starting point for (Rappleyea) is he loves Penn State.”

Rappleyea was a player Campbell knew right away was going to stay under the new coaching staff because of his passion for Penn State. However, Brahmer was a player who Campbell felt his staff “lucked into” when he committed to Iowa State.

Brahmer was initially committed to Nebraska, but the Cornhuskers were in the midst of a coaching change. That’s when Brahmer and his family made it known that he had interest in joining Iowa State.

“We knew who Ben was, and we certainly knew what he stood for,” Campbell said. “And he comes on an official visit, and our official visit was going to watch my son get pounded in a wrestling match, and that's what they wanted to do, his dad and Ben wanted to go watch that. So it was awesome.”

Team’s performance through two weeks

Even though it’s just two weeks into the season, Campbell has already learned a lot about his players and team when it comes to the games and preparation.

“I think the couple things that I've learned so far is this group loves football and they haven't wavered in terms of fall camp to practicing,” Campbell said. “There is an absolute love of the game of football and competing to play the game of football.”

Campbell mentioned the unpredictability with college football, and part of that can be handled by preparation and adversity. The Nittany Lions dealt with adversity against Temple in Week 2, but battled through it to prevent them from losing to a Group of Six team.

“You see different guys step up every week, and our sport is going to bring a lot of adversity,” Campbell said. “Sometimes on the field, sometimes internally, sometimes with injuries. Just there's so much that's going to happen, and we're going to need the whole buy-in as we continue to navigate forward through the season.”

title: Position preview | Penn State women’s hockey returns strong defensive unit
author: Aeryn Ajot | The Daily Collegian
description:
After a 33-6 season, Penn State returns with seven defensive players and three netminders in an overhauled look for this season, yet the core remains intact, with primarily gaps on the offensive side of the puck.

Here’s how that strong defensive front shapes out in another year on the ice under coach Jeff Kampersal.

New faces

Among the fresh batch, the blue and white added two freshmen to the roster this year in the goal prevention core: defenseman Megan Hosman and goaltender Morgan Stickney.

Newbies Stickney and Hosman come from extensive backgrounds and have a prime opportunity to step up to the plate for their inaugural seasons. In between the pipes, Stickney arrives from U18 Team USA, where she contributed to a silver medal finish with 12 saves over a pair of shutout performances. Prior to joining the Nittany Lions, the 5-foot-10 righty Hosman also followed a similar suit, playing defense in three games in Girls U19 Nationals.

Savanna Muir arrives in net from SUNY Cortland and Bishop Kearney, where she became NYSAHA District Champions and participated in the USA Hockey National Tournament, placing third. The former Pittsburgh Pens Elite alum slots in on Kampersal’s staff as a depth piece with real upside to see time in the crease.

For her final season, Happy Valley welcomes Ashley Kokavec, a prominent defensive transfer from Palm Beach, Florida. Arriving from Vermont, Kokavec played 74 career games in two seasons with the Catamounts after leaving Maine. The blueliner has claimed many achievements in her journey, including NEHWA All-Star and Hockey East Third Team All-Conference, as she now takes that prestige into Happy Valley.

Key returnees

Returning for their second consecutive season, Maddy Campbell, Danica Maynard, Sophie Morrow and Shelby Shane are ready to hit back onto the ice.

Goaltender Campbell made a strong lasting impact in her first season behind program stalwart Katie DeSa, and likely takes over as starter in her absence. The Courtice, Ontario native appeared in 11 games, started in eight, with a .935 save percentage that contributed to her intriguing season.

Defenseman Shane is another sophomore returning to be tabbed for an uptick in duties after she played a large role in her rookie year. After appearing in all 39 games with the blue and white, the Kutztown, Pennsylvania, native tallied a nine-plus-minus along with a goal and three assists.

The blue and white also welcome back Maynard to the defense, who was named to the All-USCHO Third Team and All-AHA Rookie of the Year for her premier season while appearing in all 39 games. Morrow also joins her as a blueliner, returning after a summer competing with USA Hockey’s National Women’s Collegiate Select Team.

Juniors Grace Tullock and Taya MacDonald aren’t new to the Nittany Lions front pairing, with both appearing in all 39 games and maintaining the defensive line en route to a historic Frozen Four season.

Named a captain for this upcoming season, MacDonald is the only player in the Nittany Lions’ leadership group to be a member of the defense, returning as one of the only upperclassmen in the defensive unit.

Tullock showed out last year, with 34 blocked shots and a 23 plus-minus to conclude her sophomore season, after earning a spot on the All-AHA Rookie Team in her debut campaign.

Penn State had a show-out season, now receiving a preseason No. 4 USCHO ranking for this upcoming year, next to top schools like defending champion Wisconsin, who the Nittany Lions took to overtime in last year's Frozen Four. Also rounding out the top teams is last season's runner-up Ohio State, along with Minnesota.

With international representatives and junior standouts donning the blue and white, Penn State has a golden opportunity to continue its upward trajectory.

title: Column | ‘Brave New World’ proves AI reliance stems from an addiction to convenience
author: Kippi Hall | The Daily Collegian
description:
At a coffee shop in downtown State College, I found myself sandwiched between two students: one using Claude to write an essay, the other using ChatGPT to finish their math homework.

The tsunami wave of artificial intelligence has broken on campus, seemingly wiping out critical thinking in its wake. While Penn State, a newly declared “AI school,” has AI literacy resources available, the apparent status across the student body is still rampant usage with minimal checks.

It’s abundantly easy and tempting to use a tool that will do the hard work for you. In a dimming light of intellectual labor and creativity, Aldous Huxley’s ‘Brave New World,’ published in 1932, stands as a pillar of caution for offloading mental and emotional effort onto technology.

The title is an ironic reference to a line in William Shakespeare’s ‘The Tempest,’ in Act V, Scene I, where the “brave new world” from the speaker’s view is a utopia of beauty and intrigue. In the novel, the “brave new world” is flipped to mirror John’s — Huxley’s protagonist who’s frequently referred to as “The Savage” — wasted curiosity and humanity in the face of a tightly controlled society.

In the beginning of the novel, John arrives at the center of an advanced society called the World State from The Reservation, an isolated area where technology isn’t available. He grapples with the moral affront of simulated feelings and lack thereof, learning that the “brave new world” he had read about is depleted of life because of a chemical dependence on comfort through a drug called soma.

Penn State is full of streamlined processes. The cashless campus encourages tapping credit cards over carrying a wallet, id+ cards can never be lost after uploading to one’s phone and ideas can now be generated through the university’s new AI Studio.

The college experience is constantly marketed like our brave new world, full of opportunities to change, discover and, most importantly, learn. But what’s the point if we’re expected to shirk the burden of thought onto a machine that cannot create ideas but only reflect existing ones?

John looks at the citizens of the World State, bred in incubators to be complacent, drugged up to avoid difficult experiences, and grows disgusted and disillusioned.

In a conversation with one of the World State’s leaders, Mustapha Mond, on the meaning of life, argues for the freedom to be imperfect: “But I don't want comfort. I want God, I want poetry, I want real danger, I want freedom, I want goodness. I want sin.”

In other words, John wants the chance to be human, warts and all.

Offloading the difficult task of critical thinking onto AI is not slowing down. According to a study conducted and co-authored by S. Shyam Sundar, a Bellisario researcher and media effects professor, users trust AI fact-checkers at similar rates to human fact-checkers. Even when attempting to do work without assistance, individuals feel less confident in their own abilities to complete assignments well, according to a multi-university study published by the National Institute of Medicine. By falling on the heuristic that AI can achieve more than a human could, AI reliance could create a “cognitive dependency.”

We have the perfect machine to find the formulas, write our essays and paint our pictures with astounding adherence to form at our disposal. When we look at ‘Brave New World’ and how the World State forces the ease of technology, it only costs us our poetry, our discomfort and our goodness. It costs us our humanity.

John, a “savage” for opting into the choice to be imperfect and uniquely emotional, retains his humanity in all of its trials and tribulations. His title as “The Savage,” implied to be primitive and barbaric, echoes the words circling online about AI’s inevitability and avoiding being as good as staying on the horse and buggy in the age of the Ferrari.

However, pushing suffering and the effort to overcome it onto an unthinking machine doesn’t give us the chance to be more sophisticated: It only leaves us underdeveloped and without stories to tell about who we are.

College is hard. It makes you feel stupid, ugly and uncomfortable. But that’s the point. Achieving higher education is a four-year-long (sometimes longer) challenge to stretch your mind beyond what it had been taught for 18 years. Excessive reliance on AI to do the stretching for us leads to less memory retention and increased “cognitive atrophy,” according to a study from the MIT Media Lab. It doesn’t encourage learning.

John quotes Shakespeare’s ‘Hamlet’ when making his case for suffering: “Getting rid of everything unpleasant instead of learning to put up with it. ‘Whether 'tis better in the mind to suffer the slings and arrows of outrageous fortune, or to take arms against a sea of troubles and by opposing end them’...But you don't do either. Neither suffer nor oppose. You just abolish the slings and arrows. It's too easy.”

Perhaps our sea of troubles looks like the cold-but-friendly greeting of ChatGPT, and our opposition takes the form of closing the tab. We won’t know until we make the attempt to bear the unpleasantness of life on our own, seeking a brave new world after the tide reels back.

title: Know Your Rights:   What students should know amid increased immigration enforcement activity
author: Fabiola González-Cruz | The Daily Collegian
description:
Over the past few years, changes to federal immigration policy, including increased immigration enforcement, have raised questions about what rights immigrants have when interacting with law enforcement.

In July, the State College Borough Council passed an ordinance preventing borough resources and personnel, including police, from collaboration or involvement with U.S. Immigration and Customs enforcement.

Here’s what Penn State students should know about their rights.

Federal and Pennsylvania law

People in the United States have certain constitutional protections regardless of their immigration status, including protections involving searches, seizures and interactions with law enforcement.

According to the guidance published by the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania, individuals stopped by immigration authorities in a public place have the right to remain silent and do not have to answer questions about their immigration status or birthplace.

Individuals can also ask an immigration agent for their name, badge and agency and ask if they are free to leave. If the agent says yes, the individual may walk away.

Individuals also have the right to say, “I do not consent to a search.” However, Pennsylvania guidance states that individuals should not physically resist an officer conducting a search.

Those who do not understand English can also request an interpreter.

U.S. citizens are not required to carry documents proving their citizenship. However, non-U.S. citizens who are over 18 and have valid immigration documents are required under federal law to carry them, and may be required to show them if asked.

If immigration authorities come to your home, dorm

Dorms, apartments and other living areas are considered private “nonpublic areas” and are subject to different treatment from immigration authorities.

Individuals do not have to open their door when immigration agents arrive, according to guidance from the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania. They can ask agents to identify themselves and ask to see a warrant through a window, or even have it slid underneath the door.

Agents are required to have a warrant signed by a judge to enter a home without permission, according to the Commonwealth. If the warrant is not signed by a judge or does not contain the correct name and address, you do not have to let any agent in.

Immigration enforcement at Penn State

Penn State has issued university-specific guidance regarding federal actions and immigration enforcement.

University Police and Public Safety officers do not inquire about individuals’ immigration status, though the department communicates with other law enforcement agencies as appropriate, according to a community update from Penn State last updated in Feb. 2026.

The university asks members of the Penn State community who become aware of immigration-related law enforcement activity at a Penn State location to notify University Police and Public Safety.

Students and university employees should also be aware of protections surrounding student records and personal information. Penn State states that student information is protected by the Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act, or FERPA, according to the update.

University employees approached by federal agents seeking student or employee information are directed to contact Penn State’s Office of General Counsel.

Penn State recommends that international students and scholars carry or have electronic copies of their biographical page of their passport, their most recent I-94 admission record, and their Form I-20 for F-1 students or DS-2019 for J-1 students. Penn State states that there is no need to carry a copy of a visa stamp seeing as it is relevant for entry.

International students at Penn State

Penn State spokesperson Tyra McGarvie said in a statement to the Collegian that “the University remains committed to keeping our community informed and supporting those who may be affected while complying with applicable federal laws and regulations.”

She said Penn State advises international students and other students with concerns on immigration matters to consult the Penn State Global website. The university continues to monitor potential changes affecting its international community and advises individuals seeking guidance about their rights or interactions with immigration authorities to consult a qualified attorney, seeing as Penn State cannot provide legal advice on individual cases.

Penn State Global informs that F-1 students must enroll in a full-time course load unless approved for a reduced course load, meet in-person requirements and obtain appropriate work authorization.

Similarly, J-1 students should maintain full-time enrollment and update their local U.S. address within 10 days, as well as meet mandatory health insurance requirements.

However, Penn State Global currently warns that its standard F-1 and J-1 regulation pages may not reflect the latest guidance since the university is reviewing a new Department of Homeland Security final rule ending “Duration of Status” for both F-1 and J-1 statuses.

According to Penn State Global, the new DHS rule eliminating Duration of Status for F-1 students and J-1 exchange visitors is scheduled to take effect September 15, 2026. Penn State has created a separate webpage to provide information and updates regarding the change. Penn State Global is continuing to review the rule and recommends that international students monitor university communications and its Duration of Status webpage for the latest information.

Getting help at Penn State

Penn State directs international students on F or J visas, as well as J scholars and university-sponsored faculty who need immigration assistance, to Penn State’s Global International Student and Scholar Advising Office.

Students with other immigration-related concerns are directed to Penn State Student Legal Services.

Additionally, the UPUA lists a number of resources available in the community and online on their website.

title: Weekly Recap | Penn State women’s soccer splits low-scoring week
author: Zach Schroder | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State began conference play this past week. The Nittany Lions started their week and year in the Big Ten on Thursday in Columbus, where they lost 1-0 against the Ohio State Buckeyes.

The blue and white would then return to Happy Valley and Jeffrey Field and secure a 1-0 win against Minnesota. Defeating the Golden Gophers made Penn State even on the week and brought the first Big Ten win of the season. After the recent stretch of play, the blue and white are now 3-2-2 on the season and 1-1-0 in conference rankings.

Here’s what stood out from the blue and white’s week.

Spamming shots

The Nittany Lions put up their second and third-most shots this year since their blowout win against Brown earlier this season. They had 16 against Ohio State and 18 against Minnesota.

Junior forward Audrey Kulpa led the team in shots this week, totaling nine, with five of those coming against the Buckeyes. That was also a season high for the Cromwell, Connecticut, native, en route to scoring the lone Penn State goal of the week. Sophomore midfielder Kennedy Ring also registered a career high of three shots in the loss to Ohio State.

Minnesota transfer Paige Kalal finished the week with six shots in total. The senior forward recorded one shot on goal and played a total of 153 minutes between both games. Freshman midfielder Paige Pasinski, junior defender Bella Ayscue and Kulpa all had two shots on goal against Minnesota, with freshman forward Ellie Kocher having the lone on-target kick against the Buckeyes.

Freshman forward Olivia Robinson also came off the bench in the clash with the Golden Golphers, showcasing tenacity in front of net as she registered three shots in a little over 20 minutes of play.

Don’t mess with Gress

Redshirt senior goalkeeper Mackenzie Gress continued her dominant performance this past week and stellar start to the season. The Lyndhurst, New Jersey, native upped her save count by six with four against Ohio State and two against the Golden Gophers

The victory over Minnesota brought Gress her first true shutout of the season, as she was relieved by freshman keeper Lily Selvy in the blue and white’s other shutout this season. The Lyndhurst, New Jersey, native started in the shutouts over Bucknell and Brown, but was taken off in the 71st and 75th minutes, respectively. Gress thwarted a breakaway opportunity late in the game, and graduate student defender Lily Boyden made sure the save was completed.

Despite the result over the Golden Gophers signaling Gress’ first complete game shutout, she had a lot of assistance from her backline, as those two saves against Minnesota marked the lowest total in the figure for the netminder this season.

Cards and fouls

The blue and white led in fouls in both contests; it also received two yellow cards in the win on Sunday. Kulpa and Ayscue drew bookings in the second half against Minnesota, which marked the first time this season that Penn State received two yellow cards in a match. The Nittany Lions totaled 17 fouls through the week, with eight against the Buckeyes and nine against Minnesota.

Penn State still sits in the bottom five of the Big Ten in total team fouls, and so does its next opponent, the Terrapins. The Nittany Lions travel to College Park to face off against Maryland at Ludwig Field at 5 p.m. this Friday.

title: Wakey wakey, eggs and bakey | The best on-campus breakfast spots
author: Rebecca Fein | The Daily Collegian
description:
As you slowly stretch awake, delicately crack your knuckles and get up to use the bathroom, you’re interrupted by a loud, ear-shattering growl — from your stomach.

You recall last night, wondering when the last time you ate was. When your mind goes blank (not because of the copious amounts of alcohol that were in your system), you realize it's been a while since nutrition graced your body.

It’s breakfast time.

On The Edge

When Bagel Crust sounds like the move, but the walk is too treacherous and DoorDash is too expensive, don’t fret.

All five resident halls — East, South, North, West and Pollock — have the wonderfully delicious Edge.

If a bacon, egg and cheese is the only thing on your mind upon rolling out of bed, this little shop has everything you could ever dream of.

From seasonal pumpkin pastries to everyday confectionaries, Edge has the best sweet treats in town, not to mention the Penn State Bakery food that can be found there, featuring different sandwiches and various kinds of bagels with a myriad of spreads.

Sausage, egg and cheese on a croissant got you thirsty? Fear not, because Edge serves Starbucks beverages. Pair your sandwich with an iced latte or fruity refresher for a satisfying breakfast combo.

Edge is breakfast done right.

Dependable Dining Hall

The dining hall is one of Penn State’s most hidden gems.

Woke up at noon? That’s perfectly okay. If you catch the dining hall on a weekend, it serves brunch until 2 p.m. to accommodate the much-needed sleep after a night out.

The dining hall serves the same classic breakfast staples every single day: scrambled eggs, waffles with syrup, cereal, including Froot Loops, Krave, Frosted Flakes and so much more. Each dining hall has a complementary toasting station filled with sourdough bread, english muffins and bagels, complete with cream cheese, butter, jelly and peanut butter to match your spread mood of the day.

In addition to the repeating items, the dining hall switches it up daily, adding three different items. This consists of a type of potato, like tater tots or hashbrowns, a form of protein, like bacon or turkey sausage and of course one sweet breakfast item — in addition to the daily waffles, there’s usually pancakes or French toast.

All of these main courses can be eaten with your choice of yogurt, granola, a variety of pastries and fresh fruit.

To wash it all down, there's any fountain drink you desire, every juice imaginable, coffee, tea or copious types of milk.

For allergy-ridden people, there’s a special fridge filled with dairy-free yogurt, cheese and milk.

Sleep in, but don’t sleep on the dining hall.

Majestic Market

Lastly, the market. This one may seem like an obvious choice, but it’s often forgotten in a hunger-induced haze.

Just like Edge, each residential area has a market filled with just about anything you would find in a real grocery store.

Try something quick, like pre-packaged fresh fruit, a protein bar, a smoothie or pre- portioned cereal boxes. Have a bit more time? Pick up a microwavable breakfast item in the refrigerated section.

There are tons of options, including microwavable bacon and sausage. If you want the real deal, there are pre-made breakfast sandwiches and burritos that are only a bite away.

There is also, of course, creamery ice cream located conveniently in the freezer next to it. If that’s breakfast, we won’t tell.

title: Preview | Penn State field hockey takes on 2 ranked opponents, first Big Ten matchup
author: Annie Gleba | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State enters the upcoming weekend after a close 2-1 loss to No. 3 Princeton. The Nittany Lions are now at a 3-2 record before heading into their first Big Ten matchup against No. 5 Maryland at home on Thursday. The game against Maryland will also be in support of THON.

After the home game against the Terrapins, the blue and white will go on the road to face No. 19 Monmouth.

Maryland

Maryland comes into this matchup 6-0, having beaten four other teams in shutouts and winning a game against one ranked opponent, No. 8 Duke. Penn State will also be Maryland's first Big Ten opponent this season.

The Nittany Lions are coming into this matchup with a strong collaboration between their offensive line, as goals and points have been spread amongst multiple players.

Even with the spread of points across a majority of the unit, two athletes stand out: Ella Gaitan and Sienna Dunn. Gaitan has built up nine points at the start of the year, leading the Nittany Lions in goals with a total of four.

Gaitan will face her former team. In her two years at Maryland, she was named to the 2024 Big Ten All-Freshman Team and was also a conference All-Second Team selection in this same season.

Just after her, Dunn currently leads the blue and white in assists with a total of six. These two players have shown to be a great combination and a key to the Penn State offense.

On Maryland's side, there are two offensive players who have taken over the field, Babs van Hest and Francisca Eschoyez. Both women are international students entering their junior year with the Terrapins.

Van Hest is the top offensive player with a total of 14 points, including four goals and is tied for the team lead in assists with six. Eschoyez is the team leader in goals with six, having a shots-on-goal percentage of 0.706.

There are two goalies for Maryland, Alyssa Klebasko and Ryleigh Osborne. The senior Klebasko has three times the playing time of Osborne and has started five Terrapins games, slotting in as the expected netminder Penn State is tasked with besting.

The Odenton, Maryland, native allowed only three goals over the five contests, yet faced heavy action with 12 total saves to achieve a 0.800 save percentage.

The two Big Ten teams will meet Thursday at 5 p.m.

Monmouth

After Thursday’s game, Penn State takes on Monmouth at noon on Sunday. Monmouth will be the second-ranked opponent the Nittany Lions will go on to face this weekend.

Monmouth sits at 4-1, taking a key win from then-No. 17 Rutgers in its home opener, 5-1. Its only loss this season came in a close matchup with Delaware, which ended 2-1. Aside from its loss, it has beaten each of its opponents with four or more goals, even taking two wins by scoring eight goals.

On the offensive side of the ball, the Hawks' breakout player seems to be Milla Frye. The Ratingen, Germany, native has achieved 19 points, spread across eight goals and three assists. She has also started and played through each game and enters as a chance to be a centerpiece of the Monmouth offense.

Other key offensive players are Alicia Vanderlyde and Stella Goddard-Despot. Vanderlyde has nine points, with Goddard-Despot not too far behind her at seven. The pair each have one assist and have contributed a combined seven goals this season.

Monmouth also has two goalkeepers this season: Charlie Bowman and Djoeke van Helsdingen. Bowman has started every game this season, allowing four goals and making 10 saves. The junior has played the full 60 minutes only two times: in the Hawks' season opener against Rutgers and a 4-2 win over Temple.

The Hawks' second goalkeeper, van Helsdingen, has played 30 minutes in two games this season, only allowing two goals while keeping up with four saves.

On the Penn State side, Aby Deverka is building up her save percentage, now averaging a .767 percentage, only allowing seven goals with an astonishing 23 saves.

As Penn State heads into the weekend, it looks to take on two ranked opponents back-to-back, making it a challenging weekend for the Nittany Lions.

title: What's here to stay, what's on the horizon for fall fashion trends
author: Ally Sons | The Daily Collegian
description:
As the leaves start to fall and the weather starts to change, Penn State students brave the transition from warm 80 degree days to cool, windy 50 degree ones. With the fall equinox next week, there's no better time than now to start shopping for your trendy fall wardrobe.

Luckily, State College has a large number of trendy fashion places right downtown, so you don’t need a car to find these items. Or if you choose to shop secondhand as well, you can find these items without breaking the bank.

We’ve watched many trends come and go over the last year, from kitten heels to jorts and foldover track pants. It’s been a big year for the fashion industry and self-expression through clothing.

So what’s around the corner for this fall?

Capris

These are the perfect pants for those days where it’s not too hot, but you’re still trying to move on from shorts. Falling right at the mid-calf, capris have made their comeback since their previous moment of stardom in the early 2000s.

Whether it’s a tight-fitting or a wider-leg jean material, these have been a staple on the streets of State College in recent weeks, typically paired with flip-flops or sandals.

A popular place to look for capris is Urban Outfitters located at 234 E. College Avenue, a convenient downtown location. They have a large number of choices, from gaucho pants to more fitted looks.

Polka dots

Polka dots might just be one of the top patterns you see when you walk out of your apartment or dorm. They’re a fun, simple way to bring pattern into your wardrobe without taking too big of a leap.

While polka dots are not a new trend, they seem to be here to stay for the fall season, with many students using them as an opportunity to show off their blue and white spirit for gameday.

This is a big trend at stores like Connections and Pitaya, and the former just dropped a new collection of polka dot matching sets.

Ballet sneakers

A new addition to streetwear that has been seen more and more on campus is none other than ballet sneakers. One of the most popular brands is Penn State's new sponsor Adidas, but every name brand is producing this trend, too.

A strappy shoe, it falls somewhere between a velcro sneaker and a classy ballet flat. Subsequently, they can be easily dressed both up and down for both professional settings and everyday life.

If you’re looking for a multi-facated shoe that you can find almost anywhere right now, start looking toward ballet sneakers.

Business casual streetwear

People desiring a little more of a professional look that’s also comfortable for hanging out with friends or heading to the bars seem to have landed on a business casual, streetwear hybrid: The perfect middle ground.

Business casual day-to-day can look like button-down crop tops and short, pleated skirts. For a more masculine outfit, nicer dress pants, Polos and loafers.

Some spots with plenty of options are Uptown Cheapskate and Urban Outfitters, both located on College Ave.

Dark-wash denim

Dark-wash denim is hitting college students like a true wave. Summer heat is abandoning the air and taking with it its lighter wash for a darker, more fall-aligned vibe.

It’s got a pumpkin patch stamp of approval, and students can easily pair it with basic tops, sweaters and cardigans. It adds contrast to an outfit and pairs nicely with almost every kind of belt or accessory.

It’s appearing in full swing in lots of local boutiques, making it an easy-to-find fall staple for your closet.

Monochrome sets

If you’ve walked to class in the cooler seasons on campus, it's almost impossible to not see at least one person in a matching set. Despite this having trended for a while, it’s unlikely to be leaving us anytime soon.

It’s an easy and put-together outfit you can just throw on without too much preparation or planning. You can look like you’ve got it all together while still being comfortable.

If you want to find these without spending too much, don’t count out stores like Walmart and 5 Below. They have a variety of matching sets that come in almost every color and size.

Men's jewelry

From rings to necklaces and earring studs, men’s jewelry has been an ever-growing trend. People are migrating from the early 2020s bigger chains toward smaller jewelry that’s less of a statement piece, and better for everyday wear.

The diamond stud and simple rings are all the rage right now, adding more character to plain outfits.

Looking for more simple jewelry is the perfect opportunity to shop secondhand. You can even expand your search to antique stores for true vintage pieces — harder to find, but so much easier to wear once you do.

title: No. 9 Penn State women’s volleyball stays hot, defeats Villanova in four sets
author: Elliott Inscho | The Daily Collegian
description:
After Penn State traveled to Philadelphia on Friday night, Villanova made the opposite trip on Tuesday to face the Nittany Lions for an in-state clash.

The blue and white dropped their first set since falling to No. 3 Kentucky on Sept. 6, but battled to secure the 3-1 win over the Wildcats and rack up another nonconference victory.

Ryla Jones started the match hot, notching its opening kill and combining with Whitney Lauenstein for a block. Back-to-back points by the Wildcats saw them even the score at 2-2, but two errors and a kill by Lauenstein gave the Nittany Lions a 5-2 lead.

Three kills by Gabrielle Nichols and an ace from Lauenstein forced Villanova coach Josh Steinbach to call his first timeout with the Wildcats trailing 10-4. Coming out of the break, Finley Krystkowiak made her first kill of the match, Villanova committed three consecutive errors and Lauenstein made her second ace to give Penn State a 15-4 edge at the media timeout.

Lauenstein’s service ace out of the break ended the blue and white’s 9-0 run, the longest of the campaign so far. Wildcats’ outside hitter Cat Young reciprocated with a bad serve of her own, but Villanova won three of four points to follow.

Kills by Jones and Lauenstein preceded back-to-back points from the Wildcats, but Kennedy Martin answered with her second kill of the night on a thunderous swing. Trailing by eight points, Selah O’Connor sailed a serve past the back line, and a block from Jones brought the Nittany Lions to set point.

While Chloe Kelly kept the frame alive for the Wildcats with her second kill of the match, Martin responded with a finessed shot that found the floor and clinched the 25-14 set for Penn State.

Villanova was competitive in the second set’s opening stages, jumping out to a 5-3 lead on two errors by the Nittany Lions and kills from three different Wildcats. Lauenstein and Krystkowiak notched kills to help level things, but a service error from Nichols, ace by Young and attack error from Martin gave Villanova a 9-6 edge.

Abby Harrell posted a kill and ace to bookend an attack error by Lauenstein, before Taylor Lewis’ third kill gave Villanova a 15-10 lead at the second-set reprieve. Penn State struggled to finish down the stretch, as four consecutive Villanova points came on errors by the blue and white, giving them a 21-14 advantage.

The Nittany Lions wouldn’t go down without a fight. Nichols and Alexis Stucky made kills as part of a three-point run, but a bad serve from Stucky and a kill by Lewis handed Penn State its first dropped set since Sept. 6 against No. 3 Kentucky.

It was more of the same at the start of the third set, as Harrell ripped off a kill and ace to help Villanova take a 3-1 lead. Penn State closed the gap, as Haley Burgdorf, the newly-named Big Ten Freshman of the Week, made her first two kills of the match to help the blue and white battle back and knot the set at 6-6.

The Wildcats won four of five points to follow, three of which coming on kills by Harrell, to take a 10-7 lead and draw a timeout from Katie Schumacher-Cawley. Harrell finally faulted when she made a service error, and it inspired a four-point run by Penn State that gave the Nittany Lions a 12-11 edge.

A block by Jones and an ace from Burgdorf led to Steinbach using another timeout with his team trailing 18-14. Two Penn State errors, Campbell McKinnon’s first ace and a failed block allowed Villanova to level the set.

Kills from Jones, Stucky and Nichols helped push the blue and white back into the lead. A three-point streak by Villanova evened the set back up at 22-22.

Martin delivered another powerful swing that the Wildcats couldn’t rebound before notching her second consecutive kill on a slower shot. Villanova scored on set point to lengthen the frame, but Stucky set up Burgdorf who powered the ball through the defense, claiming the third set.

Martin and Stucky opened the fourth with a kill and ace, respectively, as Penn State took an early 5-0 lead. Villanova finally got on the board when a swing from Martin rebounded off of the Wildcat block and toward the student section.

Burgdorf kept the Penn State momentum rolling with her fourth kill of the match, and a spike by Nichols helped to fuel the blue and white to a 10-2 advantage that made Steinbach call for another pause. It didn’t do much, as the Nittany Lions cruised to a 15-6 lead at the media timeout.

As the match meandered towards its finish, Villanova went on a three-point run to keep things interesting. After two from Penn State, the Wildcats ripped off another trio, but Caroline Jurevicius and Burgdorf brought the blue and white within three points of claiming the victory.

Jones made an emphatic swing to bring the Nittany Lions to match point, but sailed her serve, keeping the evening alive. Nichols made kill No. 13, breaking a tie with Martin for the team lead, securing the third set and match victory.

Now 7-1 on the season, Penn State has just two nonconference matches to play before opening its Big Ten slate against Michigan on Sept. 25.

Up Next

Penn State will face South Florida on Friday night at Rec Hall. Labeled as a “Beach Bash,” the match will be televised on Big Ten Network with first serve set for 6 p.m.

title: Penn State continues emphasis on working through struggles in run game
author: Andrew Deal | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State’s running backs entered the season with a lot of hype after the expectation of a four-running back system, and the camaraderie of the unit to get the best out of each other.

Those expectations have not come to fruition yet, but the belief in the room is still there from the players and coaching staff to figure it out.

“Obviously, to say that I wasn’t thrilled with where the run game's at would be an understatement,” Taylor Mouser said Tuesday. “Feel like there's a lot of growth to be had there.”

The emphasis to get the run game going was clear in the Nittany Lions’ victory over Temple, as they ran the ball more than they threw it despite the success the pass game had against the Owls.

It’s likely to help the room “continue to work itself out as we work through the weeks and work through these games,” as Campbell said Tuesday.

The lead back thus far has been Iowa State transfer Carson Hansen, who’s gotten a bulk of the carries. However, he hasn’t shown explosiveness or consistency in his runs, leading to the struggle to move the ball in the run game.

Mouser isn’t necessarily putting the blame on anyone, even putting some of the blame on himself, as he feels he’s not doing enough to showcase what Hansen and the rest of the running backs can do, but the rushes have been “a hair off” all around.

“For whatever reason, we’ve been a hair off, either he's missed it and blocked it well, or we haven't blocked it well, and there's been (missed assignments) on the ground that we need to clean up for him to be better,” Mouser said.

The big absence in Week 2’s game was Quinton Martin Jr., who proved in Penn State’s Pinstripe Bowl win last year that he can run the ball with consistency. Martin didn’t step onto the field at any point against Temple despite the inconsistency from the other running backs.

Despite Martin not recording a snap, the belief is still there from the coaching staff that he can produce at a high level. Campbell “has great belief” Martin will be one of the “many guys throughout the season that are going to pop up and showcase themselves.”

Whether that’s in Week 3 against Buffalo or later in the season during the Big Ten schedule is unknown, but the trust in Martin to make an impact when he enters the game is still there from the coaching staff.

“He's good enough to help our football team, and we're going to need that guy to make big plays with big moments this year,” Mouser said. “And his time's coming, and I have all the trust in him to go out there and play.”

No matter which running back is next to Rocco Becht, the staff knows the ground game is a work in progress within the team. The work continues to be put in to get to a point where the running game is successful, joining the passing success that’s already been established.

“That's something that we want to get better at, and we want to be able to run the ball whenever we want to run the ball for sure,” tight end Gabe Burkle said. “So we're attacking that every day in practice, and I don't think we're far off at all.”

title: Penn State professor awarded $400,000 grant for pediatric cancer research
author: Anisa Daniel-Oniko | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State professor and Four Diamonds researcher at Penn State College of Medicine, Dr. Sinisa Dovat, has received a $400,000 2026 Scholar Hope Grant from Hyundai Hope on Wheels, according to a news release from Penn State College of Medicine.

Dovat, a Penn State professor in the Department of Molecular and Precision Medicine, received the grant Sept. 15 while attending a special ceremony. During the ceremony at Penn State Health Golisano Children’s Hospital, Dovat was given a commemorative lab coat and honored for his commitment to pediatric cancer research.

After the formal ceremony, young patients participated in a handprint ceremony hosted by Hyundai Hope on Wheels, a non-profit organization which raises funds for childhood cancer research. Painted handprints, symbols of the fight against childhood cancer, were placed by children on Dovat’s lab coat and a Hyundai vehicle.

Dovat, who is also vice chair for basic science research in the Department of Pediatrics, will use the funding to test a two-drug treatment approach for pediatric acute myeloid leukemia.

Children diagnosed with the aggressive childhood cancer face high risks of relapse and death, and Dovat’s research aims to discover new treatment approaches that could improve their outcomes.

Golisano Children’s Hospital’s Division of Pediatric Hematology/Oncology also received a $100,000 Hyundai Hope on Wheels Impact Award for pediatric cancer research and care. Hyundai Hope on Wheels has awarded $2.8 million to Four Diamonds at Golisano Children’s Hospital since 2006.

At Four Diamonds, Dovat’s research focus is translational pediatric cancer research. He focuses on how disruption in gene regulation drives the development of leukemia. Four Diamonds partially supports his research, which aims to identify targeted therapy that will restore gene function.

title: Penn State notebook | Tanisha Wright discusses women’s basketball team offseason, nonconference schedule
author: Noah Radio | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State coach Tanisha Wright spoke to the media on Tuesday for the first time since her introductory press conference. In the 14-minute Zoom meeting, Wright touched on her reintroduction to State College, the talented, but slim roster and numerous other topics with less than a week before her first official preseason practice.

Welcome to State College

Wright graduated from Penn State in 2005, and as she returns to her alma mater, she has enjoyed becoming re-entrenched in the Happy Valley community.

“It's just getting out in the community,” Wright said. “I think being connected to the community is going to be a big piece to what we're doing and how we're building moving forward. It's always been a big piece of Lady Lion basketball, and so I think reigniting that and getting out there and sharing in that excitement of this new era of Lady Lion basketball is really important.”

In the last month, Wright and her team have spent time at The Village, a local retirement community, at the Lion Bash with the State College Borough and with the Nittany Valley Legends, a State College area girls basketball program.

Roster and staff

The Lady Lions have just 10 players listed on their official roster, and Wright has established her desire to play fast on offense and tenaciously on defense.

“I think any coach would say, ‘yeah, they'd love to have more depth, right?’ But that's not where we are right now. We have what we have,” the former WNBA champion said. “I'm excited about what we have and the players that have committed to our program and have committed to being great and being a part of this as we rebuild this to what we've always known it to be and expected to be.”

Penn State doesn’t return a single player from 2025-26, so Wright was tasked with reshaping the entire roster for her first season.

Wright will also roll out almost an entirely new new coaching staff in 2026-27. The staff features Penn State’s all-time leading scorer, Kelly Mazzante, who played three of her seasons in the blue and white with Wright.

Wright and Mazzante share a unique goal of restoring their alma mater to its former glory.

“We all love this place. We spent so much time here, have so many great memories here, blood, sweat, tears here in these gyms in these same places, and so we want to do well,” Wright said. “We want to do well for ourselves, we want to do well for our program, we want to do well for the community, but we also want to do well for the new Lady Lions who are here. This place is important to us, and getting it back on track is really important to us.”

Wright completed her staff on Sept. 9 with the addition of assistant coach Marlo Davis, who joins Wright, Mazzante, assistant coaches Octavia Blue, Olivier Cadet and Danielle Edwards, along with graduate assistant Nevaeh Tot.

Nonconference schedule

While scheduling news has trickled out over the summer, Penn State has just two games officially listed on its website. Wright was asked about the status of her nonconference schedule and kept her plans close to the vest.

“Be patient, it’s coming,” she said multiple times. “It’s coming out, and we’re excited about the games and the teams that we have on it.”

Of the Penn State matchups that have been announced by opponents, the headliner is a road test against TCU on Sunday, Dec. 13. The Horned Frogs have made back to back NCAA Regional Finals and will serve as a strong early campaign benchmark in a season full of unknowns.

The Lady Lions’ Big Ten schedule will come out on 5 p.m. Wednesday on the Big Ten Network.

title: Penn State notebook | Matt Campbell provides injury updates, discusses Max Granville's injury
author: Andrew Mercer | The Daily Collegian
description:
Matt Campbell took to the podium at Beaver Stadium in the wake of Penn State’s road victory over Temple.

Campbell discussed improving the running game, gave a few injury updates and spoke about the loss of defensive end Max Granville.

Here’s what he said on Tuesday.

Running backs

Penn State’s run game has featured a heavy reliance on Carson Hansen as the bell cow with James Peoples as the second string. Campbell has grappled with whether to go with someone built momentum at practice or feature a guy who has routinely proved themself in the past.

On Tuesday, Campbell said there is still a lot of room for improvement in the running back room. Not because of Taylor Mouser’s playcalling, but because of his players’ execution of those plays.

Campbell said he’s liking where Hansen’s development is going, primarily because he’s rarely losing yardage.

“But that guy, the explosion, those finality of finishes, there's still a lot of room for growth there,” Campbell said.

Campbell briefly spoke about Quinton Martin Jr., who didn’t see action Saturday. He said he has faith in Martin, but there is a lot of competition in the room.

He expressed his excitement to see the running backs continue to compete in practice, stating he’s “grateful that there's a lot of guys that can do a lot of things with the ball in their hands.”

“We have a lot of playmakers, and that's why practice is so critically important right now,” Campbell said. “There's still some gray, and that room is going to continue to work itself out as we work through the weeks and work through these games.”

Injury updates

When asked about player availability, Campbell said Armstrong Nnodim and Alijah Carnell will be playing against Buffalo on Saturday. He noted both players were close to 100% during warmups at Lincoln Financial Field, but he didn’t want to run the risk of re-injury.

However, he said linebacker Cam Smith is a “question mark,” but he practiced Tuesday.

Campbell stressed making a distinction between being healthy and being game ready. He said getting more reps at practice and easing back into game reps is critically important to the return process, recalling how some players coming back from offseason injuries were healthy in early fall camp, but limited in Week 1.

“We're getting healthier, which is positive,” Campbell said. “There's a difference between being healthy and being ready to play. Those are things where you know it's going to be critical to get those guys back and continue to see what are they.”

Max Granville

Campbell announced Saturday Granville suffered a season-ending injury in practice leading up to the Temple game. On Tuesday, Campbell went deeper into detail on losing Granville so early in the season.

He said it’s especially difficult to lose Granville because of what he’s already gone through. The redshirt sophomore returned from a season-ending injury he picked up prior to 2025 and returned in the season-opener against Marshall, breaking up one pass.

“It's really tough losing a guy like Max, more than you know because of what his capability and high-end ceiling is,” Campbell said. “It's just what he's already been through. Nobody worked harder to get back and be on the field, and that's a gut punch. It was a gut punch for our staff. It was a gut punch for him.”

Campbell said he’s confident that Granville will come back stronger next season, highlighting his commitment to faith and trusting the process.

In his stead, Campbell said Jackson Ford and Liam Andrews are going to “get some great opportunities.”
