title: Penn State notebook | OC Taylor Mouser takes blame for run game struggles
author: Noah Aberegg | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State’s offense was dominant in the season opener against Marshall, but had a slow start in Week 2 against Temple.

Days after the 27-9 victory, Taylor Mouser took the podium in Beaver Stadium on Tuesday, discussing the struggles from the running backs, Rocco Becht’s performance and more.

Here’s a look at what Mouser had to say.

Running back struggles

Before the season, Mouser said the offense will feature a four-running back package of Carson Hansen, James Peoples, Quinton Martin Jr. and Cam Wallace.

Through two games, Hansen has taken the bulk of the reps, but hasn’t seen the results he wants. He’s averaged just 4.4 yards per carry — the same number the running backs are at this year.

“I’m obviously not super thrilled with the run game,” Mouser said. “I’m still very sick with myself in a lot of ways for some of the things in the first two games.”

With Hansen taking a majority of the carries and Peoples seemingly slotting in as the No. 2 running back, Martin hasn’t seen the snaps that many have expected.

During the summer and fall camp, Mouser and the staff praised Martin for his work ethic and play. However, he didn’t see the field against Temple.

“Quinton has earned the right to get touches in the offense, it wasn’t a reflection of our lack of trust in Quinton or where he’s at,” Mouser said. “His time’s coming, and I have all the trust in him to go out there and play.”

While Matt Campbell has discussed the offensive line missing blocks and Hansen talked about being more decisive, Mouser took the blame for the struggles through two weeks.

“We’re all frustrated with the level of mediocrity that I would call the run game, and that starts with me,” Mouser said. “I’m more mad at myself than I am the Oline.”

Rocco Becht’s success

With the run game failing to get things established early on, the offense has relied on the passing game in the first two games.

Becht threw for 271 yards and four touchdowns against Marshall, seeing a slight decrease in Week 2 with 268 yards and three touchdowns. His performances have cemented himself as Penn State’s leader.

“He’s one of our best, if not our best player,” Mouser said. “I’m pleased with him. We put a lot on that guy’s shoulders every single play, and he’s done a good job.”

Against Temple on Saturday, Becht had a slower start compared to Week 1 with an illegal pass downfield and a bad miss on fourth-and-goal.

Despite the early miscues, Mouser continued to applaud Becht, including on his third-down pass to Zay Robinson, who Becht threaded the needle to in between five defenders.

“I think the throw that he made to Zay Robinson on the third down was probably the best throw I’ve ever seen that guy make,” Mouser said. “I think that guy’s playing with as much confidence as I’ve seen that guy play with.”

Tight end room

Throughout the offseason, tight end Gabe Burkle didn’t see the practice field as he recovered from a torn ACL suffered last November. After continuing to recover during Week 1, Burkle made his return against Temple in a limited role.

“Gabe has been on a pitch count this last week and it’s frustrating because I’ve been very vocal about how much I love Gabe and what he brings to our offense,” Mouser said. “He’s done a great job to prepare and (I’m) excited for his number to get called moving forward.”

Burkle didn’t record a reception against the Owls, but saw 20 snaps in a blocking role.

Another tight end who earned praise from Mouser was redshirt junior Finn Furmanek, who hasn’t seen much playing time early in his Penn State career. Under Mouser’s offense, Furmanek has been part of the tight end-heavy formation and play style.

“He’s one of those guys that no matter what you ask him, he loves Penn State,” Mouser said. “He’ll be a captain here for this place one day. Every job that we ask him to do, he does it at an elite level.”

While Furmanek hasn’t recorded a reception either, he was close to scoring a touchdown against Marshall, which was ultimately batted down.

“We’re going to get him in the end zone,” Mouser said. “We’ll find a way to because he deserves to, just from the sacrifice and what he brings to the tight end room.”

title: Community ofrenda, cultural night | Events to commemorate Hispanic Heritage Month at Penn State
author: Anisa Daniel-Oniko | The Daily Collegian
description:
National Hispanic Heritage Month, celebrated from Sept. 15 to Oct. 15 each year, is officially underway.

Penn State campuses across the commonwealth will further the annual tradition of holding events to celebrate Hispanic and Latino communities and honor their heritage and history. This year, the theme is "La unidad es nuestra fuerza," which translates to “Unity Is Our Strength."

Here are some of the scheduled events.

Wednesday, Sept. 16

Immigration: How the Past Shapes the Present

On Wednesday, sociologist Nancy Foner will deliver a talk sponsored by the Department of History and the Latina/o Studies Program.

Foner, who wrote a book named "Immigration: How the Past Shapes the Present," will discuss current policies, experiences and debates about immigration against the backdrop of America’s immigration history.

The event will run from 4 to 6 p.m. in Room 202 of the Susan Welch Liberal Arts Building.

Thursday, Sept. 17

Community Ofrenda at the Paul Robeson Cultural Center

The Paul Robeson Cultural Center has invited Penn State students to take part in a community ofrenda. This year, it will run from noon to 2 p.m. in room 21 of the HUB-Robeson Center.

Ofrendas are ceremonial altars traditionally dedicated to loved ones who have died, designed to honor and celebrate their memory.

Students can visit the ofrenda, leave a gratitude note or have a bite free food offered by local vendors. The completed ofrenda will be on display through Oct. 9.

Sunday, September 27

The Penn State Dolores Huerta Day of Service

Part 1: Honor Dolores Huerta: Harvest at the Student Farm

Huerta, a labor leader, civil rights activist and co-founder of the United Farm Workers, was known for her organizing work and her legendary cry of “¡Sí, se puede!,” or “Yes, we can!”

Part one of this event honors her legacy by encouraging students to give back to their community.

At the Dr. Keiko Miwa Ross Student Farm from 11 a.m. to 1 p.m, students will be able to volunteer and give back to the community by harvesting produce and flowers for St. Andrew’s Community Cafe.

Thursday, Oct. 1

Part 2: Serve the Community: St. Andrew’s Café

Since 2009, St. Andrew’s Community Café has offered free meals weekly, no questions asked.

In the second part of Dolores Huerta’s Day of Service, volunteers will aid in serving dinner at St. Andrew’s Episcopal Church from 5 to 7 p.m.

To volunteer or learn more about the event, reach out to Victoria Prewitt-Rodriguez at vjp111@psu.edu.

Saturday, Oct. 3

Children’s Day

Penn State student organizations will be at the Schlow Library Community Room from 10:30 a.m. to noon on Saturday, offering face painting, crafts and children’s games.

The event will also include traditional snacks and opportunities to learn fun facts about Hispanic and Latino/a communities.

Student organizations can contact jmb1040@psu.edu to sign up for the event.

Tuesday, Oct. 6

Café con Leche: Unity Across Difference: Let’s Talk About It!

The Latino Caucus, Paul Robeson Cultural Center and Center for Social Change and Belonging are offering an evening of complimentary coffee, conversation and confectionery.

From 5:45 to 7:30 p.m., guests can explore how different communities can come together while still honoring unique and diverse experiences and perspectives.

The event will take place in the Flex Theater at 134 HUB-Robeson Center.

Wednesday, Oct. 7

Trailblazers of Penn State: A Celebration of Hispanic Heritage Month

Penn State community members are invited to view a poster gallery led by the Eberly College of Science, the College of Health and Human Development and the College of Information Sciences and Technology.

The gallery aims to celebrate the voices and legacies of Penn State faculty, students and alumni who have contributed to the university and beyond.

The event is scheduled for 3:30 to 5 p.m. at the Westgate Building.

Friday, October 9

Fun Friday at the Paul Robeson Cultural Center

Free food, art, games and a space to hang out is available for students at Fun Friday.

Fun Friday is a PRCC tradition and focuses on fostering community care, a space for connection and celebration of culture.

The event will take place in Heritage Hall of the HUB-Robeson Center from noon to 3 p.m. No RSVP is needed and students can expect to meet new friends.

Hispanic Heritage Month Cultural Night

To conclude Hispanic Heritage Month, Cultural Night offers a night cultural celebration with free food and entertainment.

The night will feature a performance from the Caliente Dance Team, an organization focused on sharing Latino cultural heritage on campus.

Additionally, the event will host Eladio B. Bobadilla, an assistant professor in the Department of History at the University of Pittsburgh. Bobadilla studies immigration and social movements, including community organizing and cross-border activism.

The event runs from 6 to 8 p.m. at Heritage Hall. Seating at the event will be first-come, first-served.

title: No. 12 Penn State women’s volleyball to face Villanova
author: Gavin Leonard | The Daily Collegian
description:
After cruising past Ohio in a 3-0 win on Saturday, the Nittany Lions will host Villanova at Rec Hall for a ‘Keep It In PA’ game on Tuesday.

In a game where many of the white and blue’s best players played minimal sets, the Nittany Lions’ depth was shown to be valuable.

Whitney Lauenstein, Alexis Stucky and Kennedy Martin each played one set in the sweep of Ohio, which opened in more minutes to teammates. Eight players notched more than three kills on Saturday, with Caroline Jurevicius and Haley Burgdorf leading the team with six.

While kills were spread throughout the team, Danielle Whitmire stole the show in her own category, totaling 21 assists in two sets, as the freshman capitalized on her increased role on the court.

Defensively, the Nittany Lions played well both at the net and in the back row. Penn State’s blockers disrupted Ohio’s attacks with a .138 opponent hitting percentage, while keeping their attacks alive with 24 digs.

In their next matchup, Penn State will have a chance to replicate that defensive success against a respectable Villanova squad.

The Wildcats enter the contest with a .225 hitting percentage and a roster filled with multiple legitimate offensive weapons.

Junior middle blocker Campbell McKinnon headlines the group and has racked up 95 kills along with a .450 hitting percentage, as Villanova’s offensive firepower could pose a threat to Penn State’s defense.

However, in Villanova’s last match against a ranked opponent, the Wildcats had one of its worst performances of the season. Against then-No. 3 Arizona State, they committed 32 attack errors and a hitting percentage of -0.010.

While their performance wasn’t up to par, their schedule shows that the Wildcats are used to playing elite competition.

Not only are they accustomed to facing talented programs, but they’ve shown a knack to winning close matches, with three of Villanova’s five wins this season coming in five sets.

While the Wildcats have proved that they’re able to win tight contests, they’ve also displayed an inability to win key moments in their losses.

Against Iowa State, Villanova hit .273, which was nearly identical to the Cyclones’ .277, and both teams totaled eight blocks. The Cyclones still swept the Wildcats by winning the critical points and serving better, recording six aces to Villanova’s one, while also having four fewer errors.

The deciding factor will be whether the white and blue can force Villanova into the kind of offensive mistakes that Arizona State did, instead of playing down to their competition and assuming the Wildcats’ 5-3 record means they're an easy opponent.

Historically, Penn State has dominated the series, winning all 11 of their matches against Villanova all 15 matchups against the Wildcats in a history that goes back to 1985. The Nittany Lions last faced Villanova in 2015, earning a sweep, which marked four consecutive sweeps in the all-time series.

Now, the Nittany Lions will get a look at whether they can extend their regular-season win streak and remain unbeaten against Villanova when the two face off on Tuesday.

title: Nittany Lions in the NFL | TEs flourished, Saquon Barkley breaks first big run of 2026 season
author: Andrew Mercer | The Daily Collegian
description:
The 2026 NFL regular season is officially underway, and there were many Penn State lettermen who got off to a quick start.

Fans saw four former Penn State tight ends reach the end zone alongside a wide receiver that converted positions in the NFL, while contract negotiations continued to play out and Kaytron Allen made his regular season debut.

Here’s how the former Nittany Lions did in Week 1 of the 2026 NFL season.

Former Penn State tight ends

The alumni of “Tight End U” were on point throughout Week 1.

Mike Gesicki, Tyler Warren, Brenton Strange and Pat Freiermuth all scored touchdowns against their respective opponents. Former Penn State wide receiver and now-tight end Juwan Johnson found the end zone as well.

Gesicki scored his first touchdown of the season for the Cincinnati Bengals against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers. He received a short pass from Joe Burrow and fell into the end zone for a 2-yard touchdown before hitting his infamous “griddy” celebration.

Gesicki closed the game with 78 yards on five catches en route to a 33-27 win over Tampa Bay.

Warren, now in his second NFL season, utilized his 6-foot-6 frame against the Baltimore Ravens, turning a short pass on first-and-goal into a diving touchdown through traffic. Beyond that, however, Warren was quiet, ending the game with 13 yards on three receptions.

Strange scored a 14-yard touchdown in the second quarter as the Jacksonville Jaguars ran away with a win against the Cleveland Browns. Trevor Lawrence hit Strange in the middle of the end zone to give the Jaguars a 24-0 lead. He had two catches on three targets for 23 yards.

Johnson scored a 9-yard touchdown on his birthday, burning Detroit Lions linebacker Jack Campbell with an over-the-shoulder grab in the back of the end zone. He finished with 54 yards on three receptions.

Freiermuth put the Pittsburgh Steelers ahead of the Atlanta Falcons in the second quarter when Aaron Rogers found the former Nittany Lion in the back of the end zone for a 6-yard touchdown.

Jaquan Brisker and Joey Porter Jr.

Jaquan Brisker intercepted an overthrown pass by Atlanta quarterback Cooper Rush intended for former Penn Stater Jahan Dotson and returned it 10 yards in the second quarter, setting up Freiermuth’s eventual touchdown on the subsequent drive.

Brisker had a strong day overall with six total tackles, four solo tackles and one pass defended.

Joey Porter Jr. sat Week 1 out due to a back injury that kept him off the field for most of camp. The Steelers’ cornerback has been seeking a contract extension and talks haven’t resulted in a deal yet, adding a layer of complexity to the situation.

Parker Washington, wide receiver, Jacksonville Jaguars

A day after it was reported Parker Washington and the Jaguars are unlikely to agree to a contract extension, the former Penn State wide receiver made a statement in the first quarter against the Cleveland Browns.

Lawrence threw a leading pass from the 30-yard line, and Washington made a diving grab in the front corner of the end zone. It was the first touchdown by a former Nittany Lion this season and the first of the year for the Jacksonville Jaguars.

Washington finished the game with 83 yards on five receptions, aiding the Jaguars to a 34-10 victory over the Cleveland Browns.

Saquon Barkley, running back, Philadelphia Eagles

Saquon Barkley had a quiet outing in the Eagles’ season opener against the Washington Commanders with the exception of an explosive 42-yard rush in the second quarter. He bounced off contact and broke a series of tackles on his way inside the 15-yard line.

Other than that instance, Barkley struggled to get the ground game going and didn’t reach the end zone. He ended the game with 83 rushing yards on 15 carries, averaging 5.5 yards per carry by the final whistle.

Kaytron Allen, running back, Washington Commanders

Kaytron Allen made his NFL regular season debut against the Eagles with four carries in the second half.

Allen got his first carry at the end of the third quarter and earned five yards. The following three carries were on the Commanders’ last touchdown drive in the fourth quarter, featuring back-to-back 4-yard gains and a 3-yard gain to finish the game.

Allen ended Week 1 with 16 yards, averaging four yards per carry.

title: Sports Editors Weekly | Is No. 9 Penn State women’s volleyball back as contenders after 3 consecutive sweeps?
author: Collegian Sports Editors
description:
Editors' Note: Sports Editors Weekly is a dueling column written by Collegian Sports Editors Gianna Dowling and Myles Hannak. It aims to provide timely debate on Penn State sports performance and news each week.

For the first time since the 2024 National Championship season, the Nittany Lions have won their last nine sets.

Penn State highlighted its three-game winning streak with an upset over No. 4 Stanford at the Palestra, joining sweeps over Ohio and DePaul. With a perfect run of form ahead of the blue and white’s weekend back in Happy Valley for the Penn State Classic, the Nittany Lions have been impeccable after a down campaign last year.

Sitting at 6-1, with only five total sets dropped on the season, is Katie Schumacher-Cawley’s unit finally back on the national stage?

Gianna Dowling: Definitely back in the conversation

There were plenty of questions heading into the 2026 season for the Nittany Lions, especially since they caught a bad case of the championship hangover a season ago. However, as of late, it appears the blue and white are shaping up to be a strong contender this year.

There were a few hiccups at the start of Penn State’s campaign, including narrowly surviving an upset from High Point in the first weekend of play.

Two games later, the Nittany Lions lost their first match of the season to No. 3 Kentucky in four sets, but kept things close for the most part. Since this loss, the blue and white have been on a roll.

Throughout Penn State’s nine-set streak, its most impressive sweep was that against No. 4 Stanford, who already had two top-15 wins under its belt this season.

The Nittany Lions have shown that they have strong tools in the toolbox, especially when it comes to the strong swingers on the outside of the net. Right-side hitter Kennedy Martin and outside hitter Whitney Lauenstein each have over 70 kills this season. The duo combined for 25 kills in the win over the Cardinal.

This veteran pair isn’t the sole reason for Penn State’s success, as its young core has also proven to be lethal. Freshman outside hitter Haley Burgdorf recorded 10 kills against Stanford, marking the best performance of her young career. Additionally, freshman Finley Krystkowiak and sophomore Gabrielle Nichols have also recorded double-digit kill performances this season.

A fair mix of new and experienced talent is a key ingredient for being a championship contender.

Another reason the Nittany Lions can have a promising season is because their offense is led by veteran setter Alexis Stucky.

Stucky has done a great job of setting up her offense for success, including a season-high 37-assist outing in the blue and white’s win over DePaul, followed by a 36-assist performance against Stanford.

The Nittany Lions have one more nonconference weekend before heading into the ever-so-scary Big Ten slate, but if Penn State’s success continues, then there’s no reason to doubt what this year's squad is capable of.

Myles Hannak: Hold the horses

The Nittany Lions have no shortage of attacking star power, with most of their kill figures and hitting percentages signaling an incredibly efficient offense that can sustain a real push for glory.

Yet the blue and white still show they have a few gaps in their performances before the play reaches the caliber needed to become a juggernaut, most notably on the defensive side of the net. As it stands, Penn State averages 13.67 digs per set, a figure around the 150th in the category nationally and is tied with a 90th-best block-per-set figure, both not good enough to make a national push.

Those figures are worrying, and teams that have suffered to more adverse season starts have outperformed Penn State in both metrics, which tracks given the change of personnel and underclassmen taking on a role in defensive areas for the Nittany Lions.

Regarding blocks, three players notched over a block per set in Penn State’s historic 2024 season, yet only Ryla Jones has surpassed such a margin this year, as that defense has been the main Achilles' heel for the blue and white.

In the loss to Kentucky, Penn State had no match at the net, surrendering a hitting percentage that was over .100 points better than its own behind a leaky defense that also was outblocked by four by the Wildcats. High Point gave the blue and white a run for their money with a similar approach, using fine defensive margins to help neutralize the high-scoring Penn State attack. In both these close matches, the blue and white allowed more digs than their opponents, so there’s still a level of chemistry to be built.

Give it time, and let the errors iron out; this is a very new squad, after all, and the potential for greatness does shine through. As of now, it’s clear individual talent has propelled Penn State this far. It just needs a deeper level of cohesion to address the flaws and propel them to the next level — even though this remains only a possibility and not yet a certainty.

title: Off the Record | How to practice safe sex
author: Miss Behave I The Daily Collegian
description:
Editor’s Note: Off the record is a weekly column written by a fourth-year Collegian staffer writing under an alias. It aims to promote a space for honest conversations about love, sex and relationships. Those interested in sharing their experiences or submitting a topic are invited to do so through this anonymous form.

It’s important for anyone in college, sexually active or not, to prioritize their health and know how to practice safe intercourse. Risks may be overlooked, but with knowledge of possible implications and cautionary measures, it’s easy to implement practices to protect your body.

What’s an STI?

An STI is a sexually transmitted infection that can be transferred through vaginal, anal and oral sex. An STI can later develop into an STD, a sexually transmitted disease, if not treated properly. It’s important to prevent the initial infection to reduce long-term effects.

Students can get tested at University Health Services. You may receive testing for numerous reasons: if you have symptoms of an STI, you’ve been exposed or if you’re unsure what tests you may need. Testing may come in the form of oral and rectal testing and could involve collecting a urine sample; throat, cervical, vaginal, or rectal swabs and blood work.

Common STIs include gonorrhea and chlamydia, which are curable. Herpes and human papillomavirus (HPV) are treatable but not curable.

It’s possible to contract an STI with little to no symptoms, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. For this reason, it’s recommended to get tested for STIs if you’re having sex in order to stay proactive and catch potential infections early.

STI prevention

Abstaining from sex is the only way to prevent STIs entirely. However, there are a number of ways to reduce the risk.

If you are in a monogamous relationship and both you and your partner have tested negative for STIs, it’s safe to assume you won’t contract one.

Limiting one’s number of sexual partners can also help prevent contracting an STI, and it’s important to talk to your partners about their health history. It’s an awkward conversation, but necessary nonetheless.

An important practice when engaging in sexual intercourse is utilizing a condom, correctly and consistently. Not only does it prevent your risk of contracting an STI, but it also lowers your chance of becoming pregnant.

Gynecology care

Regardless of the circumstances, women need to take their gynecology care seriously.

Urinary tract infections (UTIs) are common among women and are treated with prescription antibiotics from a healthcare provider. Urinating after sexual activity, hydrating and keeping up with hygiene can help prevent UTIs, according to the CDC.

Vaginal yeast infections and thrush in the mouth and throat are fungal infections that may cause itchiness and soreness. Pain and discomfort should never be ignored when it comes to your health and body.

You don’t have to have sex to get a UTI or yeast infection, but you are at higher risk of contracting one or developing worse symptoms when you engage in sexual activities.

For sexual health, addressing issues early is essential to prevent the need for prolonged treatment.

Birth control

In order to prevent pregnancy, there are a number of ways both partners can be proactive.

There are various types of birth control methods that men and women can utilize to ensure all parties are safe.

Oral contraceptive pills and reversible contraceptives such as intrauterine devices (IUDs) or Nexplanon allow women to engage in sex without fear of pregnancy. Male birth control options are limited, but condoms, vasectomies and abstinence limit pregnancy risk.

No birth control is 100% effective, regardless of what you were taught in school.

If proactive measures are not taken, emergency contraception is an option. Plan B can be found over-the-counter in drug stores, including Target, CVS and Walmart.

Plan B must be ingested up to 72 hours after intercourse, but the sooner it is taken, the more effective it is likely to be. Plan B is a last resort, and proper preparation should be prioritized.

While it can be easy to overlook the importance of sexual health and precautions, it’s just as easy to stay informed. There are ample resources to get tested for STIs and purchase contraceptives. Staying on top of your health is one of the best things you can do to support yourself long-term.

title: Protesters gather in opposition of ICE activity in State College
author: Jacob Godshall I The Daily Collegian
description:
A group of protesters gathered at Old Main on Monday night to protest Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) activity in State College, on campus and at the State College Regional Airport. Protesters called for the university’s administration to cease cooperation with ICE officials.

The event was organized by the Student Committee for Defense and Solidarity (SCDS) and the People’s Defense Front. Members of the People’s Defense Front and SCDS arrived at the steps of Old Main toting signs and banners with slogans like, “ICE and Klan go hand-in-hand” and “Shut down Moshannon.”

Besides members of the People’s Defense Front and SCDS, a group of students and State College residents gathered to watch or join in.

“I think ICE has been doing horrible things to this community and to this country,” Curtis Johnson, 19, of Allentown, Pennsylvania, said. “And so I wanted to show my solidarity with the people here.”

Johnson says that similar protests have taken place in his home county, and that there were “a lot of movements,” protesting police and local government involvement with ICE officials.

Johnson also said that he doesn’t want his taxes going towards ICE.

“Ideally, the money I pay to this state, to this university, to my local government and to my state governments are not going to go to an organization killing U.S. citizens and also illegally deporting people,” Johnson said.

After spending a while protesting on the steps of Old Main, the group unravelled their banners, raised their signs and marched through campus, along Pollock Road and into the HUB-Robeson Center.

The group stood inside the HUB for several minutes, continuing their chanting as students watched on, some cheering along with the protest. After a few minutes the group walked out the door facing the HUB’s lawn, and marched back to Old Main.

Behailu Streit, 35, of State College, followed the group and observed throughout their protest.

“The topic has been pretty contentious in my opinion for especially recently over the last couple years. I know that regulation needs to be incorporated when it comes to new citizens, and obviously there needs to be more dialogue with how that should be,” Streit said. “That's why students are here voicing their opinion with this area specifically.”

Streit said he has read about several incidents involving ICE, and while he has never witnessed anything himself, he believes regulation needs to be put in place. Streit said that regulations should specifically include “keeping families together,” if there are children involved.

Giancarlo Torres, 19, of Souderton, Pennsylvania, said that the university should be doing a better job creating a safe environment for its students.

“I think Penn State, as a school, as a university, as an institution, should feel safe. As a student, you should feel safe, as a worker, you should feel safe,” Torres said. “Anybody who's on Penn State campus should not be in fear of persecution. You should be here to either learn or work.”

title: Students show how they’re using artificial intelligence at second annual AI showcase
author: Jonathon Chiu | The Daily Collegian
description:
Dozens of students filled the sixth floor of the Eric J. Barron Innovation Hub on Monday as part of the Nittany AI Alliance’s second annual AI showcase to highlight to representatives of at least 17 corporations how they are utilizing artificial intelligence as part of various projects.

A total of 41 projects were displayed by students belonging to the College of Information Science and Technology (IST), Smeal College of Business, College of Engineering and other colleges. Some projects focused on how AI can be used to assist with post-stroke brain imaging, help college advisors better help students with course planning, provide possible diagnoses to medical symptoms and recommend the correct care option and even find the most ideal location to build a data center.

Andy Gatto, Nittany AI Alliance’s innovation ecosystem and partnership strategist, said the first AI showcase, held in September 2025, was in response to the expression of struggles by Penn State’s industry partners to find students adept at using AI.

“A lot of companies were starting to see that it's really hard to do that at traditional career fairs,” Gatto, 46, of State College, Pennsylvania, said. “We opened up the filter really wide and just allowed students who'd done any sort of applied AI project to submit posters and have an opportunity to market themselves as people who have practical AI skills that companies would be interested in.”

Along with taking suggestions from participants on how to improve future showcases, Gatto said he hopes the event will inspire other students, regardless of major, to pursue their own AI projects.

He said he felt there were “almost no excuses” left for students to not at least attempt to see how artificial intelligence can be used to solve problems they care about, especially with the recent increase in AI resources available from the launch of AI Studio.

“With tools that are available now, it's not just engineering or comp sci or developers. You don't have to be a coder to build something real with AI,” Gatto said. “It doesn't take long to learn these tools and build something real, to be able to put a poster together, be in the showcase and demonstrate to these employers what AI skills you have.”

For Adim Ogbolu, 21, of Stroudsburg, Pennsylvania, the showcase was an opportunity to present his project of using physical neural circuits to control robots and other autonomous systems, which he began last year.

He said the findings from his research — which he already has tested by using his neural circuits to train two robots to avoid light sources and obstacles, respectively — will help to highlight how AI can be applied to hardware able to advance the capabilities of machine and deep learning.

“It's like a rabbit hole,” Ogbolu, a fourth-year studying electrical engineering, said. “Essentially, you’re trying to recreate a brain and you'd be surprised at the things you can learn doing that.”

With his current goal being to ultimately be able to control a drone using his neural circuits, Ogbolu said he also hopes to upgrade them so their modular nature can be utilized in new ways.

“These neurons all have weights in them that you can tune for their synaptic outputs but currently right now they're fixed. They can't vary,” Ogbolu said. “I've already experimented with versions that can vary outputs. Now it's just a matter of characterizing it and really getting it to work.”

Also among the projects being presented was Andy Salvo’s company Raptor, which seeks to use AI to create bespoke software that helps streamline a business’ operations.

Salvo, 20, of Little Silver, New Jersey, said he founded Raptor four weeks prior to the showcase and hopes it can be used to help more business owners adapt to the age of AI while ensuring that their data remains within their systems.

The issue of data retention was important for Salvo as he believes this issue will only become more pressing as more instances arise of artificial intelligence being trained using data that was scraped without knowledge or consent.

Despite this, Salvo said he still views human innovation as the key to continuing to see AI advance to both become more powerful and more applicable to whatever industry it’s used in.

“When you branch off of all of these and take a look at each project individually, you can see different lenses of thinking and looking at the day as a whole, it's just a bunch of innovation that's going on and it's fascinating to see,” Salvo, a second-year studying corporate innovation and entrepreneurship, said.

Brandon Deutsch, who attended the showcase as part of a team of representatives from Lutron Electronics, said even though this was the first AI showcase he has ever attended, he found many of the projects — such as Raptor — to be “interesting” demonstrations of how AI can be used to solve problems.

Deutsch, 23, of Allentown, Pennsylvania, said he was excited to come back to future showcases to see how students come up with different ways to implement AI as the technology continues to evolve.

“We always come to the career fair events on the IST career affairs, the Penn State career affairs, and we were trying to look at some more smaller opportunities to really see what we're doing here in Penn State,” Deutsch said. “We're hoping that with some of these use cases, we can potentially find ways that we can use AI more because it's new territory for everybody and making sure that you understand what AI is doing and what it's capable of is pretty huge in today's world.”

title: Penn State student dead after motorcycle crash
author: Grace Levy | News Editor
description:
A Penn State student has died after a motorcycle crash on Friday, according to a statement from Ferguson Township police.

The crash occurred at approximately 8:46 p.m. at the intersection of Blue Course Drive and Westerly Parkway involving a Hyundai Elantra and a motorcycle, the statement said.

The police department’s preliminary investigation found that Rashid Alnuwaymi was stopped around the 1200 block of Blue Course Drive, heading northbound, and was struck from behind by the Hyundai also traveling northbound.

The driver of the motorcycle was identified as a 20-year-old undergraduate student. He was flown by a medical helicopter from the scene to UPMC Williamsport, where he was pronounced neurologically deceased after life-saving efforts.

"We are deeply saddened by the tragic accident of Rashid Alnuwaymi, a third-semester student studying engineering at Penn State, and extend our heartfelt thoughts to his family and friends during this unthinkable time," a Penn State spokesperson said in a statement.

The cause of the crash is still under investigation, according to the Ferguson Township Police Department. Anyone with information should contact the police department at 1-800-479-0050 or via email at police@twp.ferguson.pa.us.

title: Penn State women's gymnastics adds 2 staff members
author: Myles Hannak | The Daily Collegian
description:
Jennifer Green has made her first additions as head coach of the program.

After the program hired the new boss earlier this summer, Green has finally added her support staff for her debut season in Happy Valley. The team announced Sharon Kelley as an associate head coach and Tim Levandowski as an assistant coach for the inaugural staff next season.

Kelly spent the previous season as Green's associate head coach at Air Force, where the tandem posted one of the most bountiful seasons in program history. Prior to her time officially on staff, Kelly was a consulting coach for Air Force and has spent decades in the sport in various roles before her coaching career.

Levandowski completes the staff, with no prior shared teams with either of the pair, and arrives after serving at Kent State and Brown. The new assistant coach aided the Golden Flashes in a historic 2025 campaign in which they won the MAC Conference Championship and posted an undefeated regular season.

title: Penn State men's lacrosse earns commitment from 4-star goaltender Hayden Myslinski
author: Elliott Inscho | The Daily Collegian
description:
Jeff Tambroni has secured the first piece of his 2028 recruiting class.

Hayden Myslinski, a four-star goaltender out of Trinity-Pawling School in New York, took to Instagram to announce his commitment to Penn State on Sunday.

The 5-foot-10, 185-pound netminder was ranked No. 4 at his position and as the No. 57 overall prospect in his class, according to Inside Lacrosse. On the club circuit, Myslinski played for SweetLax Upstate.

In the outlet’s evaluation of Myslinski, Inside Lacrosse noted that his patience and leadership in the crease stood out as defining characteristics, while he also possesses strong punch speed and rebound control.

Myslinski is the only goaltender currently committed to Penn State, as Tambroni’s nine-player 2027 class is yet to add one. That group is, however, headlined by midfielder Ayden Matthews, a five-star New Jersey native that’s currently ranked as the No. 5 overall recruit in his class.

title: Rothrock Coffee brings unique drinks to State College
author: Talia Rittenhouse | The Daily Collegian
description:
Right in the driving route of Penn State students at 1736 S. Atherton Street is Rothrock Coffee.

You can purchase different flavors of lattes, cappuccinos, matchas, pastries and dishes for breakfast or a quick study snack. The menu has many items to choose from, so there’s surely a pick for you at Rothrock.

It’s the perfect place to lock in on your procrastinated work after the excitement of the first few weeks back at school, with a row of tables to sit at and a great playlist always sounding out throughout the café.

If you need some caffeine to get through your day, or even just a fun drink to make your days a bit lighter, come with your friends and try out some of their drinks.

StrawB Milk and Honey Latte

If you love strawberries or have tried a strawberry latte at another cafe, this one’s perfect for you. The strawberry flavor allows for a more subtle coffee taste, so if you love fruit flavors, but aren’t sure if you like coffee yet, this one may be worth a shot.

With their strawberry milk, you get a beautiful ombre of pink and deep brown espresso in a cup; you may not even want to stir it and mess with the coloring — but it’s worth the sacrifice. It has the sweetness of the strawberry mixed with the honey and any milk of your choosing, topped with espresso.

This latte brings me a nostalgic feeling, reminding me of drinking strawberry milk as a child, but with a more mature taste, as it’s mixed with the coffee we need to get through the long days of class.

Rating: 9/10

Peaches n Cream Toast

This one is a great dish to have if you missed breakfast and want a sweet yet filling treat when getting in your study hours.

The “Peaches n Cream Toast” has an airy, crunchy piece of toast, with smooth sweet cream layered on top. There’s a layer of crunchy granola mixed with almonds and many sweet, juicy peach slices. And to top it all off: a layer of cinnamon.

For me, I think there were a lot of flavors in the mix. But each ingredient was delicious, and they created a very fall-flavored meal nonetheless.

Rating: 7/10

Iced Mango Latte

As someone who loves coffees with fruit flavors, I was interested in this latte when seeing it on the menu.

The “Iced Mango Latte” is one of Rothrock’s summer seasonal items, alongside the “StrawB Milk and Honey latte,” the raspberry matcha and the “Cococano.”

After having a few sips of the mango iced latte, I realized that the flavor combination may not be my favorite, due to the mix of espresso and mango.

However, if you enjoy unique flavors, this one is worth a try, or maybe as a matcha if they make the accommodation. It’s definitely an acquired taste.

Rating: 2/10

Affogato

Vanilla ice cream and espresso — what’s not to like?

If dessert is your favorite meal of the day, getting a little scoop of ice cream with espresso poured on top might just do the trick. If you’re having a bad day, you can get a quick serotonin boost with some affogato.

The sweet, creamy, rich ice cream is a delicious combination with espresso, providing the taste of almost everyone’s favorite caffeinated beverage and summer night treat.

I haven’t seen many cafes selling affogato (I usually see them at restaurants), so this was a pleasant surprise. To make it even better, you can get it to go. Nothing says summer more than the windows of your car rolled down and an affogato in your hand, right?

Rating: 9/10

title: Ending a friendship? Here’s how to cope.
author: Alli Satterfield | The Daily Collegian
description:
The media gives us plenty of examples of how to handle ourselves when faced with the end of a romantic relationship. When you’re left heartbroken from a failed love, you know you can deface your ex’s car like Carrie Underwood or sample an entire chocolate box like Elle Woods. Yet we haven’t been socialized to handle friendship breakups in the same way.

How should we act when we know an important friend won’t be in our lives anymore? Here are my suggestions for handling the breakup and its aftermath.

Have open, healthy communication

When dealing with the end of a friendship — or any type of conflict or disagreement, really — it’s important to keep communication open and healthy. Giving the other person space to air their grievances and work through any issues the two of you might have lingering could be the deciding factor in saving a friendship.

Be amicable in interactions, even if you’re upset with the person you’re talking to. Try to keep an open mind about what they’re conveying to you. It’s important to give your friend space to speak when working out issues.

Keep in mind, though, that healthy communication means different things to different people. Somewhat universally, though, avoiding interrupting the person you're speaking to, raising your voice and being rude — even when you’re upset — can keep communication healthy. Or, at least, healthier.

Take accountability

In line with giving someone space to speak, give them the freedom to share their grievances with you. It’s important to take accountability for how your behavior impacted them. There can be large spaces between what we intend to do and how we actually impact people.

As such, when trying to remedy relationships, recognizing the gap between intention and impact can be crucial. Explaining your intent and apologizing for the way you impacted your friend can make them feel seen and make you seem less malicious, both of which can help save your friendship.

One time, in a tiff with my father, I felt that he had taken my words and the situation out of context, since he felt I had disparaged him personally in our argument. Even though I didn’t call him stupid, as he felt I did, I had obviously made him feel that way. So, I apologized for that effect on him, even though it was never my intention.

Surround yourself with people who want to be around you, too

If all hope is lost and you’re smack-dab in the middle of a friendship breakup, there are always ways to cope. If you’re dealing with the realization that one of your friends doesn’t want to be around you anymore, it’s understandable that you may feel unwanted.

One quick way to cope with that feeling is to remind yourself that others do want you and enjoy your company. Surrounding yourself with people who want to be in your life can serve as a great reminder that your entire life doesn’t hinge on one single relationship, but rather a collection of people who truly appreciate you.

Get your favorite treats

You can always try to eat your feelings away.

Well, actually, that may not be the healthiest thing to do. But getting yourself a treat or a small pick-me-up from one of your favorite restaurants can give you a quick dopamine hit and steer your day in a better direction.

Be open, stay social

The biggest piece of advice I can give you when going through a friendship breakup is to stay open to being social. The loss of one social connection doesn’t mean you should sacrifice your entire network.

Go out with your friends, go to a club meeting or do your homework in a public space to make new connections, and you should keep an open heart and mind so that new people and places can fill the gaps.

Stay busy

It’s important not to sit around and wallow. There’s of course a buffer period where lying in your bed with your comfort food of choice is completely acceptable.

However, burying yourself in your grief for a long period of time will only make you feel it more deeply. At some point, you have to get up and move past it, even if that can be a long process.

A quick way to jumpstart that process can be picking up a new hobby, going to the gym or, even, getting up and showering. Little actions for yourself can go a long way.

title: Big Ten roundup | Power conference losses headline Week 2
author: Andrew Deal | The Daily Collegian
description:
The Big Ten had a much more daunting schedule conference wide in Week 2 compared to the opening slate, with multiple ranked and Power Four matchups on hand.

The conference finished with an 11-6 record over the weekend, with all six losses coming against other major conference opponents.

Here’s what headlined Week 2 in the Big Ten.

Top 10 teams go down

While Indiana handled business against Howard, the other two highly ranked teams in the conference had other results.

Then-No. 6 Oregon traveled to Oklahoma State, and the newly put together Cowboys seemingly figured it all out against the Ducks, defeating them 38-31,

Oklahoma State competed with Oregon as if it hadn’t lost to Tulsa a week prior, putting together one of the best games in the Week 2 slate. Oregon put up 31 points, but Dante Moore had an underwhelming showing, going just 14-for-29 for 191 yards and two touchdowns. The projected first-round pick was outdueled by Oklahoma State quarterback Drew Mestemaker.

Moore and the offense had a chance to tie the game with 3:11 left, but a fumble from running back Dierre Hill Jr. ended any chance of escaping Stillwater with a victory.

Six hours later and about six hours south, No. 1 Ohio State took on No. 4 Texas in what was hyped up to be one of the games of the year. While Ohio State went out to an early lead, and a big one at that, Texas didn’t go away easy.

Leading 20-3 at the half and 23-3 at the end of the third quarter, the Buckeyes were looking like they were going to run away with the win and solidify themselves as the top team in the country. But Texas quarterback Arch Manning had other plans, leading consecutive scoring drives.

Ohio State had a chance to put the game away, but kicker Connor Hawkins missed a 45-yard attempt wide left, giving Texas the chance to take the lead with a touchdown.

Manning and the Longhorns, with all the momentum on their side, went 12 plays for 73 yards with running back Hollywood Smothers capping off the drive with a rushing touchdown, giving Texas its first lead of the game.

Julian Sayin’s chance to lead a winning drive ended quickly, throwing an interception with 17 seconds remaining. The Buckeyes dropped to No. 6 in the AP Poll after the loss.

Power Four woes

Big Ten teams didn’t perform well against power conference teams in Week 2.

Michigan moved to 2-0 on the season with an upset victory over then-No.11 Oklahoma in a low-scoring 17-10 win that wasn’t all pretty.

Outside of that, the losses racked up in those types of games. Wake Forest and Purdue went down to the wire, needing double overtime, with a failed two-point conversion being the only difference.

Wake Forest quarterback Gio Lopez ran it in from three yards out, and then completed the 2-point conversion with a run, as well, giving the Demon Deacons the 38-36 victory.

Minnesota couldn’t handle dynamic Mississippi State quarterback Kamario Taylor, who passed for 227 yards and three touchdowns with another 86 yards on the ground en route to a 38-13 domination over the Golden Gophers.

Despite 271 yards and three touchdowns from Illinois quarterback Katin Houser, it wasn’t enough to keep up with Duke’s offense. The Fighting Illini fell to the Blue Devils, 31-27, after a quiet fourth quarter that featured only a field goal from Duke.

Night time meetings

The conference was featured in two other major prime time games, with Boston College and Rutgers meeting on Friday night, and Iowa and Iowa State facing off under the lights of Kinnick Stadium on Saturday.

Rutgers attempted to get back on the right foot following an upset loss to UMass in Week 1., but Boston College had other plans after getting out to an early double-digit lead.

Despite a late comeback attempt led by the Scarlet Knights’ stars — wide receiver KJ Duff and running back Antwan Raymond — the deficit was too much and Rutgers dropped to 0-2 with a 28-21 loss on Friday night.

The next night, the Big Ten found success with the annual Cy-Hawk game. The Hawkeyes found their starting quarterback in Hank Brown, and while he didn’t put out any standout numbers, he also took care of the football.

Trailing 13-10 entering the fourth quarter, special teams played a big part in the come-from-behind win. Iowa kicker Caden Buhr capitalized on a game-tying field goal from 32 yards out. Buhr had the chance to end the game with 15 seconds left, hitting a 42-yard field goal to send the Hawkeye faithful home happy.

title: Stock up, stock down | Benjamin Brahmer scores, Carson Hansen’s struggles continue
author: Noah Aberegg | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State’s Week 2 contest is in the past after pushing through a slow start to beat Temple 27-9.

The Nittany Lions had several positive trends carry over from the season opener, but also showcased several weaknesses throughout the contest.

Here’s a look at who’s trending up and who’s struggling after two weeks of action.

Stock up: Benjamin Brahmer

Tight end Benjamin Brahmer has continued to showcase his connection with Rocco Becht, bringing his touchdown tally to three on the season.

After finding the end zone once against Marshall, Brahmer scored in the second and fourth quarters against Temple, leading the team in receiving yards, touchdowns and tying wide receiver Chase Sowell for the most catches.

With 18 seconds left in the first half, Brahmer was crucial in giving Penn State some needed momentum. Becht found Brahmer for a short, 9-yard pass, before connecting with him again for a 23-yard touchdown strike before the half.

“I think we just caught them on their toes and got past them,” Brahmer said.

After dropping what could’ve been a touchdown in the third quarter, he returned for yet again another score to cap off Penn State’s 19 points, reeling in another 23-yard pass from Becht.

Stock down: Carson Hansen

Running back Carson Hansen’s Penn State debut was underwhelming against Marshall, averaging 4.4 yards per carry.

Going into practice this week, Hansen discussed several aspects of his game he was looking to improve, including making better reads and being decisive with his action. Against Temple, however, those areas didn’t appear to have much change, as he averaged 4.4 yards per rush yet again.

Hansen was fed the ball 19 times against the Owls — a significant increase from his 11 rushes the previous week — but recorded just 84 yards and failed to find the end zone for the second week in a row.

“I don’t know (what went wrong),” Hansen said. “I would just say myself. I just need to be a little better with the little details.”

Stock up: Zay Robinson

Penn State’s receiving corps has mainly featured more veteran players, including Sowell, Brett Eskildsen and Brahmer. However, redshirt freshman Zay Robinson has gotten his fair share of playing time the last two weeks.

Robinson found the end zone on his sole reception in Week 1 before returning for three more catches against Temple.

The former Iowa State receiver recorded 34 yards on the day, including a game-long 22-yard reception.

Robinson made the highlight reel when Becht found him surrounded by five defenders, zipping the ball in for one of his three catches.

In addition to his receiving success, Robinson has served as the team’s primary kick and punt returner. He has averaged 12.6 yards per punt return and put his agility and footwork on display with multiple spins and cuts for more yardage against Temple.

Stock down: Run defense

While Penn State held Temple to just nine points, it gave up several big yardage plays on the ground.

Former Nittany Lion and Owls quarterback Jaxon Smolik rushed for 71 yards, averaging 10.1 yards per carry. Smolik’s ability to scramble left the defense chasing after him, allowing him to earn a game-best 41-yard rush.

“We had a lot of pursuit and guys flying around, but I think he was poised,” Tony Rojas said. “He made the big plays that he needed, and I think that’s where all the rushing yards came from.

Running back Keveun Mason added another 76 yards, while quarterback Ajani Sheppard found the end zone with his legs for Temple’s only touchdown.

Stock up: Tony Rojas

After tearing his ACL amidst what was shaping up to be a breakout season last year, many were unsure of what form Tony Rojas would return to in his redshirt junior year.

Through two games, Rojas has proved to be one of the most dominant players on Penn State’s defense. He’s tallied 14 tackles, two tackles for loss and a sack so far this year.

However, one of his biggest moments came against Temple on Saturday, when Rojas intercepted Smolik on the Temple 18-yard line, returning the ball to the 5-yard line.

“Obviously, I haven’t gotten a pick in a while, so just getting that feeling good again,” Rojas said.

title: Week 2 report card | Offense takes time, defense keeps steady in Penn State’s win over Temple
author: Andrew Mercer | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State improved to 2-0 on the season on Saturday by defeating Temple, 27-9, at Lincoln Financial Field in Philadelphia.

The Nittany Lions didn't dominate the game in the same way as when they played Marshall, but they still got the job done on the road.

Here’s the grades I’d give Penn State’s offensive and defensive units after beating Temple.

Overall grade: B+

Coaching staff: A-

Matt Campbell preached handling adversity all offseason long, and that was put on display at the Linc. Although Temple kept the game closer than many would’ve expected, the Nittany Lions never seemed to lose their heads.

However, there were some head-scratching playcall decisions early in the game, such as running the ball up the gut three-consecutive times in the red zone. The Owls saw it coming, forcing fourth down, which Penn State went for on the 2-yard line and failed to deliver.

Offense: B

Early game woes saw the Nittany Lions scoreless until a field goal with 6:51 remaining in the second quarter, but that problem quickly went away in the “middle eight.” While Becht’s passing game rekindled its flame after the slow start, the running backs once again didn’t produce a spark.

Quarterbacks: A-

Becht had another quality performance, going 21-27 with 268 passing yards and three touchdowns. Becht has still yet to turn the ball over, and he threaded a tight needle on some of his passes.

Alex Manske entered the game late in the fourth quarter, but didn't attempt a pass. He had one rush for five yards.

Passing game: A-

Penn State found most of its offensive success through the air. From the first play of the game — a 56-yard completion to Koby Howard — to all three of Becht’s touchdown passes, the Nittany Lion receiving options are shaping up well.

The Nittany Lions’ receiving production was also once again balanced. Benjamin Brahmer was the top pass catcher with 79 yards and a pair of touchdowns. Chase Sowell scored the other touchdown on a screen pass.

However, Penn State had other opportunities to score, as Becht missed Andrew Rappleyea on fourth-and-goal in the first quarter, Sowell wasn’t able to bring in a deep ball in the end zone and Brahmer dropped a would-be touchdown reception.

Run game: C

Instead of using the advertised four-running back system, Carson Hansen was the clear first string followed by James Peoples for the second straight game. Neither has yet to find the end zone, but it wasn’t for a lack of trying, as Penn State was determined to get the room moving.

Hansen averaged just 4.4 yards per carry on 19 attempts, struggling to break tackles and stay on his feet, leading to many rushes failing immediately after first contact. Peoples’ six yards per carry were more efficient, but his consistency wavered.

Offensive line: B

Becht sometimes felt the heat in the early game, and he was sacked in the first quarter, but he adjusted to making short passes. However, the difficulties in the ground game often stemmed from a lack of clear openings.

Defense: A-

Penn State held Temple to just a field goal until Sheppard’s fourth-quarter touchdown. However, a lackluster pass rush and many missed tackles will give the Nittany Lions a lot to think about ahead of facing Buffalo.

Pass rush: B

Penn State wasn’t able to contain Jaxon Smolik’s dual-threat playstyle and let Sheppard run into the end zone, too. Smolik was easily Temple’s most efficient ball carrier, ending the game with 71 rushing yards and averaging an incredible 10.1 yards per carry.

Yvan Kemajou was the only Penn State player to record a sack Saturday and Ike Ezeogu was the only other player with a quarterback hurry, as Smolik routinely picked up on schemes for big gains.

While Smolik’s scrambling was successful, the same couldn’t have been said about Temple’s passing game, with tight end Peter Clarke’s 31 receiving yards leading the Owls.

Defensive backfield: A

Cornerbacks Zion Tracy and Audavion Collins were effective at eliminating Temple’s passing game with a combined three pass breakups. Collins was key in the third quarter with a touchdown-saving tackle on Keveun Mason’s 22-yard carry and a breakup on third down.

Clarke’s 15-yard reception was the Owls’ longest, and Temple only had three completions over 10 yards.

Linebackers: B+

Tony Rojas caught his first interception of the season in the first quarter and took it 13 yards to Temple’s 5-yard line. He led the Nittany Lions with seven tackles, while Cael Brezina also put in a solid day, making six tackles.

However, the first half was littered with missed tackles, and that’s an area that must be cleaned up if Penn State’s defense wants to keep Big Ten opponents off the board.

Special teams: A-

Ryan Barker’s lone miss on his first of three field goal attempts was the only smudge on an otherwise brilliant special teams performance by the Nittany Lions.

Barker converted on all of his following kicks, Nathan Tiyce’s singular punt was downed inside the 5-yard line and Daryus Dixson even blocked a field goal attempt.

title: Penn State field hockey’s second-half push falls short in 2-1 loss to No. 4 Princeton, stops streak
author: Owen Lomotan I The Daily Collegian
description:
Following Penn state field hockey’s third straight win against the Delaware Blue Hens last Sunday, the Nittany Lions had a chance to continue their success against the No. 4 Princeton Tigers at home Sunday for their annual Youth Day game.

The blue and white may’ve come in as the underdogs on paper, but coach Hannah Prince’s group fought hard until the end.

After a game that was full of whistle blows and physical play, the Nittany Lions came up short in a narrow 2-1 loss.

However, the final score didn’t tell the full story of the blue and white’s performance. After Princeton built a 2-0 lead in the second quarter, Penn State responded with a more aggressive second-half effort that brought them within one score of the nationally ranked Tigers.

The comeback, while not fully completed, highlighted Penn State’s ability to respond to adversity, especially through its late penalty corner opportunities and tight defensive pressure.

Although the Nittany Lions were unable to find the equalizing goal, their second-half push kept the game competitive until the final whistle.

After a slow first half for both the blue and white and the Tigers, Princeton’s offense began to find its rhythm in the second quarter, as junior forward Pru Lindsey scored twice to give the black and orange a 2-0 lead. Penn State junior goalkeeper Aby Deverka helped keep the deficit manageable, making a double-save with just under 50 seconds remaining before halftime.

Deverka’s performance came shortly after she was named the NFHCA Defensive Player of the Week, an honor recognizing her defensive contributions during Penn State’s recent stretch of games.

Despite trailing by two, the Nittany Lions entered the break with an opportunity to find a way back into the game, signaling Prince’s fight-until-the-end mentality.

Penn State responded early in the third quarter. With 13:16 remaining, junior forward Ella Gaitan converted a penalty corner to cut Princeton’s lead to 2-1. The goal gave the blue and white an immediate spark and seemed to shift the momentum towards the Nittany Lions, who began to create additional opportunities.

Penn State’s penalty corners became an important part of their late-game push to force overtime. After Gaitan’s goal, the Nittany Lions earned additional chances to score, including attempts by freshman forward Chloe D’Hage and Gaitan. Neither resulted in a second goal, but those opportunities demonstrated Penn State’s continued pressure against one of the nation’s top teams.

The intensity increased in the fourth quarter, with both teams battling through a more physical stretch. Penn State continued searching for their second goal, earning two more penalty corner chances with 1:22 and 41 seconds remaining in regulation. Gaitan took the resulting shots on goal, but neither found the back of the net, allowing Princeton to keep its one-score advantage.

The defensive effort was just as important to Penn State’s comeback as its offensive pressure. Deverka’s early save on Princeton’s penalty corner and her double save before halftime prevented the Tigers from extending their advantage even further. Those key stops gave the blue and white an opportunity to enter the third quarter within striking distance of making the game close again.

Penn State’s ability to generate late penalty corners has been a factor all season long and was showcased against the Tigers more so than ever. The Nittany Lions continued to fight for possession and search for openings in the defense even as whistles started to blow.

Even though Penn State’s efforts came up short against the black and orange, the Nittany Lions’ ability to draw fouls in the circle became crucial for their wins against Delaware, Villanova and Lock Haven.

The Nittany Lions will now get an opportunity to regroup and prepare for their first Big Ten conference matchup of the season against the Maryland Terrapins on Thursday, at 5 p.m. in Happy Valley.

title: Penn State defeats Minnesota in a back and forth battle, earns first Big Ten win
author: Ava Aguiar | The Daily Collegian
description:
After suffering a loss against Ohio State in their first conference matchup, the Nittany Lions sought redemption against Minnesota this Sunday on a sunny afternoon at Jeffrey Field. Coming ready to fight, Penn State won the match in a 1-0 win after a back-and-forth battle.

The Golden Gophers came into the game with a 5-1-1 record against Penn State’s 2-2-2, giving the blue and white a chance to establish themselves early in the conference and reset after their loss earlier this week.

First Half

A slow-rolling start for the Nittany Lions saw a back-and-forth game between the two teams. An early shot was taken by forward Nicole Crane but just missed.

Penn State saw back-to-back fouls on Lilly Burger and Nicole Crane, with two free kicks awarded to Minnesota’s Tenley Senden and Sarah Martin.

Multiple shot attempts were taken on both sides, as Nittany Lion Bella Ayscue tried to shoot up the field, but a weak kick was caught by Golden Gopher goalie Sarah Martin. Paige Kalal had another missed shot attempt, as Martin remained strong.

Similarly for the blue and white, goalie Mackenzie Gress didn’t let up, blocking all shot attempts taken on her by Minnesota to keep them off the board through the first half.

In the 33rd minute, Penn State saw its first goal as freshman Olivia Robinson was able to break away with a pass to Aubrey Kulpa, who blasted the ball into the bottom right of the goal, putting the blue and white up 1-0.

The Golden Gophers tried to respond, but were yet again blocked by Gress. Struggling to bring it back, a foul on Crane gave her a free kick that looked like it would be another goal but just missed up the right side.

Second Half

Immediately following halftime the game picked back up as both teams faced off in an offensive battle, with an aggressive line of midfielders fighting for the ball.

An early offsides call for Penn State saw Kulpa receive a yellow card for “unsporting” conduct, putting her on watch for the rest of the half.

Kulpa fired up and attempted a shot, but was off target and missed. A corner kick by Penn State put the pressure on the Golden Gophers as all players were surrounding the goal, but saw another missed attempt by forward Anna Babcock.

Another corner for Penn State put the pressure back on Minnesota, but the Golden Gophers couldn’t make a statement. Minnesota quickly got back on the ball, but received and missed a shot on a corner kick.

The Golden Gophers yet again got another chance in the corner, but were shot down by the Nittany Lions as the blue and white quickly took possession of the ball before a foul on Lily Boyden gave a free kick back to Minnesota’s Caroline Birdsell.

The second half continued to be a back and forth battle, as both teams had throw ins within the 71st minute, and a near goal by Robinson for Penn State just missed off the save from Martin.

A yellow card on Minnesota’s Ellen Neuharth for "unsporting" saw a Nittany Lion go down as play time stopped and trainers came on to the field. All players were cleared and the game resumed.

Kulpa took possession of the ball and took another shot but was blocked by Martin in the bottom left of the net.

Minnesota came into the second half seeing multiple corners and stronger offensive plays, but couldn’t get themselves into the Nittany Lion box.

A huge hope for another Penn State goal came via a shot attempt by Paige Pasinski, but the Nittany Lion midfielder just missed the net as Martin continued on a roll of protecting her goal.

It was a half full of opportunities for both teams but neither could follow through to put a goal on the board.

Ayscue saw her first yellow card with another “unsporting” call, giving a free kick to Golden Gopher Ava Westlund. Westlund, clutching her back, stopped the clock and was subbed out, as both teams took the break and reset in the last 4 minutes of the game.

The Nittany Lions took the win after a hard fought battle to get their third win and improve their record to 3-2-2 after their second conference match-up this season.

title: Penn State field hockey drops battle to Princeton, suffers 2-1 loss
author: Annie Alberts | The Daily Collegian
description:
The Nittany Lions take another loss to No. 2 Princeton, 2-1, resulting in their second defeat of the season.

Penn State kept their heads in the game for the first quarter. Junior goalie Aby Devorka made her 13th save of the season, from an assertive shot by Princeton’s Molly Nye.

Quarter one, for the most part, was anticlimactic for both teams. Princeton’s shot on goal was blocked, and Penn State did their best to keep the Tigers away from the shooting circle.

Coming off of a defensive high from quarter one, quarter two challenged the Lions. Four minutes and 20 seconds into the quarter, Princeton junior Pru Lindsey scored her first goal of the season.

Three minutes later, Lindsey struck again with a penalty strike goal. From then on, Princeton was on fire.

The orange and black controlled the pitch for the next few minutes. At 28:57 minutes in, Molly Nye and Izzy Morgan made three shots in nine seconds. They weren’t a match for Deverka, who scrambled to save them all.

After halftime, the Nittany Lions returned with a brighter, more eager energy.

A minute after they were accosted by a Lindsey shot again, Penn State graduate student Cam Standish made a vigorous corner shot.

Five seconds later, Penn State is back in the game. Junior forward Ella Gaitan scored her third goal of the season, with helpful assists from Sienna Dunn and Standish.

Gaitan’s goal put the team in a combative mood. Standish had the opportunity to make another corner penalty shot, which went in. But the goal was under review and later deemed not to count.

Penn State followed with three more shots, each made by Standish, Gaitan and freshman Chloe D’Hage.

The third quarter was Princeton’s quietest section of the game, only making one shot and zero corners.

Quarter four was a battle for the ball. Penn State tried to seal a win, while Princeton was struggling to maintain its hold.

At the last minute of the game, Penn State had one more shot to tie the game, with a penalty corner shot, as all eyes were on Gaitan. Her shot went high, but the Nittany Lions kept the ball in the circle.

Gaitan got another penalty shot, but it didn't go through. In the final, Penn State lost to Princeton 2-1, resulting in their second loss of the season. Both were losses to ranked teams, the first being Virginia, which ended 4-3.

Up Next

Penn State returns Thursday with a game against Maryland, which is set to start at 5 p.m.

title: No. 12 Penn State women’s volleyball earns 3rd consecutive sweep, bests Ohio at Rec Hall
author: Elliott Inscho | The Daily Collegian
description:
25 hours after their sweep of No. 4 Stanford in Philadelphia, the Nittany Lions made the trip back to Rec Hall looking to pick up another win against Ohio.

No. 12 Penn State swept its third consecutive match, and fifth of the season, in a dominant showing over the Bobcats.

Penn State was able to keep Friday’s momentum rolling into the opening of its clash with the Bobcats, jumping out to a 6-2 lead in the early stages of the first set. Gabrielle Nichols made two kills in the stretch, and Whitney Lauenstein notched her first after notching 11 against Stanford.

Ohio scored back-to-back points on an attack error from Alexis Stucky and a kill from Rowan Kelly, cutting Penn State’s lead to three. The Bobcats returned fire with a blistering, six-point run to storm back and take the lead over the Nittany Lions.

In the run, Ohio made two aces and a pair of blocks that fired up a contingent of visiting fans sitting in the rows behind the Bobcats’ bench. A block by the blue and white halted the surge, but Ohio won the ensuing point to hold a one-point lead at the media timeout.

A Nichols kill and attack error from the Bobcats thrust the Nittany Lions back into the lead. Back-and-forth action to follow kept things neck-and-neck, but an ace from Kennedy Martin forced Ohio coach Kenzie Brinkman to call the match’s first timeout with her squad trailing 20-17.

It sparked a two-point run by the Bobcats to bring them within one point, but Lauenstein and Ryla Jones delivered back-to-back kills that reestablished the edge. Ohio won two more points on a kill and an ace before a service error and a kill from Stucky brought Penn State to set point.

Stucky delivered again, with a strong swing that deflected off an Ohio player to seal the set for the Nittany Lions.

The Bobcats earned the second set’s opening point; Emmi Sellman got Penn State on the board with her first kill of the match. After Ohio responded, Nichols made a kill and an ace before an error from the Bobcats capped a three-point run for the blue and white.

Bailey Blair stopped the run with a kill of her own. Penn State won three of the next four points, two of which came off of swings by Haley Burgdorf, who notched ten the night before.

Sellman’s spike caught the lip of the net and rolled over, but when the Bobcats sent the ball back to her, she flicked it into a wide-open corner of the court to give her team a 9-6 lead in the set.

In the middle of the second set, Ohio never let Penn State get too far ahead. It kept within two points of the lead until the blue and white extended their advantage to 15-11 at the second-set break.

That gap got wider to follow, as the Nittany Lions won three of four points to go up by six. A three-point Ohio run shrunk it back down, but blocks from Nichols andKendall Northern electrified the arena and forced another timeout from Brinkman with Penn State up 20-16.

In similar fashion, the Bobcats won two consecutive points out of the break, but kills from Sellman and Caroline Jurevicius widened the edge to four. Katie Schumacher-Caweley called for a timeout of her own when Rose Mahin and Gentry Brown made back-to-back kills in the second set’s late stages.

Ohio won three of four points to follow, evening the set at 23-23. Jurevicius made a kill, and after her strong serve on the ensuing set point, Ohio’s return sailed over the net and back to the Penn State side of the court. Finley Krystkowiak leaped into the air and clinched the set with a powerful swing.

Early action in the third set was tightly contested until Penn State went on a four-point run capped by consecutive aces from Jurevicius. A kill by Brown ended it, but a kill from Burgdorf and back-to-back blocks by the blue and white saw them take a 10-4 lead.

After an Ohio timeout, the streak continued. A Northern kill was sandwiched with attack errors from Mahin, and the Bobcats called for yet another reprieve after another Burgdorf kill and an error by Blair.

With Penn State holding a 15-4 lead, the eight-point run finally ended when Northern sent a ball past the Ohio back line. Alexis Ewing notched her first kills of the season and Danielle Whitmire made four consecutive aces to extend the Nittany Lions’ dominant lead to 22-6.

The Bobcats put up a bit of a fight with a three-point run late in the set, but an emphatic swing from Burgdorf ended the set and clinched the match for Penn State.

Penn State faces Villanova on Tuesday in the second match of a four-game homestand. The in-state clash will be broadcast to a national audience, with first serve set for 7 p.m. on FS1.
