title: Ella Langley sells out Bryce Jordan Center
author: Brennan Kramp I The Daily Collegian
description:
On Friday, country singer, Ella Langley, played a sold out show at the Bryce Jordan Center as part of the second leg in her new Dandelion Tour.

Langley released her third studio album, “Dandelion,” in April 2025 and went on a headlining tour almost immediately after, starting in May for the first leg of the tour. Now, Langley is selling out shows all over.

“She’s got so much talent … her voice is, obviously, just very beautiful,” Waylon Carlson, 22, of Virginia Beach, Virginia, said.

Supported by openers Gabriella Rose and Muscadine Bloodline, Langley’s fans were waiting expectantly to see her walk through the doors underneath the drummer’s mini-stage and belt out some new-age country tunes.

Sporting leather cowboy boots and various colored cowboy hats, most women wore dresses, skirts or jeans with fringe. For the men in the audience, denim jeans and graphic t-shirts sporting logos from Coors Light to “Ella’s Fellas” (worn by Langley’s fan-club) were the go-to.

During the intermission between Muscadine Bloodline and Langley, the stage was decorated with moss, grass and dandelions scattered on the steps and around the catwalk. Fans chatted with each about what songs they wanted to hear, trying to guess the lineup down to the last note.

Emily Wilson, 25, of Uniontown, Pennsylvania, practically had Langley’s whole discography memorized as she listed off some of the hits and B-side tracks she hoped to hear most.

“'Hell At Night,' 'Butterfly Season,' 'Weren’t For The Wind' and 'Bottom Of Your Boots,' for sure,” Wilson said.

When the intermission ended, the lights faded out and the stage illuminated dark red. A sea of phone cameras shot in the air as fans became almost feral to capture Langley’s commanding entrance.

The entire set amplified the crowd more and more with every song, especially on tracks like “Bottom Of Your Boots,” “20-20,” and “Somethin’ Simple.”

In every section, the crowd refused to sit — mothers held their children wearing soundproof earmuffs bobbing up and down, guys slung their arm around the shoulders of their girlfriends as they swayed, all gazing at Langley on center stage in a brown floral dress with shiny, leather cowboy boots.

With each song, her voice seemed to grow stronger and stronger as she was invigorated by the energy of the crowd which had morphed into one giant karaoke session.

“Seeing how songs I wrote for me are being sung by all of you, it’s a very special thing,” Langley said to the crowd.

At the conclusion of the show, fans departed with wide grins, hats in hand while they took off their boots on the sides of the road. There was no doubt that every attendee needed to relieve their feet after the continuous standing ovation that occurred throughout the show.

One fan, Oaklee, 5, from Loganton, Pennsylvania, had the privilege of seeing Langley for her first concert ever. Her overall reaction to how her first show went was simplistic and a fitting answer for a young concertgoer like her.

“Good,” she said. “Awesome.”

Even though most of her fans came to hear her voice, Langley left the audience with a lasting message that conveyed even more than what she had sung about.

“Do the damn thing that’s weighing on your heart,” Langley said, “I’ll play a show like tonight and remember why I’m doing what I’m doing.”

title: Latin-American culture takes center stage at Happy Valley Latin Festival
author: Colleen Cratty | The Daily Collegian
description:
On Saturday families, students, local residents and more crowded South Fraser Street for the annual Happy Valley Latin Festival, which celebrates the diversity and vibrance of Latin-American culture.

The festival started with a parade showcasing traditional costumes from a variety of Latin cultures. Featured in the parade were members of the State College community such as students and professors.

“My favorite part of the festival has always been the beginning of it,” Umbayi Moret-Léede, a member of the festival’s organizing committee, said. “We have a parade of typical dresses from all over. It’s just so beautiful. I get goosebumps every time I see it.”

After the parade, State College mayor, Ezra Nanes, gave a speech about the upcoming Hispanic Heritage Month. Nanes spoke about the rich culture of Latin people and how they’re the fastest growing minority in Pennsylvania.

He commended the organization and growth of the festival as it's in its sixth year.

“I’ve been living here since I was eight,” Moret-Léede said in an opening speech. “And, I’ve never seen something where it just brings the whole community together, whether it's Latin-American, Indian or something else. We just come together. It definitely unites us as a community.”

Moret-Léede said the festival and parade isn’t just for Latin-Americans.

“Because we have so many friends from all different places in the world, we started inviting them,” Moret-Léede said. “One was from South Africa, one was from India, another one was from China. We were like ‘Hey, if you have a dress from your country, just parade with us.’”

Several local businesses such as Folds and Stitches Earrings, which sells handmade jewelry inspired by origami and crochet, were present at the festival.

“We wanted to participate here because we feel welcome, this is our culture,” Steven Velásquez Chancí, owner of Folds and Stitches Earrings said. “We wanted to show what we do as artists.”

Chanci said the festival is a unique way for him and others to celebrate their culture, share experiences and introduce people to their traditional food and products.

“I think it's important to recognize that we are equal, but we also have our cultural differences,” Chancí said. “It’s an experience that enriches people’s perception of other people’s lives.”

The festival also featured student groups that celebrate diversity such as the Community Diversity Group and Boricua Grads. Penn State’s Department of Spanish, Italian, and Portuguese was also in attendance, including many professors.

“The best part is the community,” Daniel Sanguino, a Penn State Spanish professor, said. “We have people from every Spanish-speaking country. It’s beautiful to come together and celebrate.”

Moret-Léede mentioned that the festival also includes a different honoree every year in which they “honor them and give them their flowers.” She remarked on the first year of the festival, when the honoree was Maria Sweet.

“Maria was one of the pioneers who came here, she was Puerto Rican and she worked in Old Main,” Moret-Léede said. “She opened so many doors for all of us. It didn’t matter who you were, where you were from, she always took the time to talk to you.”

The rest of the festival included dance and music performances. There was a Norteña Dance Lesson, a Zumba class and a performance by La Fiesta Band. DJ Elbow Knee Knee performed during the entirety of the festival, playing Latin classics.

“It’s vibrant, colorful, and celebratory,” Sanguino said. “Its really good to showcase how diverse our community is.”

title: Penn State RBs struggle to establish ground game despite road victory over Temple
author: Andrew Mercer | The Daily Collegian
description:
PHILADELPHIA — In the first quarter of Penn State’s Week 2 road matchup against Temple, James Peoples and Carson Hansen lined up for three consecutive rushes in the red zone. They found themselves short each time before the offense failed to convert on fourth down.

Despite flashes of possibility, Penn State’s running backs weren’t able to produce at a high level for the second straight week.

“I thought we were really physical at the point of attack today,” Matt Campbell said postgame. “I thought we took a step forward, but the team that we want to be and the team that we were today are still not equal to what we want to become.”

Although the preseason conception was that four running backs would see ample time on the field, the coaching staff has been using a traditional depth chart. Carson Hansen was the bell cow, and Peoples slotted in as the No. 2 running back.

But this strategy didn’t work once again, as the run game was underwhelming. Neither Hansen nor Peoples have scored a touchdown yet this season.

After his slow start to the contest, Hansen brought his average up to 4.4 yards per carry, totalling 84 yards.

Hansen attributed this result to how himself and the room need to clean up some of the smaller details that make the biggest difference. Stiff arms and swatting arm tackles were specific examples he gave. However, Hansen also said that in the heat of the moment, his only thoughts are about “getting downhill.”

“I need to be able to break some of those tackles in the red zone,” Hansen said. “I’ve got to hold myself accountable for this and have urgency this week to be able to break tackles and go for long runs.”

After the game, Hansen solemnly swayed side-to-side as he took responsibility for some of the mistakes made on the field. He said that offensive coordinator Taylor Mouser tries to pin it on himself, but Hansen rebuffed that — to him, it was about “coming together as a team.”

Peoples, meanwhile, was more efficient, averaging six yards per carry for a total of 42 yards, and he was at once point in the fourth quarter as high as 7.6 yards per carry. However, Peoples’ point of contention was his consistency, as three of his seven carries were three yards and under.

Tight end Benjamin Brahmer didn’t put the blame on anyone’s shoulders. Brahmer said that Hansen just needs to “hammer away” at practice.

“Carson runs the ball really well. He's never going to lose yards for us. He's always in the gap one, two, three, four yards,” Brahmer said. “We know we can do good in that aspect of the game.”

Hansen shared that he and Peoples have been continuously pushing each other in practice, competing day-in and day-out to improve their game. While it hasn’t shown up on the stat sheet yet, Hansen knows what needs to be done and is ready to put his nose to the grindstone at practice.

“We have to have a better start off the rip and be able to finish in the red zone,” Hansen said. “I know we can do it. I believe that we can do it. So, we're gonna fix it this week and be ready for Buffalo.”

title: ‘Nobody flinched’ | Penn State answers adversity questions in win over Temple
author: Andrew Deal | The Daily Collegian
description:
PHILADELPHIA — This offseason, Matt Campbell was confident in how his team was coming together, but it was how the team dealt with adversity that he felt would truly define his first team at Penn State.

Campbell wanted to see “how we respond to imperfect” to really know what the team has. He felt the Nittany Lions were “a closer football team to being ready to respond to those adversities,” on Aug. 25, just over a week before the season.

Penn State answered that task at Lincoln Financial Field against Temple when it trailed 3-0 towards the beginning of the second quarter. The Nittany Lions responded to the deficit with 27 unanswered points, but it was how the team dealt with the adversity that stood out to Campbell.

“I would just say that's probably the proudest that I can leave, and it's what I told our guys in the locker room,” Campbell said. “I felt like nobody flinched, nobody wavered. There was no complaining.”

Rocco Becht was the catalyst once again in the spark, with his talk on the sideline continuing to boost players up and keep the belief that success will come despite the slow start.

“He kept coming around to us, even though obviously things weren't going his way,” wide receiver Chase Sowell said. “He was still picking us up, telling us like, ‘Hey, I still believe you. I still got trust in you. I'm coming to you.’”

With Becht at the helm and finding a groove, Penn State was able to pull away with major success in “the middle eight,” as Campbell put it — the final four minutes of the first half and first four minutes of the second half.

Defensively, it was linebacker Tony Rojas and cornerback Audavion Collins who stood out to Campbell as players that stepped up to handle the adverse situation, allowing the offense to score two touchdowns in that time frame.

“I think we won (the middle eight) obviously, and that boosted that momentum going forward,” Sowell said. “But like I said, we got to start faster.”

The victory over Temple didn’t just answer the adversity question, but also showed the connection and closeness of the team is paying off. In those moments, the team stuck together and remained as one to get out of the slow start and start fully controlling both sides of the ball.

“We all just stayed together,” defensive end Yvan Kemajou said. “We all take energy off each other and just make sure we all just play together.”

A lot of questions were answered under Campbell’s leadership for the first time, and while it came against a team in a nonconference game, it does have some benefits. Sowell would much “rather it now than when we get later into the season” against a Big Ten team where it may be harder to find those answers to adversity.

But the Nittany Lions responded to the slow start in front of a Penn State-heavy crowd and will try to use the early struggles they dealt with in Saturday’s game to get out to quicker starts later in the season.

“Our eight players stepped up in eight moments and made eight plays, which is what you hope will happen in adverse situations,” Campbell said “I thought those guys did a great job of that for sure.”

title: ‘The heartbeat for us’ | TE Benjamin Brahmer leads Penn State with 2-touchdown performance
author: Noah Aberegg | The Daily Collegian
description:
PHILADELPHIA — With eight minutes and 32 seconds left in the third quarter, tight end Benjamin Brahmer dropped what would’ve been a touchdown-scoring pass from Rocco Becht at the 3-yard line.

Roughly 15 minutes later, he found himself in the end zone again, this time scoring the touchdown. Brahmer’s reception marked his second score of the day, third of the season and sixth in his last six games dating back to 2025.

“I just have to flush it and continue to play hard and not worry about it,” Brahmer said. “Go get it the next time it comes.”

Brahmer’s big day came amidst a slow start for the Nittany Lions against Temple. While Penn State came away with the 27-9 victory, some aspects of Penn State’s game struggled at the beginning.

Despite Brahmer’s big drop — a drive which ultimately ended in wide receiver Chase Sowell finding the end zone — the tight end was one of the positives from Saturday’s game.

“He’s always going out there doing his job and he’s a good person,” Becht said. “That’s why we love him.”

After a slow first quarter where the offense completed just one pass, Brahmer became involved in the passing game early in the second frame with a four-yard catch.

The following drive, Penn State was in the middle of a two minute drill, prompting a Nittany Lion timeout. Coming out of the break, Becht found Brahmer for a quick, eight-yard gain.

Instead of calling another timeout, Matt Campbell opted to leave the clock running, but it didn’t come back to bite him. Becht gathered the offense and delivered another strike to Brahmer, this time for a 23-yard score, marking Penn State’s first touchdown of the day.

“Rocco and I were on the same page and just setting the tone for the rest of the game going into half, it’s huge,” Brahmer said. “I think we just caught them on their toes and got past them.”

Brahmer’s last-second touchdown provided a lot of momentum for the Nittany Lions going into half, helping continue their scoring stretch for 27 straight points.

“Ben kind of showed that today, those guys are the heartbeat for us,” Becht said.

Throughout the third quarter, Brahmer continued to be an important presence in the passing game. He recorded a 20-yard reception, breaking three tackles in the process.

However, he also was a key blocker in the run game, along with fellow tight ends Andrew Rappleyea and Gabe Burkle. After averaging less than two yards per carry through the first quarter, the run game saw significant improvement, ending the day with 4.4 yards per attempt.

There were several plays where the Nittany Lions utilized 14-personnel, which allowed for several run plays to develop.

“Those guys do a lot of things and certainly some personnel stuff that gives you an advantage,” Campbell said. “I thought those guys did a great job handling all that today.”

Brahmer’s connection with Becht showed its success again in the fourth quarter, as he capped off Penn State’s scoring for the day with his second 23-yard touchdown of the day.

“I think we’re just always on the same page,” Becht said. “I think that’s just repetition and reps that we’ve got over the past three years, and he’s a really great player to have and throw to.”

Brahmer finished the contest leading the Nittany Lions in nearly every receiving category. He recorded a team-high 79 yards and two touchdowns and tied Sowell with five receptions.

Through two games as a Nittany Lion, he also leads the team with three touchdowns on the year, showcasing the impact he has on Penn State’s offense.

“It’s been great, just keeping my head down and working,” Brahmer said. “I know the ball will come to me when it happens, and I just got to be ready for that. I just got lucky today and got it a couple times.”

title: Penn State DE Max Granville out for season
author: Andrew Mercer & Lexie Linderman | The Daily Collegian
description:
PHILADELPHIA — One of Penn State's key players on defense will have to wait to suit up again until next season.

Defensive end Max Granville suffered a season-ending injury at practice this week, Matt Campbell announced after defeating Temple on Saturday.

Campbell did not disclose the nature of the injury.

Granville missed the entire 2025 season after picking up an injury while working out at home over the summer. This is now the second straight year Granville will be sidelined.

"A really tough blow for our football team, and really, most importantly, a really tough blow for Max," Campbell said postgame. "The thing I love about Max is he's kind of been a pillar of glue for the unity of our football team over the last nine months. Who he is, what his character is, and I think that's why I think we're all really convicted that he'll come back better than ever."

The redshirt sophomore returned to the field for the first time since last year's injury against Marshall in Week 1, tallying one pass breakup. He briefly went down during the matchup, but later returned.

Granville made headlines in 2024 after reclassifying to join Penn State a year early, appearing in seven games. He filled in for Abdul Carter in the Fiesta Bowl on certain plays, showing the trust the staff already had in him.

Two seasons later, Granville was poised to make an impact as one of the top three defensive ends in the rotation.

"Max is like a rock to us, and he will be for the future," linebacker Tony Rojas said. "Just having him along with us on away games is going to be awesome for us and something we need."

title: 3 takeaways from Penn State's road win over Temple
author: Andrew Mercer | The Daily Collegian
description:
PHILADELPHIA — Penn State traveled for the first time in the 2026 season, heading east to Lincoln Financial Field on Saturday.

The Nittany Lions had a slow start but managed to get the job done in the second half, claiming a 27-9 victory. While the scoreboard gives a rose-tinted view of the game, there were aspects of Penn State’s game that fell short. Despite that, Matt Campbell’s squad improved to 2-0 on the season.

Here’s three takeaways from Penn State’s first road trip victory of the season.

Dual-threat quarterbacks could pose issues for Penn State

Temple’s top ball carrier on the day was still Keveun Mason, but quarterback Jaxon Smolik wasn’t too far behind.

Smolik, a former Nittany Lion, ran all over Penn State’s defense throughout the game and finished with 71 rushing yards. While the Nittany Lions contained the passing game, holding Temple to just 107 passing yards — half of which came after they had pulled away from the Owls — Smolik saw open lanes on the outside zone to pick up yards when the rest of the offense faltered.

Penn State even let the Owls' other quarterback, Ajani Sheppard, find the end zone with two minutes remaining.

“I thought we did some really good things in the secondary, but again, defensively, you can't allow the running game to be able to take the advantages that they had in the game,” Matt Campbell said postgame.

The Nittany Lions’ inability to contain Smolik’s running capabilities could be a weakness that comes back to bite them later in the season when Penn State plays Big Ten teams with dual-threat quarterbacks. Upcoming opponents Washington, USC and Michigan each have a mobile starting quarterback.

Down the stretch, the Nittany Lions have to put more of an emphasis on the quarterback as a rushing option, as getting into the pocket was a notable missing piece against Marshall as well.

Benjamin Brahmer proves why he’s TE1

Last week, Taylor Mouser’s tight end room wasn’t as flashy as some expected. But against Temple, Benjamin Brahmer showed a glimpse at what Penn State’s top tight end could be.

Brahmer was the Nittany Lions’ top pass catcher, finishing the matchup with 79 yards on five catches for a pair of touchdowns. He has six touchdowns in his last six games dating back to 2025.

Penn State ran as many as four tight ends at once against the Owls, but found the most success when it was just Brahmer and either Andrew Rappleyea or Gabe Burkle. Brahmer showed why he was a semifinalist for the John Mackey Award last year.

Brahmer was the biggest threat when he found open lanes up the middle, which he did multiple times, making Rocco Becht’s life much easier. Becht finished with 268 yards, three touchdowns and a 78% completion percentage.

“I've been playing with Rocco for three, four years now, and just knowing what he's thinking and his reads on every play, I usually know when I'm when the ball's coming to me in the passing game,” Brahmer said. “I wasn't perfect. I take responsibility for that, and just continue to get better with it.”

James Peoples’ playmaking outshines Carson Hansen

Penn State’s run game is once again a topic of concern, primarily because a lot of potential gains were lost at the point of contact.

James Peoples, however, checked into the game as the second running back and did well after contact. While he didn’t have as many reps as Carson Hansen, Peoples made the most of his chances, finishing the win with 40 rushing yards, but a great six yards per carry.

On the other hand, Hansen appeared to struggle with staying on his feet. When he took a hand-off, he routinely fell forward onto the turf. Peoples showed a better sense of balance, and running backs coach Savon Huggins may look to reward that.

“I need to be able to break some of those tackles in the red zone,” Hansen said. “I’ve got to hold myself accountable for this and have urgency this week to be able to break tackles and go for long runs.”

Peoples showcased his creativity as well, shocking the crowd with a leaping huddle over a Temple defender in an attempt to get an extra yard, proving that he’s confident in his playmaking abilities.

Hansen still had a solid showing Saturday with 84 yards and 4.4 yards per rush despite the slow start from Penn State’s No. 1 running back.

The running back room is already seeing some substantial changes with the emphasis being taken off a four running back system and leaning more into a bell cow situation. But that may change once again, this time shifting in Peoples’ favor.

“Last week we were a hair off on some things, and I thought there was good growth,” Campbell said. “I thought we took a step forward, but the team that we want to be and the team that we were today are still not equal to what we want to become.”

description:

title: Penn State men's soccer overwhelmed on the road, falls to Washington in first Big Ten matchup of season
author: Chase Mitchell | The Daily Collegian
description:
Through four regular-season matches thus far under the direction of first-year coach Rob Dow, Penn State has gotten off to a rocky start, going 2-2 after run-ins with Mercyhurst, Missouri State, Pitt and Yale, with back-to-back losses coming in the middle of that stretch.

Looking to ride the hot hand, the Nittany Lions traveled cross country to the Emerald City to take on the reigning, defending champions of the college soccer world, Washington.

A couple thousand miles worth of travel may have played a factor on Friday night, though, as the Nittany Lions couldn’t survive the defending champions, falling 4-2 to the Huskies in a game that wasn’t decided until the final minutes.

First Half

It didn’t take long for the game’s first foul, as just 25 seconds in, Washington midfielder Wyatt Lewis was called for a violation, awarding the blue and white’s Nehan Hasan a free kick.

Right around the six and eight minute marks, the Huskies found themselves set up nicely with corner kicks, with one coming quite close to finding Penn State’s net, but nothing came of the attacks. The offensive units on both sides were clearly still feeling each other out as the 15-minute mark rolled around with a bunch of zeros on the scoreboard and the stat sheets.

Yet another Huskies midfielder, senior Connor Lofy, was called for a foul and given a yellow card early on after delivering a Conor McGregor-esque kick to the face of Nittany Lions defender Joe Buckly, who took the free kick which went wide left of the opposition’s net.

The first shot on goal of the night came in the 19th minute, with Washington’s Alex Hall showing off some quick feet and nice moves before sending a little blooper straight into the hands of Daniel Peluffo-Wiese, who was waiting in the Penn State goal.

Penn State had an opportune scoring chance in enemy territory in the 24th minute, but the play died out after a couple blue and white attackers got tangled up, allowing Huskie defenders to swarm Amadou Kone and recapture possession. If momentum was playing favorites, it hadn’t shown it more than halfway through the first period.

Another blue and white free kick was awarded when Lewis dragged Kone to the ground, presenting an opportune scoring chance that came to fruition when Kone sent it into the top center of the Huskies’ net off his right foot to put Penn State up 1-0 in the early running.

Just five seconds later, Washington’s Zach Ramsey let one rip from long distance and miraculously found the top corner pocket to tally his 10th goal of the season and once again tie the score at 1-1.

The Huskies continued applying pressure for the rest of the first half, finding themselves in several more scoring opportunities but unable to convert. On the other end, it felt like Penn State was lucky to get out of the half with the game still tied, with Washington holding an 8-2 shot advantage, though Peluffo-Wiese saves and six Husky fouls prevented the score from differing.

Second Half

The second half rolled around as Penn State fans in State College were getting ready for bed while the night was just beginning in Seattle, with both the home and away squads looking to pull away and ahead.

Ramsey nearly picked up his second goal of the night off another pretty Washington offensive attack, but the 6-foot-7 frame of Peluffo-Wiese snagged his shot out of the air to keep the score put.

Despite the Nittany Lions getting out of harm’s way, it was only momentarily, as Hall got one through the bottom right corner of the goal off his left foot on the assist play from Ramsey and Emmett Layman to jump out to 2-1 early in the second frame.

Just like the first half, it didn’t take long for the opposite end to strike back. Penn State freshman Beckham Brown made it a 2-2 ballgame after sneaking a right-footed goal through the legs of purple and gold defenders off a header, much to the shock of Huskies players and fans alike.

Unlike the first half, the gas pedal was pressed to the floor in the early running of the second period, with Asher Hestad picking up another goal for the Huskies off the assist from Hall. With an extended 3-2 lead, Washington went for the kill shot, but a near-miss from Ramsey left the purple and gold with just a one-goal lead.

Momentum quieted down on both ends once again after Hestad’s goal, with the action slowing down a considerable amount as the Huskies switched to a defense-first mindset while the moon came up above the Husky Soccer Stadium.

Several consecutive Washington corner kicks stretched across the 70-minute mark and brought the fans to their feet as balls were flying by and around the blue and white goal, none of which found the net but one that didn’t count due to a foul.

Some late-game corner kicks, fouls and near scores came and went for both sides, but it was another Ramsey goal that found the bottom right of the net that was the nail in the coffin for Penn State as Washington extended its lead to 4-2 in the 85th minute of the game.

The Nittany Lions held on for as long as they could on the West Coast, making things interesting for quite a while before ultimately falling short as Washington’s victory improves it to 4-2-1 on the year while Penn State’s record drops to 2-3.

Up Next

Penn State returns to Jeffrey Field on Friday to take on No. 10 Michigan State in the Mack Brady Match. Streaming on Big Ten Plus, kickoff is set for 7 p.m.

title: No.12 Penn State women’s volleyball speeds to sweep over No. 4 Stanford in Palestra
author: Lily Dorf | The Daily Collegian
description:
PHILADELPHIA – No. 12 Penn State traveled to the Palestra to take on No. 4 Stanford University at 6 p.m. for the first time since 2022, and the Nittany Lions won 3-2.

The blue and white took on the Cardinals, winning 25-21, securing a three-set sweep after a blow out game against DePaul on Monday. While Stanford is eight spots ahead of Penn State, the blue and white came in hot and fast, as the team excelled in kills and digs against their opponents. The Nittany Lions moved smoothly together, proving the loss to Kentucky was only fuel to keep working.

“We knew we needed to bounce back pretty quickly because we knew we had a really good Stanford team to prepare for,” said Penn State libero Ava Falduto. “I think we also knew that what we did against Kentucky wasn’t our best and we know we have the higher standard than that.”

Penn State began the first set with heat, claiming two points and hoping to keep their winning streak alive. However, not long after, Stanford’s outside hitter Ipar Kurt brought the score to 2-1 with a kill.

As the first set continued, both teams worked at a slow pace as the score tied, one point after another, volleying for longer and showing off each player’s skill. Especially Penn State’s libero Ava Falduto, who continuously dove to the ground, fighting to keep the ball in game.

The Cardinals came back with a punch, but Nittany Lions Gabrielle Nichols, Kennedy Martin and Haley Burgdorf took the court back, keeping the score close together as they drew closer and closer to the end of the set.

Stanford and Penn State continued to trade points as both teams fought to get ahead, one after another, keeping the score close and tying it up repeatedly.

Although the Nittany Lions continued to work together, Stanford led the set with 23-19.

Penn State passed Stanford with the help of Martin, as she made kill after kill, ending the first set victorious with a score of 27-25.

The crowd's roar could be heard and felt today by players and fans, as Penn Staters filled the stands in white and cheered after each point the Nittany Lions scored.

“I think it was just amazing how many people and how many supporters we have throughout just Pennsylvania in general,” said Haley Burgdorf. “It really got our energy going and as our energy was going up, their energy started going up too… it just kept us at such a high.”

Penn State started the second set off hot with a kill by Martin, keeping the energy from the first set up and setting a faster pace for the upcoming sets.

The blue and white conquered the court, as Martin and Burgdorf continuously kept the ball in the air, only letting it touch when scoring. The Nittany Lions passed and scored at the speed of light, reaching 21-15 in the second match as the team made kill after kill, proving to be a strong point this week.

As the second match comes to a close, with a nail-bitingly close score of 24-20, Burgdorf makes the final blow as the Nittany Lions reach victory in the second set, with a score of 25-20.

As both teams entered the third match, blue and white began to take charge, with Lauenstein, Stucky and Jones moving across the court with ease, helping the team stay ahead 4-1.

As both teams inched closer and closer to victory, the Nittany Lions moved around the court with ease, as their players worked together like a well-oiled machine, taking the lead 21-17 with five back-to-back points, with Burgdorf claiming two.

With a service ace from Burgdorf, Penn State continued its winning streak, 25-21, and kept its claim over Stanford alive.

MORE VOLLEYBALL COVERAGE

title: No. 12 Penn State women’s volleyball sweeps No. 4 Stanford in upset at the Palestra
author: Elliott Inscho | The Daily Collegian
description:
PHILADELPHIA – Penn State’s weekend in Philly got off to a fiery start on Friday night.

With Matt Campbell and company set to face Temple at Lincoln Financial Field on Saturday, the No. 12 Nittany Lions treated fans already in the City of Brotherly Love with an upset sweep over No. 4 Stanford at UPenn’s historic Palestra.

“This is a historical place,” Katie Schumacher-Cawley said. “I'm really proud of the team. It was a great team effort tonight. Stanford's a great team, and I know they'll bounce back, but we'll take the win and run.”

The blue and white fought closely with the Cardinal throughout the opening set. After the squads leveled at 3-3, the blue and white ripped off a three-point run to take an early lead before Stanford reciprocated to level things at 6-6.

The match stayed hotly contested until Penn State delivered another three-point run to take a 12-10 edge. The Cardinal won back-to-back points to level the set again, before a three-point run earned them a 15-13 lead at the opening media timeout.

Stanford got the first point out of the break, but three consecutive kills from Kennedy Martin, Gabrielle Nichols and Whitney Lauenstein, followed by an ace from Alexis Stucky, forced a timeout from Cardinal head coach Kevin Hambly with the Nittany Lions up 18-16.

After Penn State’s run, a four-point stretch from Stanford saw the Cardinal regain the lead late in Friday’s opening set.

Martin’s fourth kill of the evening momentarily halted the run, but Stanford won back-to-back points to force a timeout from Schumacher-Cawley and draw within three points of clinching the set.

Lizzy Andrew drilled the ball into the net to give Penn State life before Martin combined with Ryla Jones for a block that compelled another timeout from Hambly.

An ace from Ava Faltudo preceded an emphatic swing from Martin that drew her squad level with the Cardinal, much to the delight of a neutral-site crowd that was clearly on Penn State’s side.

“It was just amazing how many supporters we have throughout Pennsylvania,” Burgdorf said. “So many people came out here to support us, and it really got our energy going. As our energy was going up, their energy started going up too.”

The Blue Band and Nittany Lions’ presence certainly helped to develop the atmosphere in the Palestra, as well.

Julia Blyashov made a kill that put Stanford on set point, but Martin delivered again to keep the opening frame alive. After another Cardinal point, kills from Jones and freshman standout Haley Burgdorf gave the Nittany Lions a set point of their own.

Burgdorf has slotted in as a consistent starter in her first year as a Nittany Lion and finished with ten kills on a .450% clip against Stanford.

“I just knew I could go a lot of high hands,” Burgdorf said of her performance on Friday. “They weren't really a good pressing team, and it's kind of one of my specialties. And even if I did get blocked, I knew my teammates behind me had my back, so I just kept swinging away.”

Penn State capitalized on the set point to take the first frame 27-25.

The blue and white won three of four points to begin the second set before a service error and back-to-back kills gave the Nittany Lions a 7-3 lead early in the frame.

The Cardinal alternated points with the blue and white until two kills from Lauenstein gave Penn State a 11-6 advantage and forced Stanford to use another timeout.

Penn State surrendered a single point before going on another three-point run, highlighted by a kill from Nichols. Stanford won back-to-back kills before Nichols delivered a firm block to give the Nittany Lions a six-point lead at the second-set break.

An attack error from Martin and a kill by Ella Andrews cut the blue and white’s lead to four, but Martin’s seventh and eighth kills of the match brought her squad’s advantage back to six. The 6-foot-6 right-side hitter made her ninth soon after.

Stanford went on a three-point streak, but Burgdorf, Jones and Lauenstein’s consecutive kills offset the damage and put Penn State up 21-15 late in the second set. After a Cardinal timeout, they won three of four points to follow.

Martin reached double-digit kills to usher in set point for Penn State, and Burgdorf made her fifth to claim a less competitive, 25-10 second set for the Nittany Lions.

Penn State opened the third with a three-point run, consisting of a bad set by Lilly Wagner, a combined block from Jones and Stucky and finished with Lauenstein’s tenth kill. Stanford went on a heater to follow, winning seven of nine points to take the lead and force Schumacher-Cawley’s second timeout.

Out of the break, Stucky tied things up with a kill before what initially looked like a point for Stanford was overturned to a Burgdorf kill. The Cardinal continued to struggle with Penn State’s offense, making three consecutive errors to stretch the Nittany Lion run to five points.

It expanded to six on kill No. 13 for Martin, but Stanford battled back to win eight of ten points and take a 15-14 lead as the squads entered the third-set media timeout.

Alternating points brought the set into its closing stages with Stanford holding a slight edge, until a three-point run bookended by kills from Nichols and Burgdorf saw the Nittany Lions retake a 19-17 advantage.

Burgdorf made another and Martin and Nichols combined for a kill out of a Stanford timeout before Blyashov made a kill to keep the Cardinal in it. The teams alternated points before Martin made another kill to give Penn State a 23-19 lead.

Stanford earned back-to-back points on a kill from Ella Andrews and an error from Martin, but a kill and ace from Burgdorf secured the set and clean sweep for Penn State.

The victory served as an opportunity for Penn State to bounce back against a big-time opponent, after finishing a 1-1 road trip that saw them fall to No. 3 Kentucky at Wrigley Field.

“I think it was really cool to play at Wrigley against Kentucky, but we knew we needed to bounce back pretty quickly because we had a really good Stanford team to prepare for,” Faltudo said. “I think we went into practice knowing that. The coaches did a really good job preparing us for this game, and we just came in ready to work during the week.”

Up Next

The blue and white return to Happy Valley for the first time in Sept. with a one-off game against Ohio before hitting the road again. The matchup against the Bobcats is slated for 7 p.m., and it’ll be the Nittany Lions’ Team Ream match, supporting financially disadvantaged residents of the State College area.

title: ‘Unity is something our country needs now more than ever’ | 9/11 memorial commemorates 25th anniversary
author: Sarah Price | The Daily Collegian
description:
This year marks the 25th anniversary since the Sept. 11, 2001 terrorist attack. If you’ve walked past Old Main in the last few days, you may have noticed the 2,997 American flags planted on the lawn, representing each person who died during the attacks, 10 of which stand for Penn State alumni.

On Friday at 5 p.m., the Penn State College Republicans held a memorial service on Old Main lawn to commemorate those who lost their lives and to never forget that day. The memorial is held annually, however, many attendees said this year’s service was both a special and important remembrance.

“We should never forget the major events that happened in history,” Robert Bachner, 70, of State College, said. “This is just one of many. It’s a very sacred and solemn day for all.”

As the chimes of Old Main went quiet, Ryan Reichel, the director of special events for the College Republicans, began the memorial service by introducing the speakers and honoring the legacies of those who lost their lives.

“Unity is something our country needs now, more than ever,” Reichel, a third-year studying accounting, said. “This event proves that it’s possible.”

After reciting the Pledge of Allegiance and listening to the National Anthem, sung by the Penn State University Choir, student leaders, one at a time, laid a rose in front of a flag planted for the 10 Penn State alumni who died.

The first speaker was Ezra Nanes, the mayor of State College, who shared his memory of that day and what it means to him.

“If we can do one thing in addition to remembering the dead … let us take away the example of these students,” Nanes said. “Let us take that spirit of unity and purpose away, and live every day with such gratitude, because we are so lucky to be alive.”

As the memorial service carried on, unity became a common theme in not only the speeches by the guest speakers but also amongst those who attended.

“Even though it was a tragedy, it was a time that kind of brought the nation together,” Mei-Ling Liber, 40, from Alexandria, Va. said.

Following the State College mayor was Jondavid Longo, the mayor of Slippery Rock and a Marine Corps combat veteran, who also touched on his memory of that day and how our country has shifted since then. He concluded with a call to action for those in attendance to honor those who lost their lives.

“Seeing you all here on this lawn today gives me hope that you will, in fact, have answers to that day, despite being 25 years removed from it,” Longo said.

Many people who attended the memorial service had a personal reason or connection to the 9/11 attacks and felt it was necessary to show up on Old Main lawn. Liber said she went on to serve in the Air Force after watching the events of 9/11 while she was in high school.

“I know a lot of veterans, they struggle with the fallout that happened after 9/11 and whether or not their service mutually made a difference,” Liber said. “I’d like to think that it did for the time that I was there.”

After the mayor of Slippery Rock, Congressman Glen Thompson, representative of the 15th Congressional District, spoke briefly about the importance of remembering and honoring those who, not only lost their lives on 9/11, but also those who endured the debris and smoke of that day and continue to face health issues due to it.

“In 9/11, and the days that followed, we saw Americans uniting to help on another, all from our local country and in our neighborhood,” Thompson said.

The final speaker was Neeli Bendapudi, the president of Penn State, who emphasized the state of the country following the attacks and the unity witnessed across the country.

“Grief that day did not divide us, grief bound us together,” Bendapudi said.

In her speech, Bendapudi borrowed a quote from George W. Bush, the president during the 9/11 attacks. She said, “do not judge somebody by the actions of someone who looks like them,” which summarizes the message and tone of her speech. She reminded the audience that every American, no matter their identity, condemns the act that happened that fateful day.

“It’s easy to hate a caricature, a stereotype, someone you do not know,” Bendapudi said. “Please, when you are on this campus, continue to do what you are doing. Engage with one another.”

title: Preview | Penn State women’s hockey nonconference schedule rooted in contention
author: Mashiah Mitchell | The Daily Collegian
description:
The Penn State Nittany Lions schedule is heavily back-loaded in the second half of the season, with 12 conference games across the remaining 15 after the midway point.

But what about nonconference play? The return to Washington, D.C.? What about Ohio State's return to State College? The Ivy League gauntlet? Here's how those questions look to be answered in the blue and white's season outside the Atlantic Hockey America conference.

Less than a week after their early exhibition against fellow AHA program RIT, the doors of Pegula Ice Arena will swing open for the Nittany Lions' home-opening series.

The Nittany Lions start the season on Sept. 24 against none other than one of their biggest rivals, the Ohio State Buckeyes.

This will mark the first time the Buckeyes will walk into Pegula Ice Arena since 2017, which resulted in a 6-0 shutout win for Ohio State. Recently, this has become a common theme within the rivalry. The Nittany Lions haven't been able to conquer the pride of Columbus in nearly eight seasons, losing four of the last five matchups.

Penn State understands how important this series is not only to the players, but to the season itself, making it the site of both the annual White Out and banner night.

Those two themes only add fuel to the fire for both programs looking to continue their contending nature and inch closer to a National Championship. This honor preceded the Nittany Lions after a Frozen Four heartbreak, and something the Buckeyes came within fingertips of, losing to Wisconsin in a thriller.

Following this, after playing six straight AHA games back-to-back, Penn State will take a road trip to Canton, New York, on Oct. 23 to meet the St. Lawrence Saints for a short two-game series.

The Nittany Lions toppled the Saints, who entered the year as the No. 9 team in the country, in a 2-0 series sweep last season in the home opener.

This time around, St. Lawrence has added five U18 vets and will have been battle-tested by the defending champion Wisconsin Badgers, so the blue and white will have their hands more than full with a team that might surprise them at this point in the season.

After another six-game stretch of conference play, the aforementioned D1 in D.C. showcase follows, with Boston College and Minnesota awaiting in the nation's capital.

The Boston College Eagles are five seasons removed from their last NCAA tournament appearance, and 10 from their last national title appearance, an accolade that legendary coach Katie King Crowley is still chasing going into her 18th season at the helm of the program.

Nov. 27 will mark only the fifth time in each program's history that these two will intertwine on the ice, with the last matchup coming nearly five years ago.

Minnesota is coming off the bad end of an NCAA regionals upset against Northeastern, which resulted in the firing of Brad Frost, so they'll be looking to get right back into the fray of the consistent contention they became accustomed to.

Minnesota has their work cut out for them in year one of the Greg May era, who has some overtly giant shoes to fill in Minneapolis, not only being just the third head coach to lead the maroon and gold, but also replacing the greatest coach in the program's history.

With consecutive games against two hungry programs, these could make or break the season for the Nittany Lions if they take either of them lightly or don't play to their full potential.

To wrap up nonconference play, Penn State will hit the Ivy League circuit, with two games each against two of the top programs that the Eastern College Athletic Conference has to offer.

Coach Jeff Kampersal returns to his alma mater Dec. 9 when Penn State meets with the Princeton Tigers for only the second time since departing for State College in 2017. The last meeting with the Tigers was only two years into Kampersal's tenure

Since then, Kampersal has become a household name not only within the program but in the sport itself, a highly touted figure among players and coaches alike.

Princeton is ushering in a new era after a change of the guard, with former Boston Fleet head coach Courtney Kessel entering her second year as Tigers head coach, replacing Cara Morey.

Cornell has recently resurged, just two years removed from its first Frozen Four appearance of the decade. Three-time AHCA Coach of the Year, Doug Derraugh, is looking to return to the Big Red of the 2010s, when four of the program's five Frozen Four appearances landed, and even a berth in the NCAA tournament final.

The Nittany Lions play host to the Big Red for a two-game series at the turn of the new year, and hopefully in the thick of early preparations for both the AHA and NCAA tournaments, respectively.

Penn State will look to even up the historical record against the reigning Ivy League champs, with two of their three all-time wins against the Big Red coming in the previous year.

A rematch with Princeton closes nonconference play for the blue and white, this time with the roles reversed, and the Nittany Lions will welcome the Tigers to Pegula Ice Arena.

title: Column | Three key takeaways from the start of Rob Dow era
author: Ava Aguiar | The Daily Collegian
description:
After a rocky last two seasons with the Nittany Lions finishing last in the Big Ten, and seeing former head coach Jeff Cook resign, all eyes are on Rob Dow to rebuild the legacy of Penn State on the pitch.

Dow comes to Penn State after coaching at Vermont for the last nine years. Under his leadership, Dow took the team to five NCAA tournaments and won the National Championship in 2024, boasting a 129-41-21 record over his tenure. He and his staff were also acknowledged as back-to-back America East Coaching Staff of the Year.

With these accolades, expectations are high for what he can do for the program in his debut season with the Nittany Lions.

The blue and white currently sit at 2-2, starting the season strong with a 3-2 win against Mercyhurst, before falling to Missouri State and Pitt. However, just ahead of the Nittany Lions’ first round of conference play, Penn State saw a 1-0 win over Yale, where the underclassmen shone during the match.

As Penn State looks to take on Washington this Friday, here are some of the key takeaways from the start of the Dow Era.

The team is driven, but still learning

With only three returning players from last season’s roster, including defenders Morgan Marshall and Joe Sheridan, along with goalkeeper Fredrick Grundin, the team is stacked with underclassmen and new faces. In the first game of the season, 11 players made their NCAA debut.

With this comes inexperience at this level of competition, the blue and white received multiple yellow cards against Missouri State, all from rough play. Sophomore Joe Buckley was ejected from the match after two yellow cards and a hard tackle saw him leave the field.

During the same game, freshman midfielder Nehan Hassan was given a yellow for an aggressive tackle, which, when questioned by Dow, saw him instantly thrown from the match.

With more experience and time on the field, plays and calls like this are sure to be reduced as new players get more comfortable playing at the collegiate level.

They need to play as one

With an almost fresh roster, Penn State is struggling to play as one and still has to find its groove. This is something that can only come with time and practice, and according to coach Dow, they are nowhere near where they want and need to be.

“I think we’re all seeing where we can be, and that’s probably the beginner's frustration right now, but perspective is important,” Dow said on Aug. 26. “Three returning players were working a ton off the field to try to develop just relationships and chemistry, but on the field, hold the high standards.”

Most evidently, the early stages of building the team were seen in the Nittany Lions’ games against Missouri State where they struggled to get it going in the first half, despite Luca Sowinski’s first and only goal for the team during the match.

The second half threw the team for a loop, with multiple yellow cards and messy mistakes that saw the blue and white playing down a player for the rest of the game.

As the team gets used to playing together, with the talent of Amadou Kone and the promise of Hassan and Buckley, they have plenty of untapped potential waiting to be showcased on the field.

Good things take time

While this is only Dow’s first season, along with many of his players and there’s still a road to go, the team is strong and driven, consistently putting pressure on the ball and bringing the fire to each game.

In their match against Mercyhurst, the team took charge in the early minutes and won the first corner kick. While they let up the pace at first, they came back in the second, earning three back-to-back corners and possession of the ball for most of the half.

At the end of the game, it was recorded that the team earned 16 corner kicks, the most Penn State has seen in a match since 2009, further showing the ambition that this team has.

Once again in its match against Yale, Penn State put pressure on and controlled the first 15 minutes of the game, taking multiple shots and refusing to back down against the Bulldogs' offense. Penn State continued this pattern in the second half, pushing in a strong offensive battle to score and win 1-0 against the Ivy League team.

The season is long, and the Rob Dow era has just begun. While the Nittany Lions have some ways to go to be where they want to be as a team and establish themselves as a force to reckon with, the signs are already there. Dow’s team is passionate, competitive and driven, and with time could be a future NCAA contender, a dominating team in the Big Ten, and on a national scale.

title: Preview | Penn State field hockey looks to take on No. 4 Princeton after sweep last weekend
author: Annie Gleba | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State will face No. 4 Princeton this Sunday after sweeping both its contests last weekend. The matchup marks the Nittany Lions toughest opponent so far this season, with Princeton falling to No. 4 after starting week one at No. 2.

This is also the blue and white’s last game before it starts up Big Ten play, looking ahead to next Thursday's game against Maryland. Additionally, Penn State will celebrate Youth and Alumni Day that week, welcoming back former players and young girls who love the sport.

Overall, the Nittany Lions are 3-1, dropping their season opener but continuing on a three-game win streak. The blue and white won both games last weekend by two goals, including a shutout win over Villanova in their game last Friday.

Princeton sits at 1-1 after a blowout win over ODU in its season opener and a loss to No.5 North Carolina, 1-0 in shootout fashion. The Tigers will take on No. 17 Rutgers on Friday before traveling up to Happy Valley.

Taking a look at the matchups on offense, the Nittany Lions have been able to rely on many players in their starting line up and beyond. There are six players who currently hold four or more total points already this season.

The top three of the pack are Ella Gaitan with eight points, and Joji Purdy and Sienna Dunn with seven apiece. Gaitan, the top point keeper, has a team-best four goals so far this season, as the junior forward routinely pounds the defense, ending two games this season with six shots.

On the Tigers side, with only two games under their belt, it appears the upperclassmen are taking the front seat in leading the offense. Anna Faulstich, Hope Delaney and Pru Lindsey have all scored one goal. Faulstich leads the trio with three points on the season, while Delaney and Lindsey each own two.

With Princeton early in its season, the Tigers are still building their offense and looking for key players.

Looking at the defensive side, the Nittany Lions goalkeeper Aby Deverka was named the NFCA Defensive Player of the Week, becoming the first Penn State player to win the defensive award.

The award comes after the netminder made nine saves in the game against Delaware, only letting one shot go through. Deverka’s save percentage now sits at .792, totaling 19 saves on the season, as she stands as a main obstacle in Princeton’s way.

Princeton's defense is led by its own star netminder in the form of senior Olivia Caponiti, who has started and played through both of the Tigers' games so far this season. Caponiti has allowed zero goals this season with four saves.

The matchup will take place on Sunday at noon and can be found on Big Ten Plus. Penn State already has four games under its belt, looking for this to be enough as Princeton goes on the road to compete in just its second week of play.

title: Players to watch | RB Keveun Mason, 2 quarterbacks highlight Temple’s roster
author: Noah Aberegg | The Daily Collegian
description:
It’s been 10 years since Penn State and Temple have faced off, with the Nittany Lions firmly dominating the rivalry.

The Owls have several key returners on this year’s squad, but also have many new faces with 29 true freshmen and 23 transfer portal additions.

Temple started the season off on a strong note with a 38-14 win over Rhode Island. However, it will face its toughest opponent of the season in the No. 16 Nittany Lions on Saturday.

But anything can happen — as shown by Temple’s historic upset in 2015. Here’s a few players that could aid in another potential upset from the Owls.

Keveun Mason, running back

Temple’s passing attack garnered just 142 yards between Ajani Sheppard and Jaxon Smolik. Running back Keveun Mason recorded 158 rushing yards alone.

Mason was a key piece in Saturday’s victory, finding the end zone for a pair of touchdowns to end the second and third quarters. The sophomore star averaged 7.9 yards per carry, but also played a large role in the passing game with two receptions for 34 yards.

As a true freshman, Mason played in nine games, recording 167 yards and a touchdown. However, he nearly exceeded that in his first game this year.

Penn State gave up just 44 yards in the run game against Marshall. The only true runner was dual-threat quarterback Carlos Del Rio-Wilson, so Mason’s skills will introduce a new challenge for the Nittany Lions this weekend.

Ajani Sheppard & Jaxon Smolik, quarterbacks

It remains unclear who will be the starting quarterback for the Owls in Week 2. Their first game featured a mix of two quarterbacks, as Sheppard completed the first pass of the game while Smolik threw the opening touchdown later that drive.

After 60 minutes, Sheppard led the way with 85 passing yards compared to Smolik’s 57 yards. However, it was Smolik who recorded the only touchdown of the day between the two.

While many see the quarterback struggle as a problem for Temple, it may also be a problem for Penn State when game planning. Sheppard is more of a dual-threat quarterback with 23 rushing yards last week, while Smolik has operated as more of a pocket passer.

Smolik played in four games in his three years with the Nittany Lions before transferring to Temple, giving him an opportunity to shine against his former team on Saturday.

Kaleb Artis, defensive tackle

While Kaleb Artis didn’t add to the stat sheet against Rhode Island, he had a big presence in his Temple debut. He earned a 77.7 grade from Pro Football Focus — the highest from the entire defensive line.

The former Nittany Lion is coming off a season-ending injury he sustained ahead of the 2025 season. However, he showed flashes of success earlier in his career, recording seven tackles and 1.5 tackles for loss in his 26 games played.

Artis is the second-biggest defensive tackle on the team, weighing in at 315 pounds. Penn State’s offensive line has focused on preparing for those bigger defenders with the addition of four defensive tackles over 300 pounds, and has also had its practice against Marshall’s Mikailin Warren, who tipped the scale at 380 pounds.

Tyree Alualu, linebacker

Tyree Alualu has played in 21 games over his first two seasons with Temple, earning a start each year.

However, he had arguably the biggest moment of his career against Rhode Island on Saturday. Midway through the fourth quarter, Alualu extended the Owls’ lead with a pick six, returning the ball 63 yards to the end zone.

Outside of his interception, the junior linebacker also recorded a pair of tackles and a pass deflection.

Alualu’s scoring opportunity on Saturday showcased his defensive potential, creating a big matchup with his speed and 230-pound frame.

title: The Penn State-Temple football rivalry through Collegian reporting
author: Andrew Mercer | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State and Temple have a storied — albeit lopsided — in-state rivalry that’s seen its fair share of blowouts, tight contests and a single groundbreaking upset.

Take a look at Penn State’s storied history against the Owls through the Collegian archives.

1931

The Penn State Collegian reported on Oct. 13, 1931, that the Nittany Lions were shut out, 12-0, by a “heavy Owl eleven” in the opening game between the programs.

Henry Reese’s 80-yard pick six was the play of the game before Corny Bonner scored the team’s second touchdown. Kicking wasn’t what it is now, as both point-after attempts missed.

1940

The Nittany Lions first beat Temple in 1940 after sending their first undefeated team to Philadelphia in 20 years.

Dick Peters, who wrote the “Between the Lions” column, said he was confident that the Nittany Lions were ready to counter Temple’s strong passing game.

“They’ve heard, eaten and slept aerial defense all week, and if that defense comes through, plus a superior Nittany line and running attack, State will pluck the Owl by two touchdowns,” Peters wrote on Oct. 25, 1940.

1950

The 1950 rendition of the storied rivalry had a couple of firsts. Notably, it was the first time Rip Engle faced Temple as head coach, and it was the first and only tie of the all-time series, with a final score of 7-7.

However, it wasn’t Engle’s first encounter with the Owls. The Collegian reported that he’d suffered a 110-0 loss to Temple with now-defunct Blue Ridge College. He beat the Owls with Western Maryland two years later, posting a blocked punt and a pick six.

Penn State faced the Owls on Homecoming that year, and Collegian writer Marv Krasnansky said “no holds will be barred” at New Beaver Field in front of a predicted crowd of 25,000.

Despite having motivation, Penn State’s offense slumped despite using Engle’s proven Winged-T formation, and Engle had no idea why.

“I was beginning to think there was something wrong with the system,” Engle said Oct. 30, 1950. “But Brown, which doesn’t have too much, scored 27 points in one period against Colgate, and Paul Bixler has a good club.”

1978

In April 1978, the date of Penn State’s away game against Temple was moved from Nov. 18 to the season-opener on Sept. 1 at 8 p.m. At the time, it was the earliest the program had ever played a regular season game.

Joe Paterno said that the switch was to make accommodations for Penn State’s final exam schedule, per the Collegian’s Neil Rudel. However, the situation wasn’t without controversy.

Many thought that the switch was really made so that Penn State would have more experience before facing Ohio State. Paterno denied these claims.

“I don’t relish the idea of opening against Temple when I remember what happened the last two times we played them down there,” Paterno said.

Paterno’s instincts were right, as Penn State scraped by with a 10-7 victory.

1981

On Oct. 2, 1981, Ron Gardner penned a story that gave historical context to the Owls 1941 victory, reminding readers what else took place 40 years prior.

“Japanese-American relations grew strained in Tokyo, the Nazis claimed victory at Odessa, the U.S. diplomatic corps fled the embassy in Moscow and a then-undefeated Temple football team downed Penn State 14-0 in Philadelphia,” Gardner wrote.

Times had changed on the gridiron too. The Nittany Lions won the last 15 games in the series, and Penn State became a force to be reckoned with at the beginning of the 1980s.

“Weaknesses — I haven’t seen any,” Temple head coach Wayne Hardin said. “I’ve been following Penn State since 1955 when I was assistant coach at Navy, and we played against Lenny Moore and the great team that they had. And I think this is the best Penn State team I’ve seen.”

After hearing Temple’s thoughts on the 1981 matchup, Gardner likened the contest to climbing Mt. Sinai to meet God, only to find Penn State there lying in wait.

Penn State shut out the Owls the next day, 30-0, at Beaver Stadium.

1989

Mark Wogenrich wrote a story for the Sept. 12, 1989, issue of the Collegian regarding a recent string of “first-time-in-who-knows-when” upsets of Penn State before asking, “Well, how about it Temple?”

It wasn’t the Owls’ year after all, falling 42-3, per the Sept. 18, 1989 issue.

“They outfought us for the ball,” Temple coach Jerry Berndt said. “Our coaching staff worked hard all week on playing the ball and we didn’t do it.”

2015

In James Franklin’s second year as head coach, the unthinkable happened.

The Nittany Lions, who had dominated Temple for nearly three-quarters of a century, lost.

Connor Whooley reported on Sept. 6, 2015, that there were three glaring issues that caused Penn State’s downfall at Lincoln Financial Field. Christian Hackenberg got sacked 10 times and was subsequently frazzled, Nyeem Wartman-White suffered a knee injury on special teams and the offense completely stalled from the second quarter on.

After scoring the first 10 points, the Owls scored the last 27 to send Penn State home with its first loss to Temple in 74 years.

“I couldn’t tell you right now what really happened, why we went in such a drought,” wide receiver Geno Lewis said after the game. “I have to go back and look at the film to see what was going on.”

Hackenberg was short with his responses postgame. “We’re on to Buffalo,” he said.

2016

Penn State got back on track in its most recent outing against Temple.

Giana Han’s story on Sept. 17, 2016 centered around Saquon Barkley’s immense impact. Han reported that Barkley “burst past the first level of Temple defenders into the open field with less than eight minutes remaining in the game.”

Barkley’s 55-yard rushing touchdown effectively stalled any momentum Temple was building.

“I thought we did a good job against Barkley up until that last run,” Temple coach Matt Rhule said. “And obviously, you can’t win a ball game when you allow him to have a 55-yard run.”

title: Returnees, incoming recruits headline Penn State women's hockey forward unit
author: Rafael Rivera | The Daily Collegian
description:
The 2026-27 Penn State season is right around the corner and the team has a look to continue ascending after the program's first Frozen Four appearance last season. With seven players being drafted to the PWHL the Nittany Lions have to retool and find similar offensive production if they want to get back to their 2025-26 form.

Here’s a look at Penn State's forwards for the upcoming campaign.

Grace Outwater

The Picton, Ontario, native is coming off her best collegiate season yet, where she was crowned AHA Scoring Champion with 31 points in league play. Outwater finished her second collegiate season with 24 goals, 16 assists and 40 total points.

The Nittany Lions return an experienced player who has proved she's a top scorer in the nation. The junior steps into a captain role where she will be expected to be the blue and white’s top scorer in this season.

Abby Stonehouse

Stonehouse, a junior right wing from Blenheim, Ontario, Canada, has skated in every game for the Nittany Lions the last two seasons. In 77 career contests, Stonehouse has 23 goals and 15 assists.

Last campaign, Stonehouse posted a plus/minus of +28 and ranked fifth on the team in goals. In the upcoming campaign, Stonehouse aims to continue her steady improvement and become a real threat for opposing defenses, slotting in as an alternate for the Nittany Lions next year.

Mikah Keller

The Moisinee, Wisconsin, native had a productive first season for the blue and white where she put up eight goals and a whopping 26 assists, the most by a freshman in program history, leading her to be named to the All-AHA Rookie Team.

Keller has exceptional playmaking ability, and she has a chance to pair that with more goals to be on her way to a stellar season.

Matilde Fantin

In the Como, Italy, native's first season with the Nittany Lions Fantin totaled 23 points on 10 goals and 13 assists in 26 matches. Fantin missed some time while representing Italy at the 2026 Milan Cortina Olympics, scoring three goals in the tournament.

The sophomore missed about 13 games for the blue and white, but still managed to put up solid numbers. With the Nittany Lions presumably having her for the whole season, Fantin has the chance to bring a lot more with the team full time.

Sofia Ismael

Hailing from St George, Ontario, the freshman previously spent three seasons with the Etobicoke Jr. Dolphins U22 team, appearing in 125 games and totaling 71 goals and 100 assists for 171 points, making her a point-per-game scorer.

Ismael has represented Canada on the world stage twice, playing at the IIHF U18 Women's World Championship in both 2025 and 2026. In the latter she claimed a silver medal, impressing in the tournament by recording seven goals and eight assists for 15 points during only six tournament games.

She’s already proven herself on the world stage. It’s now time to see if she can produce at the collegiate level.

Kylie Amelkovich

The Glen Ellyn, Illinois, native spent five seasons at Shattuck-St. Mary's, where she appeared in 152 games while recording 76 goals and 83 assists for 159 points.

Amelkovich also has international experience, having represented Team USA at the IIHF U18 Women's World Championship in both 2025 and 2026. In 2026, she appeared in six games, recording two goals and 12 assists for 14 points while helping the United States become the first team in tournament history to complete a "perfect gold".

The freshman arrives in Happy Valley with a real opportunity to see playing time in her debut season.

Nicole Hall

The junior from Stockholm, Sweden, has totaled 18 goals and 14 assists, tallying up to 32 points in 71 games played throughout her career.

Hall competed at the 2026 Milan Cortina Olympics with Sweden and also missed a midseason stint with the Nittany Lions. The forward has gotten consistently better, making improvements in all of her numbers as the years have progressed, and she has a chance to continue that trend with an even larger role.

Lorelai Nelson

Nelson played at high school hockey powerhouse Edina in Minnesota, where she appeared in 151 games totaling 82 goals and 97 assists for 179 points. She won the highly coveted Minnesota State championship. Nelson also has National experience, representing the United States in the 2024 U18 Series against Canada.

Additionally, Nelson competed for the Minnesota Lakers Tier I program, helping the team capture the 2026 USA Hockey Tier I National Championship. The gem of the Nittany Lions’ incoming recruits, Nelson was a finalist for the 2026 Ms. Hockey Award.

McKenna Walsh

The Oswego, Illinois, native has appeared in 76 games for the Nittany Lions over two seasons, where she has scored eight goals and 14 assists, totaling 22 total career points.

In a group of new faces, Walsh turns over impactful collegiate experience to the 2026-27 roster.

Sydney McIntosh

The freshman from Langley, British Columbia, competed for RINK Hockey Academy Kelowna during the 2025-26 season, recording 13 goals and 26 assists for 39 points in 48 games.

Before the RINK Hockey Academy, McIntosh spent two seasons at Shattuck-St. Mary's, appearing in 53 games while totaling 35 goals and 31 assists for 66 points.

Alanna Devlin

Devlin, a junior transfer from Boston College, tallied nine goals and 13 assists in two seasons for the Eagles. In 2024, she represented Team USA at the 2024 IIHF U18 Women's World Championship, helping the United States capture the gold medal.

Devlin joins coach Jeff Kampersal’s team at Penn State where she has a chance to take the next step in her attacking game.

Kayla McCarthy

The Pittsburgh native previously played for the Pens Elite for six seasons. During her senior season, McCarthy recorded 20 goals and 21 assists for 41 points in 57 games.

The 5-foot-10 forward is a five-time USA Hockey National Championship qualifier. McCarthy had significant success at the club level.

title: Penn State vs. Temple preview | Betting odds, scouting report on the Owls and more
author: Andrew Mercer | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State and Temple will meet for the first time since 2016, and for the first time under Matt Campbell, at noon Saturday at Lincoln Financial Field in Philadelphia.

The in-state opponents have a storied history dating back to 1931. The Nittany Lions have since dominated the series, holding a 40-4-1 record over the Owls.

Penn State last played at the Linc, however, in the 2015 season opener and suffered a 27-10 upset. 2016 was the most recent matchup between the two squads, with the Nittany Lions getting revenge.

Here’s a deeper look into the weather, programming methods and team previews heading into Week 2.

Forecast

After a partly cloudy morning, the cloud coverage should part in time for kick off, and the teams can expect intermittent clouds throughout the contest, per AccuWeather.

The temperature will have picked up to 81 degrees with a real feel of 85 right at noon. The heat will slowly rise during the game to a high of 83 degrees with a real feel of 87.

Fans who make the trip from State College may experience rainfall on the ride home, which will start at approximately 7 p.m.

Betting, how to watch

For the second-consecutive game, the sportsbooks are anticipating a dominant win for the Nittany Lions.

Penn State is a 23.5 point favorite to beat the Owls, per FanDuel. The over-under is set at 49.5 points, so the Nittany Lions are projected to win 37-13.

The game will be broadcast on ESPN2, while tickets are available for as low as $71.75 on Ticketmaster.

About Temple

Temple took down Rhode Island, 38-14, to start the season after a 5-7 campaign last year.

The Owls’ offense begins with a pair of transfer quarterbacks, both from Big Ten programs. Former Nittany Lion Jaxon Smolik moved east, and Ajani Sheppard transferred from Rutgers.

Both quarterbacks struggled in the passing game against the Rams, combining for just 142 yards on 16 attempts. Smolik had a better day passing, throwing a touchdown pass to Jayce Freeman on the Owls’ opening drive. However, Smolik had issues protecting the football, fumbling twice.

Running back Keveun Mason far outperformed the rest of the offense with an explosive ground game. Mason accumulated 158 yards, averaging 7.9 yards per carry with a pair of touchdowns.

However, Temple’s offensive line is severely banged up, and that could hinder Mason’s ability to break free. Four of the top-seven offensive linemen are dealing with injuries, per Shawn Pastor of Owls Daily. Those four are tackles Giakoby Hills and Kevin Terry, left guard Eric King and Luke Watson.

Linebacker Curly Ordonez led Temple’s defense with eight tackles against the Rams, followed by safety Saboor Karriem with six.

About Penn State

Penn State started the 2026 season on the right foot with a 45-0 rout of Marshall in the annual Stripe Out. After the win, the Nittany Lions rose two spots in the AP Poll and are currently ranked No. 16.

The Nittany Lions used six different players to score their six touchdowns against the Thundering Herd and got to play a lot of their depth in the second half.

Rocco Becht and Koby Howard had statement performances to kick off the schedule. Becht played a clean game, going 13-for-18 for 271 passing yards and four touchdowns. Howard was Becht’s top receiver, as the sophomore racked up 161 receiving yards and a 42-yard touchdown on six catches.

The wide receivers found success largely because Marshall’s defense put a lot of emphasis into stopping the tight ends and the running backs.

Penn State’s tight end room is one of the best on the team. Benjamin Brahmer and Andrew Rappleyea played the majority of the season opener, but the room also has Gabe Burkle, a key contributor at Iowa State who is working his way back from injury.

Meanwhile, running backs Carson Hansen, James Peoples, Cam Wallace and Quinton Martin Jr. all underwhelmed against Marshall, combining for 3.9 yards per carry on 40 total attempts. Although Wallace and Martin got into a rhythm in the second half, Hansen and Peoples were routinely stuffed at the line of scrimmage.

Against Marshall, Penn State’s defense was headlined by Caleb Bacon, who made his debut at defensive end after a position switch from linebacker. He had six tackles, three tackles and one sack.

Penn State’s linebackers, Tony Rojas and Kooper Ebel, also had big days and are looking to continue building momentum against Temple. Other notable defensive starters include cornerback Audavion Collins and safeties Jeremiah Cooper and Marcus Neal Jr.

Injury updates

Campbell confirmed on Wednesday that Burkle linebacker Alex Tatsch will be playing on Saturday, both coming back from injuries sustained last season. Campbell said that the pair were “close to playing” against Marshall.

Additionally, Campbell also confirmed that LaVar Arrington II will likely be out for four to six weeks after undergoing a cleanup knee surgery.

Armstrong Nnodim, Alijah Carnell and Owen Aliciene are questionable. All three didn’t dress for Marshall but have practiced this week.
