title: ‘My voice alone isn't gonna cut it’ | Social media posts voice concerns about on-campus Flock cameras
author: Jonathon Chiu | The Daily Collegian
description:
When State College resident and political activist Ryan Caldwell first heard concerns from a friend about the nationwide presence of cameras made by Flock Safety, he knew he had to investigate further.

Caldwell viewed a map made by DeFlock, a volunteer organization that’s been tracking the expansion of automated license plate reader (ALPR) cameras nationwide since 2024, where he discovered the presence of several ALPRs in State College — including Flock cameras located on Penn State’s University Park campus.

“The first time I looked at the DeFlock map, I was like, ‘Wow, there are a lot of cameras here that I didn't know about,’” Caldwell, a second-year studying political science at George Washington University, said. “I went out there in-person and started looking for the cameras myself, because they are quite difficult to see if you're not looking for them, and then after that, I started reporting on it and kind of hit the ground running with my activism.”

Caldwell’s posts on Instagram and TikTok about the presence of ALPR cameras both on and off campus haven’t gone unnoticed. An Instagram reel he posted on Aug. 5 highlighting University Park’s Flock cameras and Leonardo ELSAG video plate hunter cameras located at the intersection of South Atherton Street and Westerly Parkway has already gained almost 4,700 likes and 289 comments.

According to DeFlock, there are over 20 Flock cameras across University Park that were mapped by contributors. The Daily Collegian confirmed their presence in the spring.

DeFlock’s map also reports that Flock cameras have been spotted at several Penn State Commonwealth campuses, including Altoona, Behrend and Harrisburg.

Penn State’s partial exemption from Pennsylvania’s Right-to-Know Law means university records related to Flock usage, which would include audit logs and data collected from the cameras, are not accessible to the public.

Penn State’s Flock cameras represent a fraction of the 120,000 deployed across the United States, according to the American Civil Liberties Union, which use artificial intelligence to analyze collected data with the findings made accessible through a networked database.

The nationwide usage of Flock’s cameras has been criticized as an implementation of mass surveillance that infringes on peoples’ privacy and doesn't provide adequate measures to ensure transparency from law enforcement.

This viewpoint is increasingly gaining traction, especially following reports of Flock cameras and their data being used by law enforcement officers to track women seeking abortions and to stalk people and by Immigrations & Customs Enforcement (ICE) for their operations.

Caldwell said he believes his posts have sparked increased discussions about Flock and other automated license plate reader cameras in State College. An Aug. 16 town hall he organized and moderated saw attendees express their concerns about Flock cameras to Pennsylvania House Rep. Paul Takac (D-Centre) and PA-15 Democratic congressional candidate Ray Bilger.

“It definitely showed, right off of the bat, how much the people cared about this issue,” Caldwell said.

Several Penn State students, faculty and staff have already expressed concerns about the university's use of Flock cameras. One student even made a website — psuprivacy.com — to document their presence both at University Park and on Penn State’s commonwealth campuses.

Inspired by Caldwell’s posts, Penn State student Parker Wallis decided to ask people their thoughts about the University Park Flock cameras. These interviews were then posted as a four-part series to Instagram and TikTok as part of his podcast, “Parcast with Parker,” which combined have received thousands of views and likes and dozens of comments.

“We never had the chance to vote on whether or not these Flock cameras should be installed in our community and so I knew I had to do this,” Wallis, a second-year studying broadcast journalism, said. “My voice alone isn't gonna cut it but if I can pass on this information online and I can get people to realize what’s going on in State College and Penn State University — why these ALPR cameras are here and how they’re being used — I can seriously do some damage and I can help to fight against these Flock cameras.”

Wallis said there is potential to push back against Penn State’s use of Flock cameras through on-campus organizations such as the University Park Undergraduate Association. But others, including Caldwell, see the only way to ensure the university cuts ties with the company is through pressuring lawmakers in Harrisburg to pass in-state legislation regulating or banning ALPRs.

The issue of Flock cameras and other automated license plate readers has already reached the halls of Harrisburg, where several bills have been proposed seeking to either restrict or ban them in the Commonwealth.

Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro has also voiced concerns about the use of Flock cameras in the state, and said he was open to signing a bill banning them statewide.

However, there are House and Senate bills in the works which, if passed, would allow the Pennsylvania Department of Transportation to issue permits for ALPRs to be installed along state-designated highways.

In lieu of clear guidance from Harrisburg, Trevor White, a member of the Ferguson Township Board of Supervisors, filed a request for the township to explore the viability of implementing ALPR restrictions within its borders. This request was approved during the board’s Sept. 1 meeting.

White said he is familiar with Caldwell’s posts about Penn State’s Flock cameras and appreciates their increased discussion via social media. However, he said these posts act more as a reflection of the opposition to ALPRs, which was already being channeled through movements like DeFlock.

“Regardless of the social media outcry, folks have been on this beat for a long time,” White said.

Because he believes opposition toward Flock cameras is approaching a “critical mass,” White said it’s important to enact local restrictions so they’re handled in a way where people aren’t influenced by social media, especially by posts calling for the vandalizing of Flock cameras, to act rashly against their usage.

“I'm looking for a solution here because there are people who want these but the vast majority of folks around here do not want ALPRs like Flock,” White said. “We just want to be able to live our lives and not be tracked by these private companies.”

title: Column | Underage haven: The Lion's Den’s reputation
author: Quentin Jurney | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State is well known for its party scene, which students have enjoyed for decades, and it consistently ranks high in polls of the country's party schools. In a 2027 top party school ranking by Niche, Penn State came in at number six.

Whether it be fraternities or the lucrative bar scene, partying is synonymous with Penn State’s name. Since the drinking age is 21, many freshmen and sophomores (and select juniors) can’t go out to the various bars downtown. As such, many turn to the internet to order fake IDs in hopes of getting a taste of the 21+ student nightlife.

Most bars are extremely strict and are veterans when it comes to verifying IDs. Bars even have built-in incentives for bouncers to confiscate fake IDs. There’s one bar that stands alone from the rest with a decades-long reputation for being notoriously loose with ID regulation, and has even earned the nickname “freshman bar” because of how easy it is to get in with a fake ID.

The Lion’s Den has held this reputation since as early as the 90s. This circulates through word of mouth, and the Den obviously doesn’t openly advertise an underage drinking policy. But with a decadelong reputation, it makes you wonder how they get away with that kind of leniency.

This isn’t a new rumor, either. I heard it long before I even set foot in State College. The Lion’s Den fiercely denies any wrongdoing, and promises that its policies are preventative enough to stop people with fake IDs from getting into their bar.

Less than five years ago, the Den posted that they were raided by Liquor Control Enforcement (LCE) and several people were cited for having fake IDs.

“Last night we were inspected by LCE due to complaints from another local establishment. Several people were cited for possessing a fake ID. We’re extremely confident that our policies have protected our establishment from any legal issues. Please be very careful, because Liquor Control Enforcement will inspect every bar at some point,” the Den said in an Instagram post.

When it comes to underage drinking and using fakes at public establishments, I don’t believe the drinking itself is the most harmful part. There are people with bad intentions who go to bars and other places where alcohol is served: Predators and other malfeasant individuals, for one, may take advantage of it. I’m not saying this doesn’t happen to people, especially women, over the age of 21 in other establishments, because it does, but a space so widely known as a sort of safe haven for underage alcohol indulgence will likely turn into a breeding ground for that kind of behavior.

What makes underage people, again, mostly women, especially vulnerable in bars is that they might hesitate to speak out against this type of behavior, since they’re breaking the law by being there in the first place. In turn, they’re more prone to being targeted because individuals know they won’t speak out, too.

There’s no Lion’s Den policy welcoming fake IDs, and they do check ID upon entering the bar. It just strikes me as strange that a well-established bar has a notorious reputation among students for allowing fake IDs and enabling underage drinking. And when the bar has, to their own admittance, been caught accepting fakes — whether they say they knew they were fakes or not — the rumors are no longer just rumors.

Whether or not allowing fake IDs is a “don’t ask, don’t tell" policy, bad training or just blatant ignorance, the fact remains that it’s known to happen, especially among students, at this establishment.

As a responsible bar owner, I would try everything possible to nip this rumour in the bud and make known that it's not true. Not only to prevent underage drinking, but to try and salvage the reputation of this bar-life staple in State College.

title: Penn State falls to No. 6 Ohio State in seasons first conference matchup
author: Sara Castrovinci | The Daily Collegian
description:
Battling under the lights at Jesse Owens Memorial Stadium in Columbus, Ohio, Penn State and No. 6 Ohio State faced off at the start of the season’s Big Ten play.

The Buckeyes took a 1-0 victory over the Nittany Lions, for their first conference win of the season.

The two programs opened up the first half of play with stints of offensive attacks on both final thirds of the pitch.

The Buckeyes’ Amanda Schlueter started off the first half with a quick attacking play in the six-yard box that was ultimately deflected back to center field by the blue and white.

Playing out of a 4-2-1-3 formation, Penn State quickly retaliated in Ohio State’s 18-yard box with a shot on goal from Ellie Kocher that was knocked away by Buckeye senior goalkeeper Peighton Northrup.

In the 17th minute, Penn State’s Kayleigh Herr was knocked down during Ava Grecco’s unsuccessful header on goal. Herr walked off the field after the play.

Herr, being the backbone of the Nittany Lions’ defensive end, constantly organizing and communicating on the pitch, was quickly sent back on the field.

With Herr back in the match, Schlueter created a counterattack from the half in the 20th minute, where she found Jadin Bonham in the eighteen. Bonham took a touch and placed a powerful shot in the back of the net, giving the Buckeyes a 1-0 lead.

Schlueter tallied the assist, making it the 26th of her career, pushing her past Lisa Grubb to record the second-most career assists in Ohio State program history.

Penn State head coach Erica Dambach challenged a play in the 30th minute, looking for a potential penalty opportunity. The effort was denied, and Dambach lost one of her two challenges for the match.

Operating out of a 4-2-3-1 formation, the Buckeyes were focusing on building through Grecco in the middle to Schlueter on the left side. The blue and white had to step on the gas to keep up with Schlueter’s fast pace and ability to split through their defense.

Ohio State continued with a high press in the final few minutes of the first half while Penn State’s game play shifted to a more compact defense, learning to sit comfortably without the ball.

Heading into the first half, both teams split time on the ball evenly, but Ohio State quickly turned the tide. The Buckeyes began winning back possession fast after losing it, balancing off each other’s movements, spacing and transitional play.

At the end of the half, the Nittany Lions tallied six corners to the Buckeyes none, but even with those offensive opportunities, Ohio State won the first half of conference play going into the final 45 minutes leading 1-0.

The blue and white continued to battle against the Buckeyes attacking chemistry entering the second half.

Bonham led a counterattack in the 47th minute but Lilly Burger tracked her down and regained possession on a clean slide tackle. This marked the second big time tackle of the night for Burger on a potential goal scoring opportunity.

Back in Ohio State’s final third, Kocher got past the Buckeye defense to cross the ball from the left to Aubrey Kulpa. Kulpa got her left boot on the ball and rocketed a shot towards the net, but just missed to the right.

In the 65th minute, Kulpa, sitting just outside the eighteen got a quick one touch shot opportunity off an aerial ball, firing it just off the crossbar.

Ohio State hadn’t had dangerous possession in the blue and whites’ final third for some time until a fast paced break away from Callie Tumilty in the 70th minute. Tumilty placed an undefended shot on goal but was deflected by Mackenzie Gress. Tumilty regained possession, but was rejected by the Nittany Lions’ netminder once more.

Penn State’s level of offensive pressure grew in the final 20 minutes of the match. Kulpa pressured up on Northrup after a huge mistouch, gaining wide open possession but skied the ball above the open net, missing an opportunity for the equalizer.

Despite desperately trying to create offensive opportunities in the final quarter of the match, the Nittany Lions were unable to break through Ohio State's solid defense. The game ended 1-0 with the Buckeyes taking their first conference match on their home turf.

Penn State returns to Jeffrey Field, facing Minnesota at noon Sunday

title: Jess Mruzik  makes USA Women's volleyball national team for Pan American Cup
author: Rafael Rivera | The Daily Collegian
description:
Former Penn State volleyball player Jess Mruzik has made the USA Women's Volleyball national team for the 2026 Pan American Cup, which will take place Sept. 11-18, in León, Guanajuato, Mexico. It’ll be the 23rd edition of the tournament; the United States has won the tournament seven times, with the last win coming in 2019.

Mruzik spent her first three collegiate seasons in Ann Arbor with Michigan and her final season in State College with Penn State. The Livonia, Michigan, native had a decorative collegiate career tallying 2,030 kills, 129 assists and 1,192 digs racking up numerous awards such as NCAA Championship Most Outstanding Player, three AVCA All-America honors first team in 2024, second team in 2023, honorable mention in 2021, four First-Team All-Big Ten accolades and finally an NCAA National Championship in 2024 with the Nittany lions.

Following her collegiate career, Mruzik opted to play professionally in LOVB’S Houston Franchise. In two LOVB seasons, Mruzik has made the Icon team twice, getting a first-team nod in 2025 and a second-team nod in 2026.

After two pro seasons, Mruzik looks to help the USA win its first Pan American Cup since 2019.

title: ‘We can really play together’ | Penn State DTs buying in to togetherness
author: Andrew Deal | The Daily Collegian
description:
When D’Anton Lynn said they’d use “four to five tackles” throughout the game on defense, it alluded to the trust in the depth at the position.

The interior of the defense, with its notable addition of size, got off to a strong start on defense, holding Marshall’s run game to 44 yards in a 45-0 win over the Thundering Herd.

“We handled that, did our job, did what we needed to do, and guys had success,” defensive lineman Keanu Williams said Wednesday.

Williams got the starting nod alongside former UCLA teammate Siale Taupaki, and the duo set the tone for the rest of the defensive lineman during the rest of the game.

“We went to school together for a long time, and now that we went through this whole process and everything of coming here to Penn State, it's awesome to see, and I'm just glad I get to finish it off with him,” Williams said.

The performance became even more impressive given that multiple defensive tackles missed the game with injury. Armstrong Nnodim and Alijah Carnell both missed the game with injuries, but that didn’t hinder the result.

Replacing them as depth pieces were Penn State returnees Ty Blanding and De’Andre Cook, who stepped in and still made the unit run as normal.

“We can play together, and that we got to just sit here and just just do the basics,” Williams said. “Don't overthink things. Don't do too much. Don't do too less. Just do what we're supposed to do and do our job and do it to the fullest potential.”

Cook is a player who’s flown under the radar, but has consistently grown through offseason work. That work was put to the test against Marshall, and he stepped up, recording one tackle.

“To see his growth over the time of these couple of months that we've been together, and he came back from injury and all that stuff too,” Williams said. “So it's been awesome. And for him to get out there and I'm playing alongside of him, it's great to see.”

The growth of Cook in the room came in part due to the leadership from Taupaki, who “always made sure guys felt accepted.” Even without players who were expected to play, it was Cook who could come in and still make a difference.

“No one gets left behind,” Taupaki said. “That's not just a football thing. That's a family thing. So to be able to see him come out on Saturday and join us, it made my heart even happier because he's been through a lot.”

With Taupaki and Williams leading the way, and injured depth players expected to be back in the near future, the defensive line group has bought into the rotation. The unit will be tasked with shutting down Temple running back Keveun Mason who rushed for 158 yards in Week 1.

However, with the momentum the defensive line has after its first performance, it could be in for another strong game in its first road game of the year.

“That was really fun to have no points on the board, and I loved it,” Williams said. “And it shows that we can really play together. So if we do our details, this is what we're capable of doing, shutting people down for sure.”

title: As the U.S. approaches the 25th anniversary of 9/11, students set aside individual politics to honor the victims
author: Annabella Chaklos | The Daily Collegian
description:
Usually, the Penn State College Democrats and College Republicans can be seen tabling, organizing protests, speaker events, and mobilizing students to vote — against each other’s party.

But on Tuesday, both organizations were found together, huddled over 2,977 American flags, each one planted in memory of a victim of the terrorist attacks on Sep. 11, 2001.

Since 2010, the College Republicans have hosted a 9/11 memorial event, including the planting of 2,977 flags on Old Main lawn a few days before the service. For the last two years, the College Democrats have joined them in placing those flags.

Ryan Reichel, director of special events for the College Republicans, said he considers having the duty to plan out the memorial events an honor. Collaborating with the past special events director, Reichel has been planning Friday’s service since the middle of summer. He said Penn State President Neeli Bendapudi, State College mayor Ezra Nanes and Slippery Rock Mayor Jondavid Longo will all be in attendance.

“There's an event in everybody's lifetime that they know exactly where they were,” Reichel, a third-year studying accounting, said. “For my grandparents, it was Kennedy’s assassination. For my parents, it was 9/11. I was talking to my dad and a close family friend, and we were talking about 9/11, and the one thing they described to me was unity.”

Reichel said he sees these memorials as an opportunity to build unity during a time of political discord. He described his parents’ memory of the year after 9/11 as a time when it didn’t matter if you were a Democrat or Republican, everyone was an American.

“Our world is facing a great divide,” Reichel said, planting another flag into the grass. “I feel like this is an opportunity to somewhat get back to that and try to use it as a building block for the years to come.”

For Madeline Shanafelt, the president of the College Democrats, the 9/11 memorials demonstrate a love for America in the face of devastation.

“I think that 9/11 was such a tragedy in the United States that we should commemorate every year, especially with this one being the 25th,” Shanafelt, a fourth-year studying education and public policy and political science, said. “It's really important for our club and for me personally to participate to show my love for the country.”

Shanafelt said that it’s important to commemorate the tragedy no matter how much time has passed so it’s never forgotten.

“I think that that was one of the first large-scale attacks on that, and I think the United States is seen as impenetrable, and when that happened, it was proven not,” Shanafelt said. “So it really changed how things worked with valuing national security a lot and really protecting the United States’ security, which I do think really changed the way that now things are funded, or our emphasis on funding the military.”

Neve McAllister, the secretary of the College Republicans, said that despite most students not being alive when 9/11 happened, it’s still a story that all people need to learn about for the future.

“It brings the community together for a bigger purpose,” McAllister, a third-year studying criminology, said. “There's still people in this community who have lost people from 9/11. So being able to do this for them especially is really important.”

In addition to bringing the community together, McAllister believes having bipartisan events like the annual flag planting brings the two organizations closer to collaborate.

“State College is a very blue area, but then we're surrounded by a very red area, which makes it a little interesting in terms of polarization,” McAllister said, with a bundle of American flags in her arms. “I think being able to have our executive boards work together and collaborate is only going to allow executive boards to come to be able to work again together.”

Keegan Jolly, the vice president of the College Democrats believes that the partisan nature of today’s politics has no place in the remembrance of Sep. 11, 2001.

“I think 9/11 shouldn't be partisan at all,” Jolly, a fourth-year studying criminology, said. “We're all Americans. We're all affected. People that passed away in this tragedy, the thing that you don't immediately think of is whether they were a Democrat or a Republican or anything in between. They're all people.”

Jolly said that despite the country feeling divided right now, it is important to continually remind ourselves that everyone is here to celebrate and commemorate a nation and people that was and continues to be greatly affected, no matter anyone’s affiliation.

“I think the reminder of no matter what party that you're a part of, we're all Americans and unfortunately, sometimes it takes tragedy to remind us of that,” Jolly said. “But 9/11 is a day where, of course, we're reminded of tragedy, but we're also reminded of how beautiful it is to band together as Americans.”

title: Penn State men’s soccer opens Big Ten play against defending national champion Washington
author: Luci Palacios | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State opens Big Ten play Friday with its toughest test yet.

The Nittany Lions travel to face the Washington Huskies at 10:30 p.m. Friday, marking head coach Rob Dow’s first Big Ten matchup since taking over the program.

Penn State enters the game at 2-2 after shutting out Yale 1-0 at Jeffrey Field. Washington comes in at 3-2-1 and is fresh off a 4-0 win over UC Davis.

The matchup also gives Penn State its first chance to take on the defending NCAA champions. The Huskies have won all three meetings between the programs, including a 2-1 victory at Jeffrey Field on Oct. 20, 2025.

The Defending Champions

Washington enters its first Big Ten game as the reigning National Champion after defeating No. 15 seed N.C. State 3-2 in overtime of the national title game last season.

The championship marked Washington’s first NCAA men’s soccer title and the 13th national championship won by a Big Ten program.

Senior defender Harrison Bertos returns after scoring the championship-winning goal against N.C. State.

The Huskies also return one of the conference’s top threats in junior midfielder Zach Ramsey. Ramsey leads the NCAA and Big Ten with nine goals this season, adding one assist through six games.

Ramsey finished last season with 24 points on eight goals and eight assists. He was also named the Offensive Most Outstanding Player of the championship match.

Fifth-year midfielder Cameron Cruz gives Washington another option in attack. Cruz leads the Huskies with four assists, tying for seventh nationally.

Washington will also rely on fifth-year goalkeeper Stockton Short. The 6-foot-3 keeper has started every game this season, recording 11 saves with a .524 save percentage and a 1.68 goals-against average.

Penn State’s Test

Penn State comes into the matchup after its strongest defensive performance of the season.

The Nittany Lions held Yale to five shots and didn’t allow a single shot on target in Friday’s 1-0 win.

The performance was a step forward for a defense that has allowed seven goals through four games. Penn State will now face a much different challenge against Washington, which has scored 18 goals through six games. The Nittany Lions will need to carry over Friday’s defensive discipline while limiting the Huskies’ chances in front of goal.

Freshman goalkeeper Daniel Peluffo-Wiese recorded his first collegiate shutout. The 6-foot-7 keeper has started all four games he has played this season and gives Penn State a major presence in the box.

Peluffo-Wiese is part of a tall defensive group that also includes sophomore center back Joe Sheridan at 6-foot-6 and junior center back Noah Förster at 6-foot-4.

The Nittany Lions will need that size against Washington's attack led by Ramsey and Cruz.

Penn State also found some offense of its own against Yale. Sophomore Joe Buckley scored his first collegiate goal, while freshman Nehan Hasan recorded his first collegiate assist.

Friday’s matchup will give Dow his first look at Big Ten competition. Facing the defending national champions this early in conference play could provide an early measure of where Penn State stands under its new head coach.

title: Staff predictions | Can Penn State continue all-time dominance against Temple?
author: The Daily Collegian Football Staff
description:
Matt Campbell will be coaching for Penn State on the road for the first time this Saturday, as the Nittany Lions head to Philadelphia to face Temple.

“I think this is going to be huge for us,” Campbell said Tuesday. “Great teams play great on the road. That's just how it goes.”

Here’s how we think Penn State will perform this weekend after a dominant Week 1 win over Marshall.

Andrew Deal: Penn State 41, Temple 6

Penn State didn’t have any growing pains in its first game of the season, leading to a 45-0 victory over Marshall.

I expect the momentum from Week 1 to continue in Week 2 in front of a likely Penn State-heavy crowd at Lincoln Financial Field.

The Nittany Lions proved the talent they have and the depth at certain positions that could cause major issues in Temple’s upset attempt. On top of that, the Owls are likely without multiple starters, including three on the offensive line, which could have Penn State’s pass rush licking its chops on Saturday.

Temple’s offense was one-dimensional in a win over Rhode Island, but it’ll have to open up the pass game if it wants to keep things close. However, the Owls have yet to name a true starting quarterback, with both Penn State transfer Jaxon Smolik and Ajani Sheppard throwing 16 passes combined. If Temple wants any chance, it’ll have to throw the ball more with whatever quarterback is in, or the run game will be shut down.

For Penn State, the key to success is to keep doing what it did last week, but also allow the run game to get going more. I think Rocco Becht will utilize all the weapons he has, and it’ll be too much for Temple to handle throughout the game.

A three hour drive, or a quick flight to the eastern part of the state, while adding the likelihood of a majority Penn State crowd, will result in the Nittany Lions cruising to another blowout victory, moving to 2-0 on the season.

Andrew Mercer: Penn State 45, Temple 7

Penn State’s season opener was an overwhelming success, but the Nittany Lions still learned a lot about themselves.

Specifically, the running backs discovered that when they falter, the passing game can pick up the slack. In Week 2, I feel like the ball will start to trend the running backs’ way, as the film on Penn State will likely cause the Owls to try containing the passing game.

Koby Howard has a big target on his back after last week, so I think Temple will put a lot of effort into stopping him. But Becht has other methods of getting on the scoreboard, and I think he’ll mirror his production.

The defensive versatility that Campbell has stressed will be put to the test on Saturday, but the Nittany Lions will once again rise to the occasion.

D’Anton Lynn’s unit dominated against Marshall, and I think Penn State’s defensive ends will make a bigger impact against Temple, bypassing potentially three backup offensive linemen en route to a flurry of sacks.

On that note, Temple hasn’t quite found its No. 1 quarterback, so for an offense that isn’t set in stone, I foresee the Nittany Lions holding the Owls to one score.

Lexie Linderman: Penn State 38, Temple 10

Penn State couldn’t have had a better start to 2026, and I expect that strong play to continue in the first road game of the year for the Nittany Lions.

Temple has some talent, but it’s hard to defeat a top-25 team without three of your starting offensive linemen. The Owls’ left tackle is out for six weeks, while their left guard and right tackle are game-time decisions.

If all three are out, it could have a serious impact on Temple’s rushing attack that shined in Week 1, as running back Keveun Mason had 158 yards and two touchdowns in a win over Rhode Island.

The game will likely be decided by how the Owls’ defense holds against Penn State’s offense. The Nittany Lions came out firing against Marshall, and they’ll look to do the same against a Temple defense that had two pick sixes last week.

So it’s important for Becht to take care of the ball Saturday, and it’s also crucial Penn State’s rushing attack gets things going, as the passing game will surely get more attention from Temple after its strong showing in Week 1.

I think it’ll be the tight ends that have the biggest impact this week as a result of the receivers being the focus for the Owls’ secondary, and the Nittany Lions will cruise to victory with depth pieces getting some more burn.

Noah Aberegg: Penn State 42, Temple 13

The Nittany Lions outperformed the betting odds nearly twofold against Marshall, winning 45-0 when the line was set at 23.5 points.

This week, the odds are the same, but I think Temple will stay truer to the prediction than the Thundering Herd. The Owls are coming off a dominant win against Rhode Island, but several bumps will keep Penn State firmly in the lead.

On Monday, Temple head coach K.C. Keeler said the starting quarterback battle is still up in the air. Both Sheppard and Smolik played last week, but three of the Owls’ starting offensive linemen are dealing with injuries, which complicate things for the quarterbacks.

Meanwhile, Penn State looked nearly unstoppable in Week 1 and will have two more key players back against the Owls in Gabe Burkle and Alex Tatsch, as confirmed by Campbell on Tuesday.

I’d expect the passing game to have another standout performance with Becht recording another 250-yard outing while Howard tallies over 100 receiving yards with another touchdown. The run game should be improved after a week of film study, but will still be far behind the success of the offensive air strike.

Defensively, the Nittany Lions will have more of a challenge, but will still hold the Owls for just one touchdown and a pair of field goals.

title: No.12  Penn State plays No. 4 Stanford, Ohio in pair of weekend matches celebrate The Palestra’s 100th Anniversary
author: Ashley Felsberg I The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State arrives for its match against Stanford, coming off a sweep against DePaul on Monday. After traveling to Philadelphia to play Stanford on Friday night, Penn State will host Ohio at Rec Hall on Saturday. The Stanford match is a part of the celebration of the 100th Anniversary of the Palestra.

After Monday’s match, Penn State has improved to 4-1 on the season and is currently ranked at No. 12. Graduate student Whitney Launstein and senior Kennedy Martin have combined for an effective offense so far this year, which continued into this week.

Against DePaul, Lauenstein hit .333 and contributed a match-high 16 kills. The graduate student also contributed 13 kills in the Nittany Lions’ prior match against Kentucky at Wrigley Field. The accomplished outside hitter now sits second on the blue and white in kills, with 59, trailing Martin by two.

Martin is another Nittany Lion who’ll pose a threat to both Stanford and Ohio on the front line. Martin nearly tied Lauenstein in kills on Monday, putting up 15. The right-side hitter also came up big on the defensive, putting up three blocks and six digs on Monday.

Stanford is currently ranked No. 4, coming off of a 3-1 win against Marquette Sunday, and a 3-1 loss against Texas A&M on Friday which was the Cardinal’s first loss of the season.

In the match against Marquette, sophomore Logan Parks recorded her season-best assist total of 49. The six-foot setter was named to the AVCA Player to Watch List ahead of the 2026 season and was named AVCA Pacific Region Freshman of the Year in her debut season.

While Parks is a threat, she is supported by a consistent offense. Cardinals players Lizzy Andrew, Ipar Kurt, Jordyn Harvey and Julia Blyashov each record double-digit kills to ensure Stanford’s Sunday victory.

Penn State struggled defensively against Kentucky’s Brooklyn DeLeye, as she put up 21 kills, signaling a similar issue the blue and white could face against Stanford’s star power, as the all-around strong kill game from the Cardinals could outmatch one of Penn State’s weaknesses.

The Nittany Lions last saw Stanford on Sept. 9, 2022, which was a competitive match and lasted five sets, with Penn State winning.

Stanford finished last season 29-5 and has the core of the team returning, as opposed to Penn State, which is largely reshaping.

Ohio is currently 4-2 on the season, coming off a sweep loss against Butler on Saturday. Prior to that match, Ohio had swept Bucknell, Niagara and Marshall in the Marshall Invitational to open up its season. The first loss for the Bobcats came on a sweep against IU Indy, who sits at .500 on the season.

Sophomore Bailey Blair and junior Emily Waddel were both named to the 2026 Preseason All-MAC team ahead of the season. Blair had a successful opening year in the 2024-2025 season, totaling 360 kills.

While Ohio struggled to put up points in the second and third sets against Butler, losing by 15 points in the final set, Blair and senior Torre Kildow contributed a joint total of 11 kills.

The last time the Nittany Lions battled the Bobcats was back in 2017, when the blue and white escaped with a sweep victory at the Penn State Classic.

While this history sways favors towards Penn State, it’s been nearly a decade since the two squads have seen each other, yet so far this season, the offensive scale seems to tilt in the Nittany Lions’ favor.

title: 'A wonderful sign of hope' | UHS, CAPS, Jana Marie Foundation unveil Stomper statue
author: Annabella Chaklos | The Daily Collegian
description:
University Health Services, Counseling and Psychological Services and the Jana Marie Foundation unveiled the Stomper statue in the Student Health Center lobby on Wednesday.

The statue is a colorful 6-foot figure made mostly of recycled sneakers named “HAVEN,” an acronym meaning “healing and validating emotional needs.” The finished product of a year-long collaboration was presented by UHS and CAPS staff and members of the Jana Marie Foundation, who gave a series of speeches.

Introductory remarks were given by CAPS senior director Natalie Hernandez DePalma and UHS senior director Rebecca Simcik, who expressed their shared wish that the Stomper would serve as a symbol of hope, not just for students seeking services, but for the staff providing them.

“Many of us know how hard the work is every day through every student or patient encounter, no matter what that might look like,” Simcik said. “We know with every year that goes by, the needs increase and the complexities increase, and yet the isolation and the distress for many of our folks is real.”

“I think that this is a wonderful sign of hope and thoughts of moving forward to a better era of wellness for students and also kind of our colleagues here within both units,” Simcik said.

Simcik and DePalma then introduced Jennifer Brauser, who they said “this would not have ever happened without the sort of wit of.”

Brauser, a UHS pharmacist, revealed the name of the statue and explained that although the project is for raising mental health awareness, it began with something more personal: the loss of her sister, Donn, to suicide nearly five years ago.

Brauser confided in the founder of the Jana Marie Foundation in State College, Marisa Vicere. When Brauser learned about the Stomper Project, she knew she wanted to share it with the Penn State community.

“I may have conceived the thought of a Stomper here at UHS, but it has taken a community to create ‘HAVEN,’” Brauser said.

Brauser described the multiple workshops held to create the statue, where students, faculty and community members were taught about mental health stigma, followed by a session where they painted each of the 200 pieces of sneakers that make up “HAVEN.” At the base of the statue are a pair of yellow converse that every Stomper wears in memory of Jana Marie Vicere.

“I hope that they feel free to take a look, and close up, and realize that it is a representation of a place where they can feel safe, secure, and that no one has to walk through mental health issues by themselves,” Brauser said. “That they should be a person that can be someone that others can talk to, and that they can talk to others.”

Marisa Vicere followed Brauser’s speech, detailing how she founded the Jana Marie Foundation 14 years ago after her sister took her own life, and all of the collaborative work that’s gone into the statue since the summer of 2025.

Vicere explained art installations like “HAVEN” are an impactful way to raise awareness because creative expression is a powerful vehicle to start conversation.

“Just its presence within the building space sparks curiosity,” Vicere said. “‘What is this? I wanna learn more.’ And in that learning more, they can learn about how we can reach out for help or other ways that we can be there and show up for somebody who might be going through a challenging time.”

After the speeches ended, the attendees were encouraged to view the statue up close and read the placard next to it, explaining the history and making of “HAVEN.” Brauer said she’s most proud of the artwork as a way to honor her late sister.

“I can’t change her story,” Brauser said, glancing at the orange laces stitched onto the statue’s side. “I can’t change what happened five years ago, but I can choose what I do with that experience moving forward. I can talk about her, I can keep her memory alive, and I can try to use what I’ve learned to help create more awareness, and hopefully, more hope for other people.”

title: Penn State RBs focusing on improvements after subpar showing in Week 1
author: Noah Aberegg | The Daily Collegian
description:
In the days leading up to Penn State’s matchup against Marshall, Taylor Mouser said the Nittany Lions would play all four experienced running backs in the season opener.

Those running backs recorded just 159 yards on 40 carries, averaging less than four yards per run. While there was a lot of confidence around starter Carson Hansen and No. 2 running back James Peoples — transfers from Iowa State and Ohio State — the pair's performance was somewhat underwhelming.

Despite the lack of explosive plays, Matt Campbell isn’t worried about his running backs’ production.

“I thought those running backs played really good last week,” Campbell said Wednesday. “I’m not too concerned about where those guys are.”

Hansen recorded 48 yards on the ground, playing a majority of the first quarter snaps. He said the biggest struggle in the run game was the loaded box that Marshall presented, although it provided strong, positive competition.

“You’re a competitive guy, and whatever they bring at you, you got to be prepared for it and that’s the mindset going into it,” Hansen said. “If they pack the box, that is what it is, and we got to go run through it.”

Campbell said Tuesday he felt there were times Penn State “fell off blocks,” which added to the struggles already presented by the loaded box. He followed up Wednesday, saying he isn’t too worried about the rushing attack in the future.

The four running backs themselves, however, have committed to fixing the little things for a more explosive game this week.

“There’s definitely a lot more room for improvement from that game,” Hansen said. “Just going back to the film, there’s a lot of things I can take from it and move forward.”

Among the areas to improve were reading and reacting to the defense, as well as being decisive in his actions. Campbell said they “practiced the right way and really have prepared the right way.”

Against the Thundering Herd, the passing game was the primary focus of the offense, recording the majority of the total yardage. However, those plays and tendencies could change any week.

“The reality is the ball, there’s only one of them and this is a great team sport,” Campbell said. “I think everybody knows that their time’s coming to be the difference maker per se in the game. I think all those guys were really excited about where we were by the end of the football game.”

As the team has turned its focus to Week 2 against Temple, the running backs have seen similar tendencies from Marshall, including a stacked box in the run game. However, Hansen feels there’s much more room to grow from Penn State’s performance against Marshall.

“We got to find those little things that are going to make this offense explode,” Hansen said. “That’s exciting because we have the potential to do that, and I’m excited for this next Saturday.”

title: ‘Earned the right to play’ | Penn State CB Josiah Zayas turning heads after 1st career start
author: Andrew Deal | The Daily Collegian
description:
The biggest surprise in Penn State’s starting lineup against Marshall came when Josiah Zayas’ name was announced on the videoboard in the place where many expected Zion Tracy’s to be.

While it was a shock to many, the Nittany Lions’ coaching staff and Zayas’ teammates knew it was coming after his hard work since arriving on campus. It helped that Zayas shined in his debut with two tackles for loss and a quarterback hurry.

“He did that since he got here and throughout fall camp, throughout spring ball,” safety Jamison Patton said Wednesday. “When you turn that tape on, he was constantly making plays.”

Zayas had to deal with multiple things in his debut. Not only was he starting in his first collegiate game, but he’s never experienced a crowd like he did in Penn State’s 45-0 win over Marshall.

But he didn’t let that get to him, doing “a great job” on the field. Matt Campbell noticed that “he certainly didn’t look or feel like” a freshman.

The former 4-star recruit rose up the depth chart in the middle of fall camp, which is when he started to really figure everything out. Defensive coordinator D’Anton Lynn noticed the light bulb went on for Zayas, and the freshman hasn’t looked back.

“I would say about halfway during camp, you just saw him thinking less, playing quicker, talking a lot more out there,” Lynn said Tuesday. “And the biggest thing is moving on from bad plays, not letting the play before affect the next play, and then he just got better and better every day in camp, and he felt like he earned the right to play.”

Zayas’ performance in Saturday’s win caught the eye of his coaches and his teammates, proving once again that the moment wasn’t too big for the true freshman.

He fit right in with the rest of the defense, a unit that’s filled with many veteran players, and his teammates noticed the way he carried himself.

“I don't know if you can say enough about what he did defensively Saturday for a true freshman,” Campbell said.

Zayas’ preparation throughout the week led to his chance to play on Saturday, and proved he’s going to be a name to watch this season, but also in future years in Lynn’s defense that “tries to put all of us in position to succeed.”

“He played like a player on our defense,” safety Marcus Neal Jr. said. “We put him out. Everybody got trust in (Josiah) to make plays. I say he plays like he's a very mature player, very smart player. You probably don't even know he's a freshman when he's out there.”

title: Penn State notebook | Matt Campbell discusses LB Alex Tatsch, road trip logistics
author: Andrew Mercer | The Daily Collegian
description:
Matt Campbell took to the podium in the Lasch Building on Wednesday ahead of Penn State’s road debut against Temple.

He discussed Alex Tatsch’s availability, gave insight into what this week’s preparation will look like and an assessment of the running back room after the season-opener.

Here’s what Campbell had to say.

Alex Tatsch

Campbell confirmed that Tatsch will play against Temple on Saturday, adding more options to Penn State’s linebacker room alongside Tony Rojas and Kooper Ebel. Tatsch was dealing with an undisclosed injury sustained before the Pinstripe Bowl that kept him sidelined this offseason.

Campbell took the time to praise how Tatsch can fill a lot of different roles at linebacker, having the ability to comfortably play at MIKE, SAM and WILL.

“He can run, he's dynamic,” Campbell said. “He's a great blitzer, and just a guy that I think can have a lot of multiplicity in what he does.”

Tatsch’s “multiplicity” was a topic of conversation Wednesday, and Campbell said the sophomore’s physical traits have been impressive. Additionally, he said Tatsch reminds him of Rojas in the way that he’s able to play “sideline-to-sideline.”

“We’re really excited to get him back,” Campbell said.

Road trip details

Ahead of Penn State’s first road trip of the season, Campbell spoke about some of the logistics that go into the week leading up to kick off.

Campbell said that there aren’t many changes to the weekly schedule, with the team having off days Monday and Friday. On Friday, Campbell said the Nittany Lions might go through a “light walkthrough.”

As for the team’s method of travel, Campbell expressed his curiosity in what Joe Paterno liked to do, which was drive down to the game and later fly back to State College.

He also said there aren’t any restrictions on how many players he could bring to Philadelphia, but that he isn’t going to dress everyone regardless. He said that everyone must “earn the right to dress.”

“There is a lot of depth, and it doesn't matter who you are,” Campbell said. “You’ve got to come to practice every day and earn the right to start. You’ve got to earn the right to play in the game on Saturday. That's the thing that probably we're excited about.”

Spreading the wealth

Despite the running back room’s underwhelming performance against Marshall, Campbell isn’t too concerned.

He noted that the room didn’t seem frustrated, stressing the importance of getting all four of them north of eight carries against Marshall while also being able to spread the wealth to the wide receivers and tight ends.

“I thought those running backs played really good last week,” Campbell said. “I'm not too concerned about where those guys are.”

Campbell’s offensive philosophy this season has revolved around getting as many players to touch the ball as possible.

“When you’ve got a lot of guys that deserve to get the ball, the tight ends, the wide receivers, the running backs, I go back to globally — we're going to try to do everything in our power to take what the defense gives us,” Campbell said.

No matter what the game plan is, Campbell said that his main concern is making sure everyone is ready for when their time comes to make an impact. As for the running backs, he said they’ve “practiced the right way.”

title: Series history | Penn State dominant all-time against Temple
author: Noah Aberegg | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State is set to travel to Philadelphia to face Temple on Saturday for the first away game under Matt Campbell.

The two programs have faced off many times since their first matchup in 1931 in a series dominated by the Nittany Lions. Still, the contests have featured many memorable moments.

Here’s a look at the history between Penn State and Temple, with the Nittany Lions holding a 40-4-1 advantage.

Early Temple success

Temple earned three of its four victories in matchup history, taking the series opener on Oct. 10, 1931, with a 12-0 win. Hank Reese recorded an 80-yard touchdown for the first score, while the second touchdown came as the result of a fullback run.

The following year marked another victory for Temple, but Penn State was able to right the ship in 1940. The Nittany Lions marched into Philadelphia and shut out Temple, earning their first victory in the series with an 18-0 win.

However, the Owls came back the next year and reclaimed their home turf, shutting out Penn State 14-0 to take a 3-1 lead on the series.

Penn State dominance

After Temple’s third victory in 1941, the Nittany Lions took control of the series for the next nine years. Penn State won seven straight contests, five of which were shutouts, to take the advantage in the matchup.

The start of the Rip Engle era in 1950 saw the first and only tie between the two teams. However, the Nittany Lions took over and never looked back following that game, winning the next 31 straight contests under Engle, Joe Paterno, Tom Bradley, Bill O’Brien and ultimately James Franklin.

Temple was close to overtaking Penn State in a few of the matchups, including the 1975 and 1976 games. After a 23-year gap between meetings, the Owls started strong with a 76-yard touchdown on the first play from scrimmage in 1975, while the Nittany Lions recorded a 100-yard kickoff return for a touchdown.

Penn State later returned a punt 66 yards, setting up a touchdown and two-point conversion on the ensuing drive. The Nittany Lions gave up a safety to drain the clock, winning 26-25.

The following year, Temple found the end zone to make the score 31-30 with just seconds on the clock. The Owls went for the two-point conversion to win the game, but ultimately failed to convert.

2015 upset

The matchup in 2015 would go down as one of the worst losses in the Franklin era at Penn State. Temple routed the Nittany Lions 27-10 at Lincoln Financial Field — the most recent meeting in Philadelphia.

The Owls’ win marked their first over Penn State since 1941 despite early success from the visiting team. Kicker Joey Julius split the uprights on the Nittany Lions first drive to put the first points on the board.

A 42-yard rushing touchdown by Akeel Lynch added to Penn State’s lead, but those were the last points for Penn State on the day.

Temple’s offense found its rhythm in the second quarter as Jahad Thomas marched into the end zone for his first touchdown.

After a field goal from the Owls and a rushing touchdown from quarterback Philip Walker, Thomas added another six points to the scoreboard before a late field goal sealed the deal in Philadelphia.

The most recent matchup

In 2016, Penn State held off a Temple squad that was hungry for its second straight win.

The Nittany Lions opened with a 10-7 lead courtesy of a 52-yard touchdown connection between Trace McSorley and Chris Godwin. They extended that to a 21-10 margin at halftime.

However, the Owls found the end zone twice to make it a three-point game before Saquon Barkley ran 55 yards for another Nittany Lion touchdown.

Temple made it a one-score game again with a late field goal, but threw a last-second interception to seal the deal in Happy Valley.

title: Breaking through the 'class friend' barrier to make real friends
author: Ally Sons | The Daily Collegian
description:
As new classes officially start feeling real, there's no better time to start truly getting to know your classmates than now. Whether it be the people in your assigned class groups or the people in your 300 person lecture hall that happen to sit next to you each day, the opportunity for friends is everywhere.

Even though it can feel scary to break out of your shell and connect with people in a school environment, it’s important to remember we’re all in the same boat: Everyone’s a little nervous, and everyone wants more friends.

We sit in class all day, so there’s no better place to meet new people. If you’re looking for some easy ways to break through that awkward “class friend” barrier, look no further than these five strategies.

Exchange phone numbers, social media for “studying”

By offering your contact info to someone, it creates a closer bond than just "classmates." It shows you're taking initiative to stay connected, but still in a casual and less intimidating way than asking them to hang out upfront.

You can suggest studying together or creating a study group for class, which takes the friendship outside of the classroom. Even if no study plans ever emerge, it guarantees you a person to sit next to for the rest of the semester.

This also gives you the opportunity to ask them to hang out socially. Whether in a big group to celebrate post-exam or asking them to grab food and gossip about class, it sets you up for success.

Overshare (slightly)

This is definitely something that’s easier said than done, but striking up conversation before class starts makes you seem like a social person that anyone would love to be friends with.

Some good conversation starters could be talking about upcoming quizzes or assignments, any big weekend plans or something exciting going on in your life. If you’re feeling brave, you could have a big reaction to a notification and then tell your classmate all about it.

Keep it tasteful. No one’s asking you to trauma-dump to a fresh group of faces who likely just want to get the class over with. But show that you have a personality outside of taking notes on your laptop.

Suggest new study spots

The easiest way to make the friendship feel less classroom-confined and less stuck on talking about the curriculum is venturing outside of Willard, Thomas or wherever you take notes for 50 minutes each week.

Instead of asking to study at the library or the HUB, you could instead suggest Starbucks, Dunkin’ or, if you’re really feeling bold, your apartment or dorm. If you’re already committed to studying at the library, you could always suggest coffee or food after and invite them.

This sets you up to be able to shift the conversation to something more personable and find common interests.

Identify mutual friends, interests

On that note, mutual friends and interests are the easiest way to have someone see you as more than just a person to share notes and exasperated sighs with in class. If you exchange social media accounts, then it allows you to check for mutuals or any organizations or clubs you have in common.

All you need is one, single mutual thing, and then you have a blossoming plan for hanging out in the future.

Ask them about going-out plans, invite them to yours

This one is straight to the point and definitely not for everyone, but has a very high-risk return.

Penn State has a pretty big going-out scene that many students engage with. Asking the people in your classes about their favorite night-life activities opens up the conversation to you guys going out together, which definitely secures a friendship.

People are so much more than just what they’re studying in class, and everyone's definitions of “going-out” are different, so, just like any of the suggestions on this list, this could expand your horizons too.

title: Meliza Fermin shares her story from Penn State to Emmy-winning visual arts
author: Colleen Cratty | The Daily Collegian
description:
In between her classes at Penn State, Meliza Fermin would rent out cameras and new technology to experiment with. From constant work in computer labs, filming around campus and practicing her artistic skills, she kept herself busy, learning and exploring.

On Sunday, Fermin was nominated for Outstanding Special Visual Effects In A Single Episode for her work as a digital matte painter supervisor on the television show “Paradise.” This was her third nomination with the Television Academy, and she won in 2009 for the show “Heroes.”

Fermin started her journey studying integrative arts at Penn State from 1999 to 2003, where she found she loved manipulating videos, whether it was 3D or after effects.

“I was making my own projects, basically, and that’s how I started learning about visual effects,” Fermin said. “I was in the computer lab there one day, and I realized, ‘Wow I really like doing this.’”

Fermin also mentioned that she loved watching movies, which led her to find visual effects as her career path. After graduating, Fermin reached out to Penn State alumni to get advice and learn about the complicated industry of film and television.

“I spoke to a lot of people around that time in her position, and I often recommended that they try and get an internship,” Forker, a visual effects supervisor at Netflix, said. “Having the right experience is really hard, I’d say.”

Fermin agreed that getting experience post-graduation was really difficult, a barrier that still prevails today.

“Before, everyone would move to LA and pursue their dreams there,” Fermin said. “But now, the entertainment industry is expanding and is not concentrated in LA, like it was before. Because of the switch to streaming now, there’s not a lot of money being made in movie theaters.”

Even through the difficulties in the growing industry, Fermin has found success in the visual arts field.

But she said awards aren’t what define achievement in her field. People are more interested in the actual work you’ve done.

“In this era where technology is always changing, new software is coming out. Who cares if you won an Emmy five years ago?” Fermin said.

When working on a new show, no one knows if it's going to get recognized, she said, and it's important to approach everything the same way: Work hard no matter what.

Fermin’s colleague, Evan Underwood, spoke to her dedication in the workplace.

He said most matte painters in visual arts just do the art aspect of the shots, and most commonly, separate artists or teams set it up. But Fermin’s knowledge of technology sets her apart from other visual artists. Since she’s multi-skilled, she’s a “one-stop shop,” Underwood said.

“Rarely does she miss the mark,” Underwood, a computer-graphics supervisor, said. “She’s very detail-oriented. She asks great questions upfront to make sure she fully understands the needs of the shot.”

Forker also said knowing technology and having the ability to adapt to new changes in the entertainment industry holds high importance. Professionals need to constantly be willing to adjust, learn and perfect new skills.

In recalling a specific shot on a project the two worked on, Underwood said Fermin’s artistic abilities superseded anything that could've been made using CGI.

“The real hidden skill is her technical chops,” Underwood said. “She has the artistic ability, which is one side of the brain, she’s an incredible artist and an incredible painter. But usually, you don’t get both. You don’t get somebody that is technically savvy as well.”

Fermin’s technical skill goes back to her time at Penn State, where she was able to use campus resources to experiment with cameras.

The access to campus computer labs also allowed her to play with software and technology she never could have afforded. The ability to try out and have fun with Penn State’s tools helped her grow in her profession.

“The advice I always give to current students is to focus on something,” Fermin said. “Visual effects is so general. And everyone always says, ‘I wanna work in visual effects, I wanna work in film.’ I’m like, ‘But what? What area?’”

Even through her whole career journey, she said her biggest achievement is simply her art skills.

“You can’t just learn a software and be an artist,” Fermin said. “You actually have to know composition, color values, all those basics — and you can’t ignore that.”

description:
The 2027 Nittany Lions’ season is set to begin early play in Nassau, Bahamas, for a second consecutive year, gracing Andre Rodgers National Stadium as part of the returning Atlantis Collegiate Baseball Series.

Penn State is one of four programs selected for participation in the international series, joined by Auburn, NC State and Michigan. The blue and white are set to play a three-game series against the Tigers, marking the first time the two programs have met in their history.

Auburn finished with a 42-22 record, an SEC tournament semifinals berth, and an NCAA Tournament Super Regional run, while Penn State missed the Big Ten Tournament for the first time under coach Mike Gambino.

The blue and white participated in the inaugural Atlantis Collegiate Baseball Series last season, dropping two contests to Indiana State and winning the finale on a walk-off.

The matchup with Auburn is slated for Feb. 19-21 before the Nittany Lions take to another landmark event, the Amegy Bank Series, at Globe Life Field, home of the Texas Rangers in Arlington in early March.

title: Jerry Sandusky withdraws recantation claim, seeks federal appeal
author: Grace Levy | News Editor
description:
Jerry Sandusky appeared remotely at the Centre County Courthouse on Tuesday morning, withdrawing the recantation claim of one of the men who alleged Sandusky assaulted him when he was young.

Presiding Special Judge Maureen A. Skerda, of Warren County, questioned Sandusky to confirm that he was informed of his rights when withdrawing the claim, which was made on his behalf by his attorney Jerry Russo.

State prosecutors also questioned Sandusky, and confirmed that he understood that he would not be able to try the claim again in state or federal court.

In a court document, Skerda dismissed the Post-Conviction Relief Act (PCRA) petition filed by Sandusky in Sept. 2025. The order says that Sandusky has 30 days to appeal.

The hearing occurred despite a request from Russo to have Sandusky’s evidentiary hearing cancelled. The hearing was expected to include the recantation testimony of one of Sandusky’s alleged victims, known in court documents as “Victim Number 10.”

In an affidavit filed in June 2025, the individual recanted his testimony against Sandusky, saying that he was told by prosecutors that his testimony was “critical to stopping a predator” despite lacking “clear or certain memory of any such conduct.” He said that his “statements were not willfully false, but induced under extreme psychological and institutional pressure.”

According to an initial report from ESPN, Sandusky plans on seeking federal relief.

“There is a pending federal appeal that has been stayed pending this litigation,” Russo said to reporters following the hearing. “We will be supplementing that extensively.”

Attorney General Dave Sunday shared a press release Tuesday afternoon, saying that Sandusky’s latest attempt to have his conviction overturned “failed.”

“This was yet another attempt by a convicted child predator to avoid accountability and escape punishment for years of abuse he perpetrated under the veil of a child-empowerment program,” Sunday said. “I commend our litigation team for challenging this alleged recantation by one victim, and putting on record that we had available voluminous evidence that debunks this highly-suspect claim by defense counsel.”

The former Penn State assistant football coach was convicted in 2012 of sexually abusing young boys. He was originally sentenced to 30 to 60 years in prison. He is currently held at Laurel Highlands state correctional institute in southeastern Pennsylvania.

title: ‘I learned everything through my OGs’ | Penn State DL Siale Taupaki using his platform to help his family
author: Andrew Deal | The Daily Collegian
description:
When Matt Campbell first contacted defensive lineman Siale Taupaki out of the transfer portal, his first question wasn’t about him or his play on the field.

Instead, Campbell asked Taupaki about his family and more importantly, his parents, which sold Taupaki right away to make the trek to central Pennsylvania despite his familiarity with the West Coast.

“I knew I could come to him about anything because he's a father before he was a coach.” Taupaki said Tuesday.

Taupaki, who transferred from UCLA to Penn State this offseason, comes from a large family, and his journey to college football isn’t like most, especially in the NIL era. He grew up “broke,” and said there was one point when he had 22 family members living in a two-bedroom house.

“Some of us had to sleep outside,” Taupaki said. “My parents, they (are) older than most of you guys. When people talk about OGs, like I got OGs. I got to learn a lot of stuff from them. Everybody learned everything through IG. I learned everything through my OGs. So that's how it is.”

The California native has had a lengthy collegiate career as this year marks his eighth. He started playing before every athlete was making money through NIL, which began in 2021. But he’s not one to spend what he’s earned as of late on big, flashy items and is looking out for his family instead.

“I'm really just trying to fill in all the holes that I have back at home, understanding the platform that I'm having, and just seeing all of that stuff and understanding how far I came,” Taupaki said. “I really try to take full advantage and opportunity that I can. I come from nothing.”

Taupaki recognizes the journey he’s taken to get to where he is today, and his family got to watch him play for Penn State in Beaver Stadium for the first time on Saturday.

Postgame, Taupaki called his father, who was able to watch the game with his mother because Taupaki paid for their internet.

“My pops told me that he had the chills just hearing about it, because he can visualize in the game,” Taupaki said. “We don't watch a lot of TV back at home.”

Taupaki and his family are still figuring out whether they can come to a game this season, as he said they’re too old to fly. He’s expecting some of his cousins to make the trip to Happy Valley at some point, though.

Regardless, Taupaki’s mind is on his family. He said when he returns home, he goes from being a football player to just being a son, and he’s going to continue using his platform to help them.

“The opportunity I got with the NIL era and the great coaching staff and all that, I'm thankful for that,” Taupaki said. “But at the end of the day, I still got stuff to do as a son. So to play my role as that, I'm forever grateful.”

title: Penn State notebook | Matt Campbell shares injury updates, why run game struggled
author: Noah Aberegg | The Daily Collegian
description:
With Week 1 in the books, Penn State has its eyes set for this weekend’s matchup against Temple.

Matt Campbell took the podium in Beaver Stadium on Tuesday to discuss notable injury updates, playing at Lincoln Financial Field in Philadelphia and more.

Here’s a look at what Campbell said.

Injury updates

Three of Penn State’s bigger depth pieces didn't suit up on Saturday in defensive tackles Armstrong Nnodim and Alijah Carnell alongside offensive lineman Owen Aliciene.

All three were praised throughout the summer. Aliciene was fighting for a starting role at left tackle, while Nnodim was considered one of the defensive line’s key pieces.

Luckily for the Nittany Lions, none of the players are dealing with significant injuries, as Campbell said they are all questionable against Temple and practiced today.

“We would love to have those guys back ready to go for us this week,” Campbell said.

Two players who had been dealing with long-term injuries, Gabe Burkle and Alex Tatsch, were doubtful heading into Marshall and didn’t see the field.

“Both guys I thought were really close to playing and just didn’t feel like it was the right decision to do that,” Campbell said. “They needed more contact collision in practice, but both guys will certainly be available this week.”

Another injury that was speculated earlier in the week, with LaVar Arrington discussing his son’s unavailability on Fox Sports Radio, was confirmed to be a longer-term injury. Campbell said LaVar Arrington II had a cleanup surgery in his knee and will likely be out for four to six weeks.

Run game struggles

Campbell had talked throughout the summer and fall camp about having four running backs they could comfortably play. On Saturday, they struggled, averaging just 3.6 yards per carry as a team.

“I feel like we felt we were going to get loaded boxes early in the game,” Campbell said. “I felt like that was something that opened up the passing game, and we felt like that was going to have to happen early in the football game to kind of get us going.”

While the running backs didn’t produce, Campbell didn’t put the blame on them. Instead, he focused on the offense as a whole, discussing the blocking struggles in the run game from the entire unit.

“That’s certainly not to say we can’t be cleaner or need to be cleaner in the run game,” Campbell said. “I thought there were times we fell off blocks.”

The Nittany Lions were able to rely on the passing game in the shutout win with 324 yards in the air. However, Campbell didn’t shy away from knowing the run game needs to improve, saying “consistency there is going to be a huge improvement for us as we continue to move forward.”

Complementary football

Penn State’s victory over Marshall was full of big plays. Koby Howard recorded several big plays with 76 yards after catch and Rocco Becht dished the ball for 271 passing yards.

However, Campbell’s favorite moment from the game came from a pair of special teams and defensive plays.

After Nathan Tiyce pinned Marshall at the one yard line, the defense allowed six rushing yards from the Thundering Herd before freshman Bryson Williams recorded the game’s only interception.

“I think those things are what great football teams have the ability to do,” Campbell said. “The ability to play good complementary football throughout the game I thought was really huge for us.”

That production was on display throughout much of the game, as Penn State’s defense forced multiple three-and-outs followed by the offense finding the end zone.

Playing at Lincoln Financial Field

Ahead of Penn State’s matchup against Temple at Lincoln Financial Field, Campbell talked to his former college roommate Nick Sirianni on Monday about playing in the Eagles’ home stadium.

Sirianni has been the Eagles head coach since 2021, leading them to a Super Bowl win and numerous signature wins in the Linc.

“Nick has been a great sounding board,” Campbell said. “We’ve gone through some of the same journeys as head football coaches, good moments and tough moments.”

Campbell discussed with the media how “It’s a great opportunity when you get to bring a football team to play in a professional stadium.”

“You're already kind of behind schedule playing a noon game, let alone on top of that having to get yourself ready for your first road trip as a team and as a program,” Campbell said. “I think this is going to be huge for us. And great teams play great on the road. That's just how it goes.”

title: Penn State notebook | DC D'Anton Lynn praises Josiah Zayas, discusses defensive complexity
author: Andrew Mercer | The Daily Collegian
description:
Ahead of Penn State’s first road trip of the season, defensive coordinator D’Anton Lynn took to the podium on Tuesday at Beaver Stadium for his biweekly press conference.

Lynn discussed the decision to start Josiah Zayas at cornerback, how he’s planning to add complexity to the defensive scheme and gave a short scouting report on Temple for Saturday’s contest.

Here’s more of what Lynn said on Tuesday.

Josiah Zayas and Zion Tracy

One of the biggest surprises among the starting lineup on Saturday was Zayas, a true freshman who was previously expected to fill a rotational role at cornerback while Zion Tracy started in the slot.

However, for Lynn, Zayas was a standout performer in the spring and earned the starting role due to his mental strength.

Lynn noted that one of Zayas’ biggest strengths is how he handles mistakes, development that happened around the midway point of the offseason and continuously improved over time.

“You just saw him, thinking less, playing quicker, talking a lot more out there,” Lynn said on Tuesday. “The biggest thing is like moving on from bad plays, not letting the play before affect the next play, and he felt like he earned the right to play.”

Going forward, Lynn said that he’s going to continue building Zayas up, giving him more reps in the slot as one of the younger impact players.

On the other hand, Tracy will be a player that bounces around different positions, as “the most versatile defensive back” on the team. Lynn said Tracy has the ability to play both nickel and safety.

“There's going to be times where Zion's going to be at cornerback, there'll be games where Zion's playing safety,” Lynn said. “So he's kind of a chess piece that we can kind of move around each week.”

Adding complexity

Tony Rojas said postgame against Marshall that the defensive plays were simple, and it allowed them to freely execute. While the defense shut out the Thundering Herd, Lynn said that the team didn’t nearly dig into its bag of tricks.

“We definitely didn't do everything that we've done in camp or everything that we've done in spring,” Lynn said. “There'll be some point in the year where we're doing some things that are new for everybody.”

Lynn also said he’ll install new concepts to add more complexity into the scheme on a week-by-week basis, but that his primary concern is getting the players to understand the “core” of the defensive system before adding new layers.

So far, he’s working on adding more schemes to the safety room, which was run almost completely in a two-high formation. He noted that a couple variations of single-high formations are on the horizon.

“We like to be in a shell just because we can do a lot of different things from a disguise standpoint as far as different split safety variations, getting into post safety coverages as well,” Lynn said. “But there also will be times where it's going to be the exact opposite. You might see us single-high and staying in it, or getting in single-high and getting the split.”

Scouting Temple

Looking ahead to Penn State’s Week 2 matchup against Temple in Philadelphia, Lynn spoke about the difficulty of playing a team who considers the game one of the most important on the schedule.

Lynn himself played the Owls four times in his career with the Nittany Lions, and he saw the whole array of results, including blowouts and nail biters.

“It's the Super Bowl for Temple, so we have to have that mindset when we go in there,” Lynn said. “We know that we're going to get there best, and we just have to make sure our guys are prepared for that.”

This year, Lynn scouted Temple’s defense and said that the Owls are a team who excel in pre-snap motion and communication. He said Penn State’s first road trip will be a test of the its communication in the heat of the moment, as Temple will often try to adjust on the fly.

“They do a good job of making a defense play on their heels,” Lynn said. “We just have to try and simplify it for our guys and make sure that we can do attack mode all game.”
